Do I love God and his people? Do I love the brethren, and am I kind to all men? Have I forgiven those who wronged me? Is there a grudge I am keeping? Do I want Christ? Is there a desire for him, and for more of him? Am I obeying? Is there new obedience, even weak and uneven, that was not there before? The Ten Commandments are the best mirror for the second question. Go through them one at a time. The Ten Commandments for a Believer sets out what each one requires and forbids.

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: How to Do It Pray first. Search me, O God, and know my heart (Psalm 139:23). Ask God to show you what you would rather not see. Be specific. Name the sin, the time, and the person. Vague confession leads to vague repentance (WCF 15.5). Keep it short each day. A few minutes at night is enough. Look back over the day, confess, give thanks, and go to bed. Go deeper before the Lord’s Supper. Take longer in the days before communion. The Catechism directs communicants to prepare themselves before they come (Q&A 171). Make it right. If you wronged someone, confess it to them and repair what you can (Matthew 5:23-24). End at the cross. Every examination should end with Christ freely offered and freely received. If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1).

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: Two Cautions Do not skip it. A man who never looks at himself can live for years in a sin he would see in a minute if he looked. The Puritan John Owen warned that a man who finds no fight in himself against his sin is at peace with it, not dying to it. If You Have Made Peace With It speaks to that man. Do not drown in it. Some believers turn self-examination into an endless loop of checking whether they really meant it. If that is you, keep the searching short and the looking to Christ long. Read Am I Really Saved? and if the same thoughts keep coming whether you want them or not, read thoughts you would never choose . Tell your elders too.

title: How to Repent
text: What repentance unto life is, godly and worldly sorrow, confessing sins by name, making things right, and coming home again.

title: How to Repent
text: What Repentance Is Repentance unto life is a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 87 It is God’s gift (Acts 11:18), and it is still your own turning, which he commands of you (Mark 1:15). The answer holds five things. A true sense of sin. Not only its danger but its filthiness, because it is against God’s holy nature and law (WCF 15.2). A man who only fears hell is sorry about the danger. An apprehension of God’s mercy in Christ. Without it, a sight of sin drives a man to hiding or despair. There is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared (Psalm 130:4). Grief and hatred of sin. You grieve that you did it, and you hate the thing itself, not only what it cost you. Turning from it unto God. Away from the sin and toward him, and from all your sins, not only the one that shamed you (WCF 15.2). Full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience. You mean to obey, and you begin. The purpose is whole even when the obedience is weak. Repentance is not penance. It is no satisfaction for sin and no cause of pardon, which is the act of God’s free grace in Christ (WCF 15.3). Your tears do not wash you. Christ’s blood does (1 John 1:7). Yet none may expect pardon without repentance. Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (Luke 13:3). A man who says he trusts Christ while he means to keep his sin does not yet know whom he is trusting.

title: How to Repent
text: Two Kinds of Sorrow For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. 2 Corinthians 7:10 (KJV) Paul was glad the Corinthians sorrowed to repentance, because it made them earnest to set things right (verses 9-11). Judas and Peter both sinned against Christ on the same night. Judas repented himself, brought back the silver, and said, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood (Matthew 27:3-4). The words were true. But he took his sorrow to the priests and not to Christ, and he went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). Peter denied his Lord three times. Then the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter, and Peter went out, and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61-62). His sorrow brought him back, and Christ restored him (John 21:15-17). The difference was not how much they hurt. It was where they carried the hurt. Worldly sorrow grieves over loss and shame and turns in on itself. Godly sorrow runs to God for mercy. If you are in that darkness now, hear this carefully. Thoughts of ending your life do not prove that your repentance is false or that you are not his. Deep depression is often an illness of body and mind, and true believers have been crushed by it (read When You Are Depressed ). But any voice that tells you Christ will not have you, or that death is the way out, is lying to you about him. Christ looked at Peter to call him back, and he has not stopped looking for you. Tell someone today, and if those thoughts press on you, call 988 or text 988 .

title: How to Repent
text: Repent of Sins by Name The Confession calls every man to repent of his particular sins particularly (WCF 15.5). Saying I am a sinner costs nothing. Saying what you did costs something. David’s prayer after Bathsheba is the pattern. He begins with God’s mercy, not his record (Psalm 51:1). Then he owns the sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me. Psalm 51:3 (KJV) He had wronged Uriah terribly, yet he says, Against thee, thee only, have I sinned (verse 4), because every sin is first against God. He asks to be washed (verse 2), for a clean heart (verse 10), and for the joy of salvation to come back (verse 12). And he knows God will not despise a broken and a contrite heart (verse 17). Confess to God first, and then to those you have wronged, who are to receive you in love (WCF 15.6, Matthew 5:23-24). Where you took something, give it back. Zacchaeus said, if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold (Luke 19:8). The law asked for the thing returned and a fifth added (Numbers 5:7). If you lied about someone, tell the truth to those who heard it. Some wrongs cannot be undone, and some confessions would only wound again or put someone in danger. Ask an elder how and when.

title: How to Repent
section: Coming Home, and Coming Home Again
text: Coming Home, and Coming Home Again Christ taught us to ask for forgiveness in the same prayer as our daily bread, Forgive us our debts (Matthew 6:11-12). A believer keeps falling and keeps returning. That does not prove you never repented. It is what repentance looks like while sin remains (WCF 13.2). If the same sin keeps winning, read When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back , and for the long fight, Struggling With Sin . Mortify can help you confess daily and fight alongside brethren from your church. And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. Luke 15:20 (KJV) Jesus told the story of the prodigal son because the Pharisees murmured that he received sinners (Luke 15:1-2). It is a parable. There was no particular son in a far country. But what it pictures is real. The son came to himself and went home to say, Father, I have sinned (verses 17-18). He meant to ask to be a hired servant, but his father never let him finish. He called for the robe, the ring, and the feast, for this my son was dead, and is alive again (verses 19-24). That is how the Father receives a sinner who comes home through his Son. If You Fear You Have Repented Too Many Times Christ told his disciples that if a brother sins against them seven times in a day, and seven times turns again saying, I repent, they must forgive him (Luke 17:4). He does not ask more mercy of us than he shows. Your pardon never rested on your count. It rests on his blood, and he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him (Hebrews 7:25). A heart that has hardened itself against God does not usually lie awake afraid of losing him. So come again tonight. Do not wait until you have stopped falling.

title: How to Repent
text: Steps for Today Come to Christ first. Repentance without him is only regret. If you have never trusted him, read the gospel and come today. Name the sin. Before God, say what you did and against whom. How to Examine Yourself can help you see it. Pray Psalm 51 aloud. Then believe the promise. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Make it right this week. Go to the person you wronged. Pay back what you took. Cut off the supply. Make not provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14). Change what made the sin easy, and tell an elder or a trusted brother (James 5:16). Do it again tomorrow. A few minutes each night, looking back over the day, keeps short accounts with God.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
text: Why a forgiven Christian still keeps God’s law, how to read it, what each commandment requires and forbids, and how to use them this week.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
section: Why a Believer Keeps the Law
text: Why a Believer Keeps the Law You are not saved by keeping the commandments. Christ kept them in your place, and he bore the curse for every one you broke (Galatians 3:13). A believer is free from the law as a way to earn life. But he is not free from the law as a rule for how to live. The Confession says the moral law binds all men forever, believers included, as a rule of life that shows them the will of God and their duty (WCF 19.5-6). The law tells a forgiven man what love looks like. If ye love me, keep my commandments. John 14:15 (KJV) So you obey because you are loved, never to become loved. And when you fail, the law sends you back to Christ, which is one of the things it is for.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
text: How to Read Them The Larger Catechism gives rules for reading the commandments (Q&A 99). Four of them do most of the work. They reach the heart. The law governs thoughts and desires, not only actions. Jesus said lust is adultery in the heart and hatred is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21-28). Every command has two sides. Where a sin is forbidden, the opposite duty is commanded. Where a duty is commanded, the opposite sin is forbidden. Thou shalt not steal also means work, and give (Ephesians 4:28). One sin stands for a whole family. Murder covers anger, contempt, and reckless driving. Adultery covers lust, pornography, and immodesty. The causes and occasions are forbidden too. Whatever leads you toward the sin is part of what the command forbids.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
text: Each Commandment in Plain Words The Shorter Catechism sets out what each one requires and forbids (Q&A 45-81). This is a short version. Thou shalt have no other gods before me. Know, worship, trust, and love the true God alone. Forbidden are atheism, false gods, and anything you love or trust more than him, money and comfort and approval included. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image. Worship God only in the ways he has commanded in his Word. Forbidden are images of God and any worship men invent for themselves. This is where the Reformed regulative principle of worship comes from (WCF 21.1). See How God Wants to Be Worshiped . Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain. Use God’s names, titles, Word, and works with reverence. Forbidden are cursing, careless use of his name, false oaths, and mocking holy things. Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Set apart one whole day in seven for God, now the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day . Honour thy father and thy mother. Give honor and obedience to parents and to everyone God has set over you, in the home, the church, and the state, and care for those under you. Forbidden are contempt, rebellion, and abuse of authority. Thou shalt not kill. Preserve your own life and the lives of others. Forbidden are murder, abortion , suicide, unjust anger, hatred, and neglect of your body or anyone in your care. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Keep yourself and others chaste in heart, speech, and behavior. Forbidden are sex outside of marriage, pornography, lustful thoughts, and immodest dress or talk. Thou shalt not steal. Get and keep goods honestly and work to provide for yourself and others. Forbidden are theft, cheating, laziness, waste, and gambling away what God gave you. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. Speak the truth and guard your neighbor’s good name. Forbidden are lies, slander, gossip, and flattery. Thou shalt not covet. Be content with what God gave you and glad for your neighbor’s good. Forbidden are envy, discontent, and wanting what is his. The full text is in Exodus 20:1-17 and Deuteronomy 5:6-21.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
section: How to Use Them This Week
text: How to Use Them This Week Learn them. Memorize the ten, then the Shorter Catechism’s questions on each. Teach them to your children. Examine yourself by them. Take one commandment each evening for ten days. Ask what it requires and what it forbids, and where you stand. See How to Examine Yourself . Pray them. Turn each one into a request for help to obey and a confession where you have not. Run to Christ. No mere man since the fall is able in this life perfectly to keep the commandments of God (WSC 82). When the law shows you your sin, it is pointing you to the Savior who kept it for you. If one commandment keeps exposing the same sin, Struggling With Sin is written for that fight.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: The regulative principle in plain words. God decides how he is worshiped, what he has commanded, what that rules out, and why it matters.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: The Principle God decides how he is to be worshiped. We do not. In worship we may do what he has commanded in Scripture, and nothing else. The Reformed churches call this the regulative principle of worship. But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture. Westminster Confession of Faith 21.1 Most churches work by a different rule. They hold that whatever Scripture does not forbid may be used in worship. The Reformed rule is narrower. Whatever Scripture does not command is left out. The question is never whether something is forbidden. It is whether God asked for it.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Where Scripture Teaches It The second commandment. God forbids worshiping him by images or by any means of our own making (Exodus 20:4-6). The Larger Catechism says it forbids all devising, counselling, commanding, using, and any wise approving any religious worship not instituted by God himself (Q&A 109). Nadab and Abihu. Two priests offered strange fire before the Lord , which he commanded them not, and fire from the Lord devoured them (Leviticus 10:1-2). The text does not say what rule they broke. It says they offered what he commanded them not, that is, what he had not commanded. Add nothing, take nothing away. God told Israel to observe what he commanded, and not to add thereto, nor diminish from it (Deuteronomy 12:32). Worship that God never asked for. Through Jeremiah God condemned worship which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart (Jeremiah 7:31). Jesus on the traditions of men. In vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9). Paul on will-worship. He warned against worship men devise for themselves, however humble or devout it looks (Colossians 2:20-23).

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: What God Has Commanded The Confession lists the parts of ordinary worship, which are called its elements (WCF 21.3-5). Prayer, with thanksgiving, in the name of Christ. The reading of Scripture with godly fear. Preaching of the Word, and hearing it with understanding, faith, and reverence. Singing of psalms with grace in the heart. The sacraments, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, rightly given and worthily received. On special occasions the Confession adds religious oaths, vows, solemn fastings, and thanksgivings. Giving to the Lord and the benediction belong to the service as well (1 Corinthians 16:1-2, Numbers 6:24-26, 2 Corinthians 13:14).

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Elements and Circumstances The principle does not mean Scripture must tell you what time to meet, how long the sermon runs, or whether to sit in pews. Those are circumstances, things common to any gathering of people. The Confession says they are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word (WCF 1.6). The test is simple. An element is a thing done as worship, and it needs a command. A circumstance is only how and when the commanded thing is done, and it needs good sense and good order (1 Corinthians 14:40).

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: What It Means in Practice No images of God. No pictures, statues, or films of the Father, the Son, or the Spirit, in worship or out of it (WLC 109). No holy days of men’s making. God appointed the Lord’s Day. The Westminster Directory for Public Worship says no other day is commanded to be kept holy. No entertainment in place of worship. No drama, dance, light shows, or performances. Worship is not a show for the congregation. It is the congregation meeting God. The Word at the center. Reading and preaching are not a short segment between songs. They are the heart of the service. Psalms, sung without instruments. The Reformed Presbyterian churches sing only the Psalms in worship, without instruments. God gave his church a book of praise, the Psalms, and commanded it to be sung (Colossians 3:16, James 5:13). The instruments of the Old Testament were appointed for the temple and its sacrifices (2 Chronicles 29:25-28), and they passed away with them when Christ fulfilled them. The New Testament church is told to sing, making melody in your heart to the Lord (Ephesians 5:19). That last point is where Presbyterians who hold the same principle part ways. Many sing hymns and use instruments, and they are brothers. This site holds what the Reformed Presbyterian churches hold, and it holds it as a conviction from Scripture, not as a matter of taste.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Why It Matters It honors God. He is the one being worshiped. He has the right to say how. It frees your conscience. God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF 20.2). No pastor or church can bind you to worship God in a way he never asked for. It keeps the church from drifting. Once worship is open to anything not forbidden, there is no line, and each generation adds what the last one would not have dreamed of. It keeps Christ central. The things God commanded, the Word, the sacraments, and prayer, are the means by which Christ gives his grace (WSC 88). Men’s additions crowd them out.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Common Objections It is legalistic. Legalism tries to earn God’s favor by works. This asks how a forgiven people should come to the God who already accepted them in Christ. Obeying his instructions for worship is not earning anything. It is love (John 14:15). The New Testament does not give a worship manual. It gives enough. It shows the apostolic church reading, preaching, praying, singing, giving, and keeping the sacraments (Acts 2:42, 1 Corinthians 11, 14, 16:1-2, 1 Timothy 4:13). Those are what Reformed worship does. God looks at the heart. He does, and he also told us what to do. Nadab and Abihu were priests offering incense to the true God. Sincerity does not make strange fire acceptable.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: What to Do Read WCF 21 with your Bible open. Check every proof text. Look at your church’s worship. For each part of the service, ask where God commanded it. Raise honest questions with your elders, kindly. Learn the Psalms. Sing them at home, in family worship , until you know many of them by heart. Come prepared on the Lord’s Day. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day .

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Why preaching matters, what God asks of a hearer, the four kinds of ground, and how to carry the Word home.

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Why Preaching Matters The Spirit of God maketh the reading, but especially the preaching of the Word, an effectual means of convincing and converting sinners, and of building them up in holiness and comfort, through faith, unto salvation. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 89 Notice the word especially. Reading the Bible at home is a great gift, but God has made the preached Word his chief means of saving sinners and growing saints. The Larger Catechism says he uses it to drive sinners out of themselves and draw them unto Christ (Q&A 155). How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:14-17). A minister lawfully called is sent. Such men are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us (2 Corinthians 5:20). When he opens the Scriptures faithfully, you are not hearing one man’s opinions but God calling you to be reconciled to him. Yet the ambassador is still a man, and he must be tested. The Bereans received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so (Acts 17:11).

title: How to Hear a Sermon
section: What God Asks of a Hearer
text: What God Asks of a Hearer The Larger Catechism sets out what God requires of hearers (Q&A 160). Attend with diligence, preparation, and prayer. Come ready, having asked God to bless what you will hear. Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear (Ecclesiastes 5:1). Examine what you hear by the Scriptures. Keep your Bible open and ask whether the sermon says what the passage says. Receive the truth with faith, love, meekness, and readiness of mind, as the Word of God. Do not sit as a critic waiting to grade the preacher. The Thessalonians received the word not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Meditate and confer of it. Think it over afterward, and talk about it with others. Hide it in your heart. Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee (Psalm 119:11). Bring forth the fruit of it in your life. A sermon is not finished when the minister sits down. It is finished when you obey it.

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Four Kinds of Hearers Jesus told of a sower whose seed fell on four kinds of ground, and then explained it himself (Luke 8:4-15). The seed is the word of God (Luke 8:11). The ground is the heart of the one who hears. Some hear, and the devil takes the word away. Some receive it with joy but have no root, and fall away in trouble. In some the cares and riches and pleasures of this life choke it. And some, in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience (Luke 8:15). The seed, the birds, the rock, and the thorns are pictures. What they picture is real. There is a real devil who wants you to forget the sermon before lunch. Real cares and pleasures crowd the Word out of real hearts in real pews. Jesus means you to ask which one you are. No heart is good ground by nature. God promised, A new heart also will I give you (Ezekiel 36:26). The Lord opened Lydia’s heart, that she attended unto the things which were spoken (Acts 16:14). If you have heard sermons for years and never come to Christ, read the gospel and come to him now. Take heed therefore how ye hear: for whosoever hath, to him shall be given; and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have. Luke 8:18 (KJV) Hearing is never neutral. The one who receives the Word is given more light. The one who lets it slide past loses even what he thought he had.

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Doers, Not Hearers Only But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed. James 1:22-25 (KJV) The glass is a mirror. James uses it to picture what God’s Word really does. It shows you your true face, your sin and your need. The forgetful hearer glances, walks off, and is the same man on Monday. The doer keeps looking and keeps obeying, and God blesses him in it. A man can love good preaching and still never do what he hears. Ask after each sermon, What did God show me in the mirror, and what will I do about it?

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: When the Sermon Seems Dull Some Sundays the minister will be tired, or the sermon plain and weak. Do not despise him for it. Look at your own heart first. Often the dullness is in the pew and not the pulpit. Did you come prepared? Did you pray? Desire the sincere milk of the word (1 Peter 2:2), and you will find less to complain of. Remember whose power it is. We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us (2 Corinthians 4:7). Look for the bread. If the text was read and Christ was set forth, there was food for your soul. Take it home. Pray for him. Paul asked the churches to pray that utterance may be given unto me (Ephesians 6:19). Keep your complaints off the table. Children who hear their parents pick apart the preacher learn to despise the Word. Dull is not the same as false. If a minister teaches against Scripture, go humbly to him or to your elders. Read How to Spot a False Teacher , and if your church has no faithful preaching at all, read How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Steps for This Week Prepare on Saturday night. Get to bed in time. Set aside quarrels and grudges, laying aside all malice (1 Peter 2:1). If you know the text, read it. Pray for the minister and for all who will hear. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day . Listen in the pew with your Bible open. Follow the text. When your mind wanders, bring it back without fuss. Bring the children in with you. God told Israel to gather men, and women, and children, that they may hear, and that they may learn (Deuteronomy 31:12). Give each child one thing to listen for, a name, a word, or a question. Do not expect perfect stillness from little ones, only that they are there and hear something. Take notes, or do not. Some listen best with a pen, and older children often do. Others find writing pulls them away from the message. Either is fine. The aim is to remember and obey. Talk it over at the Lord’s Day table. What did we learn about God? Where did the sermon point us to Christ? What does God call us to do this week? Let the children answer first. They that feared the Lord spake often one to another (Malachi 3:16). See With Children and How to Lead Family Worship . Pick one thing to do. Name one duty, one sin to fight, or one promise to hold, and come back to it at family worship during the week.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: What the Supper is, what it means to examine yourself, whether a doubting believer may come, and what to do before, at, and after the table.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: What the Supper Is The Lord’s Supper is a sacrament, wherein, by giving and receiving bread and wine, according to Christ’s appointment, his death is showed forth; and the worthy receivers are, not after a corporal and carnal manner, but by faith, made partakers of his body and blood, with all his benefits, to their spiritual nourishment, and growth in grace. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 96 On the night he was betrayed, Jesus gave bread and the cup to his disciples and told his church to keep doing it until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:23-26). It is his meal, not ours. It is not a bare memorial, as if we only thought about a death long ago. The bread and wine stay truly bread and wine, and Christ’s body is not in them or under them (WCF 29.5, 29.7). But he is present spiritually to the faith of the believer, as really as the bread is present to your hand and mouth, and the believer truly feeds on Christ crucified and all the benefits of his death (WCF 29.7). Nor is it a fresh sacrifice. Christ offered himself once for all on the cross, and the Supper remembers that one offering (WCF 29.2, Hebrews 10:10-14). The bread does not become his body, and the Confession calls that teaching, transubstantiation, contrary to Scripture and to common sense (WCF 29.6). So come expecting to meet him by faith.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: Let a Man Examine Himself Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 (KJV) Paul wrote to a church that had made the Supper an ordinary meal. Some ate their fill while the poor went hungry, and some were drunk (1 Corinthians 11:20-22). Those were the particular ways Corinth sinned at the table. Paul’s warning reaches further than their case. To eat unworthily is to come irreverently in any form, carelessly, or holding to a sin you mean to keep, treating the holy things of Christ as common. It does not mean that you must be worthy in yourself before you come. No one is. The word unworthily describes the manner of coming, not the man. A believer who comes grieved over his sin and trusting Christ’s merit alone comes worthily, though he feels himself the least of all. Notice where the command ends. Not stay away, but and so let him eat. Examination is the road to the table, not around it. Even when God disciplined the Corinthians, it was a Father’s correction, so that they should not be condemned with the world (11:31-32).

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
section: If You Doubt Whether You Should Come
text: If You Doubt Whether You Should Come Many tender believers stay away because they are not sure they are in Christ. The Larger Catechism speaks to them. One who doubteth of his being in Christ, or of his due preparation to the sacrament of the Lord’s supper, may have true interest in Christ, though he be not yet assured thereof; and in God’s account hath it, if he be duly affected with the apprehension of the want of it, and unfeignedly desires to be found in Christ, and to depart from iniquity: in which case (because promises are made, and this sacrament is appointed, for the relief even of weak and doubting Christians) he is to bewail his unbelief, and labor to have his doubts resolved; and, so doing, he may and ought to come to the Lord’s supper, that he may be further strengthened. Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 172 If you grieve that you do not feel sure, and truly want to be found in Christ and done with your sin, God counts you as having what you fear you lack. The Supper was made for weak believers too. Bring your doubts to God, ask your elders for help with them, and come, so that you may be strengthened. Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out (John 6:37). If your doubts run deep, read Am I Really Saved?

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: Who Should Not Come The table is not open to everyone. Those who are ignorant or scandalous, even if they profess the faith and want to come, may and ought to be kept from it by the power Christ left in his church, until they are taught and show that they have turned (WLC 173). The scandalous are those who live in open sin and will not leave it. Wicked men may eat the bread, but they do not receive Christ, and they eat to their own harm (WCF 29.8). That is why Reformed churches guard the table through their elders. Before the Supper the minister usually fences the table. He warns the impenitent not to come, and he invites every sinner who mourns his sin and trusts Christ to come gladly. That is care, not coldness. If you are visiting a church, speak to the elders beforehand. If you trust Christ but have never professed your faith before a church, talk to the elders about joining. And if you have never come to Christ at all, the first thing is not the table but the Savior. Read the gospel and come to him.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: How to Prepare The Week Before Prepare by examining yourself, by renewing the exercise of your graces, and by serious meditation and fervent prayer (WLC 171). Examine yourself. Ask whether you are in Christ, what your sins and needs are, and how you are growing in knowledge, faith, repentance, love, and new obedience. How to Examine Yourself gives questions drawn from this same answer. Confess what you find. Name your sins before God, and turn from them. Make peace. Forgive those who wronged you. If someone has something against you, go to him first (Matthew 5:23-24). Stir up your faith. Read Isaiah 53 or Matthew 27, and think on what it cost him. Pray for the table. Ask God to meet you there, and pray for your minister. The Lord’s Day Morning Rise in time. Do not rush in late. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day . Pray before you leave. Ask for a hungry heart and a clear eye on Christ. Hear the sermon and the fencing as meant for you. Let the warning search you and the invitation draw you. At the Table Wait on God with holy reverence, watch the bread and wine and what is done with them, discern the Lord’s body, and meditate on his death and sufferings (WLC 174). Watch and think. The bread broken pictures his body given. The cup poured pictures his blood shed. What is pictured is real. He truly died for sinners. Mourn your sin and feed on Christ. As you eat and drink with your mouth, trust him with your heart. Receive him, rest on his merit, and rejoice in his love. Give thanks and renew your vows. Give yourself to him again, and love the brothers and sisters who eat beside you (1 Corinthians 10:17). Afterward Look back on how you came and what came of it (WLC 175). If you found comfort, bless God for it. Ask him to keep it, watch against slipping back, and keep the promises you made. If you felt nothing, do not despair. Look again at how you prepared and how you came. If you were sincere, wait for the fruit in God’s time. If you were careless, be humbled, and come next time with more care. Look forward to the next time. Come often, as the Catechism urges, and keep showing forth his death till he come (1 Corinthians 11:26).

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: Why God set apart one day in seven, how to keep it, what counts as necessity and mercy, and how to make it a delight for children.

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: Why It Matters God set apart one whole day in seven as holy to himself. From the creation to the resurrection of Christ it was the last day of the week. Since the resurrection it has been the first day, the Lord’s Day, the Christian Sabbath (WCF 21.7, Acts 20:7, Revelation 1:10). It is a gift before it is a duty. The sabbath was made for man (Mark 2:27). A day kept for God is a day of rest from ordinary work and worry, and of meeting him with his people. If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord , honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words: Isaiah 58:13 (KJV)

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: How to Keep It The Shorter Catechism says the day is kept by a holy resting all that day, even from such worldly employments and recreations as are lawful on other days, and by spending the whole time in the public and private exercises of God’s worship, except so much as is to be taken up in the works of necessity and mercy (Q&A 60). Prepare on Saturday. Finish the shopping, the yard, and the chores. Get to bed in time to be awake in worship. The Larger Catechism calls for this kind of foresight (Q&A 117). Worship with your church. Be present for the public worship your congregation appoints for the day. If it meets morning and evening, the old Reformed counsel is to be at both. Public worship is the center of the day (Hebrews 10:25, WCF 21.6). Rest from your work. Leave the job, the business email, and the errands for Monday. Rest from your entertainments too. Not because they are wrong on other days, but because this day is set apart for better things. Fill the rest of the day. Read, pray, talk about the sermon at the table, sing psalms, visit the sick, show hospitality, and rest. See How to Lead Family Worship .

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: Works of Necessity and Mercy Jesus healed on the Sabbath and defended his disciples for picking grain when they were hungry (Matthew 12:1-13). Some things must be done on any day, and some ought to be. Necessity. Feeding your family, caring for animals, essential work that cannot wait such as medicine, police, and fire. Mercy. Caring for the sick, helping someone in trouble, visiting the lonely. If your job requires Sunday work that is not a work of necessity or mercy, talk with your elders about it, and look for ways to change it. Do not decide it alone.

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: With Children Make the day a delight and not only a list of things they cannot do. Keep them in worship with you. Talk about the sermon on the way home. Save special books, walks, and meals for that day. Let them see that you love it.

title: How to Fast
text: Why Christians fast, how it joins prayer, what it is not, how to begin, and when not to fast from food.

title: How to Fast
text: When Ye Fast But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly. Matthew 6:17-18 (KJV) Jesus set fasting beside giving and prayer (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16). He said when ye fast, not if. He took it for granted that his people would. Asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered with a wedding. Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast (Matthew 9:15). The bridegroom is Christ, and his disciples are the friends at the feast. It is a picture, and what it pictures is real. While he walked with them it was a feast. Now he has been crucified, raised, and taken up into heaven, and we live in those days. Christian fasting is the ache of the bride while the Bridegroom is away.

title: How to Fast
text: Fasting Joined to Prayer In Scripture fasting goes with prayer and with humbling the soul. Ezra proclaimed a fast that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way, and God was intreated of them (Ezra 8:21-23). Nehemiah wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed (Nehemiah 1:4). Daniel sought God by prayer and supplications, with fasting, and confessed the sins of his people (Daniel 9:3-5). The church at Antioch fasted and prayed before sending out Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2-3), and elders were ordained with prayer and fasting (Acts 14:23). Therefore also now, saith the Lord , turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the Lord your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil. Joel 2:12-13 (KJV) The empty stomach serves the broken heart. Hunger reminds the body of what the soul must learn, that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). The Confession names solemn fastings, with oaths, vows, and thanksgivings, as parts of worship upon several occasions, to be used in an holy and religious manner (WCF 21.5). The Larger Catechism lists religious fasting among the duties of the second commandment (Q&A 108). Because it is worship, it is done as God directs. The Westminster Assembly gave a chapter of its Directory for Public Worship to public fasting. Scottish Presbyterians long kept a fast day in the week before the Lord’s Supper, and the Covenanters kept days of public fasting and humiliation in times of trouble. If your elders call such a day, keep it with your church.

title: How to Fast
text: What Fasting Is Not It is not a way to earn God’s favor or bend his arm. In Isaiah’s day the people complained, Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? (Isaiah 58:3). They thought hunger put God in their debt, while they drove their workers and fasted for strife and debate (58:3-4). God answered them. Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh? Isaiah 58:6-7 (KJV) A fast that leaves a man as hard toward the poor and as harsh at home as before is not the fast God chose. Nor is it a show. The Pharisee told God, I fast twice in the week (Luke 18:12), and went home unjustified. The publican had nothing to offer but God be merciful to me a sinner, and he went home justified. No fast adds anything to what Christ has done. We fast as forgiven children, not to buy forgiveness. And it is not a diet or a punishment of the body. Food is God’s good gift, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4).

title: How to Fast
text: How to Fast Fast for something. A sin you cannot master, a hard decision, a sick friend, a child gone astray, the state of the church. Alone, as a family, or with the church. Keep a private fast quietly (Matthew 6:17-18). A husband and wife may agree to fast together (1 Corinthians 7:5). Older children may join by giving up one meal. Start small. Scripture shows a fast of one day until evening (Judges 20:26), and in great danger, three days (Esther 4:16). The forty days of Moses, Elijah, and our Lord were extraordinary, not a pattern. Begin with one meal, or from one supper to the next. Keep drinking water. Give the time to God. Spend the mealtime with your Bible open, in a prayer of humbling such as Psalm 51 or Daniel 9. Confess your sins by name, then pray for what you are fasting about. When hunger comes, let it send you back to prayer. See How to Pray . Break the fast gently. Eat something light and give thanks.

title: How to Fast
section: When Not to Fast From Food
text: When Not to Fast From Food The sixth commandment requires a sober use of meat and drink to keep the life God gave you (Larger Catechism Q&A 135). If you have diabetes, are pregnant or nursing, take medication, or have any serious illness, see your doctor before you fast from food. If the answer is no, fast in another way. Give up one meal if your doctor allows it, or the phone and the news for a day, or a comfort you lean on. Hunger is not the point. Humbling yourself before God is the point, and he sees the heart. If you have lived with an eating disorder, hear this gently. Going without food can feed the very thing that has hurt you and dress it up as holiness. For you the faithful path may be not to fast from food at all, and that is no lesser obedience. Set aside an evening for prayer instead, and eat as your doctor tells you. Struggling With Sin has a short word on getting help. If you are starving or purging now, see a doctor this week. If you feel driven to hurt yourself, call 988 or text 988 .

title: How to Fast
text: Your First Fast Christ fasted forty days and would not turn stones into bread (Matthew 4:2-4). Where Adam fell over food, he stood for his people. Fasting cannot bring you to God, but he can ( the gospel ). If you are his, fast as one waiting for the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), when no one will fast again. Choose one meal this week, and write down why you are fasting. Check your health first. If a caution above is yours, ask your doctor, or fast from something other than food. Spend that mealtime with God. Read Psalm 51, confess, and pray for what you wrote down. Do a mercy. Give what the meal would have cost to someone in need (Isaiah 58:7). Break the fast gently and give thanks. Leave the answer with God, and look to Christ, the bread of life (John 6:35).

title: How to Lead Family Worship
text: Read, sing, and pray. A few minutes a day, the way Reformed households have done it for centuries.

title: How to Lead Family Worship
text: Why a Household Worships God commanded parents to teach his words to their children at home, when they sit, walk, lie down, and rise up (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). The Confession says God is to be worshiped in private families daily, as well as in secret and in public (WCF 21.6). The Church of Scotland wrote a whole Directory for Family-Worship in 1647 to help households do it. Fathers, this is your charge first (Ephesians 6:4). But a mother with children, a single believer with roommates, or a couple with no children can keep it too.

title: How to Lead Family Worship
text: What to Do It does not need to be long. Ten or fifteen minutes is enough. The old pattern has three parts. Read. A short passage, read straight through the Bible a chapter or part of a chapter at a time. Ask one or two simple questions about it. What does this teach us about God? What does it tell us to do? Sing. A psalm, or part of one. Learn a few tunes and use them often. Pray. Thank God, confess sin, and ask for the needs of the family, the church, and the world. Let older children pray too. Many households add a question or two from the Shorter Catechism, or the Catechism for Young Children with little ones.

title: How to Lead Family Worship
section: How to Start and Keep Going
text: How to Start and Keep Going Pick a time you already share. Right after supper works for many families, because everyone is already at the table. Start small. One passage, one psalm, one prayer. Do it tonight. Do not wait until you feel ready. You do not need to preach. Read, sing, and pray. Miss a night, pick it up the next. Do not give up because you broke a streak. There is no streak. Ask your elders for help. Ask them what other families in your church do. Sojourner’s family worship page walks through the reading, a psalm with its tune, a catechism question, and prayer, step by step.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: Forgiven people forgive. How to confess a wrong, go to a brother, cover an offense, and what forgiveness does not require.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: Forgiven People Forgive And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you. Ephesians 4:32 (KJV) Christ taught us to pray, Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. Then he added a warning, If ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses (Matthew 6:12, 15). He told a parable to show why (Matthew 18:21-35). A king forgave his servant ten thousand talents, a debt no servant could ever repay. That servant then took a fellow servant by the throat over an hundred pence and threw him into prison, and the king delivered him to the tormentors. It is a parable, a story told to teach, but what it pictures is real. Your debt to God is beyond counting, and God really does forgive it in Christ. A heart that will not forgive the small debts owed to it is in real danger, for Jesus ends, So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses (18:35). You do not earn God’s pardon by forgiving others. Christ alone paid for sin. But a heart that has received mercy learns to show it, and God gives the grace to do so. In the fifth petition, which is, And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors, we pray that God, for Christ’s sake, would freely pardon all our sins; which we are the rather encouraged to ask, because by his grace we are enabled from the heart to forgive others. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 105

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: When You Have Wronged Someone If you remember that thy brother hath ought against thee, Jesus says, leave your gift at the altar, first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift (Matthew 5:23-24). Name it plainly. Say what you did and call it sin. I lied to you. I spoke against you behind your back. Not “if I hurt you” or “mistakes were made.” The one who offends his brother is to declare his repentance to those that are offended (WCF 15.6). Leave off the “but.” I was wrong, but you provoked me, is not a confession. It is a second accusation. Ask, Will you forgive me? Then let them answer in their own time. Make it right where you can. Under the law a man who wronged his neighbor was to confess, repay what he took, and add unto it the fifth part thereof (Numbers 5:7). Zacchaeus promised to restore fourfold whatever he had taken by false accusation (Luke 19:8). Pay back what you took. Correct the lie you told. If you have been violent at home or made your family afraid, do not press them to forgive you or to let you come back. Read My anger frightens my family . If you broke faith in marriage, read If you are the one who broke faith .

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: When Someone Has Wronged You Most offenses should simply be covered. The discretion of a man deferreth his anger, and it is his glory to pass over a transgression (Proverbs 19:11), and charity shall cover the multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). The careless word and the small slight can be forgiven in your heart and never mentioned again. Some sins are too serious to pass over, or they keep standing between you. Then Jesus says, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone (Matthew 18:15). Go gently, to win your brother, not the argument. If he will not hear, take one or two others, and then tell it to the church (18:16-17). If he repents, forgive him, even seven times in a day (Luke 17:3-4). That pattern is for ordinary sins between believers. It is not for abuse or crime. Do not go alone to face someone who has hurt you or a child. Go to the police and to your elders.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
section: What Forgiveness Is and Is Not
text: What Forgiveness Is and Is Not To forgive is to make a promise. You will not hold the sin against them, bring it up to wound them, or pay them back. Recompense to no man evil for evil, and avenge not yourselves, Paul says. Instead, if thine enemy hunger, feed him (Romans 12:17-21). It is not first a feeling. It is a choice made before God, and you may have to make it again each time the memory comes back. Forgiveness does not mean these things. Pretending it did not happen. Joseph forgave his brothers, and still told them, ye thought evil against me (Genesis 50:20). Trusting at once. Forgiveness is given. Trust is earned back over time. Staying in danger. Never. Getting safe is not a failure to forgive. Keeping a crime from the police. God gave the ruler the sword against evildoers (Romans 13:4). Reporting a crime is not revenge. Reconciliation takes two, and it may take a long time. Paul says, If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men (Romans 12:18). Some of it does not lie in you. If the other will not repent or make peace, you have done your part when you have forgiven and kept the door open as far as it is safe.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
section: When They Never Make It Right
text: When They Never Make It Right Some who wronged you will never say they are sorry. Some have died. Reformed teachers differ on how to speak of this. Some say full forgiveness waits for repentance, for Jesus said, if he repent, forgive him (Luke 17:3). Others stress that we are to forgive whenever we stand praying (Mark 11:25). Both agree on what you must do. Put away bitterness and revenge, and give the wrong to God. Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense, saith the Lord (Hebrews 10:30). He will judge rightly. Look at Christ. While they crucified him, he prayed, Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34). He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously (1 Peter 2:23). That prayer was heard. Weeks later, in the city that crucified him, about three thousand repented and were baptized for the remission of sins (Acts 2:36-41). He died for sinners and rose again. If you have never come to him for your own pardon, start there . Then search your heart. Feeling the pain again is not the same as refusing to forgive. But if you nurse the grudge and want them to suffer, that is bitterness, and God says to put it away (Ephesians 4:31). A heart that flatly refuses to forgive is the servant in the parable, and it should be afraid. Do not despair. Bring it to Christ and ask him to make you willing.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: What to Do This Week Pray the fifth petition slowly. Ask God to forgive you, and name before him the people you need to forgive. See the Lord’s Prayer as the pattern . Go to one person you have wronged. Confess it plainly with no “but,” and make right what you can. Let one small offense go. Do not bring it up again, to them or to anyone. If a serious sin stands between you and a brother, go to him alone and gently. If it is abuse or a crime, go to the police and your elders instead. Pray for someone who wronged you. Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you (Luke 6:28).

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: Know the message, pray for people by name, tell the bad news and the good, call for repentance and faith, and bring them to church.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: Why Every Christian Tells Others Christ sent his church to every nation (Matthew 28:19-20). Preaching belongs to ministers, but every Christian can tell what he knows and invite others to hear it. People cannot call on one they have not heard of (Romans 10:14). You do not save anyone. You tell, and God gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). That takes the pressure off. It also takes away the excuse. God uses the plain words of ordinary believers.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: Know the Message You cannot give what you do not have. Be able to say the gospel in a few minutes. God. He made us, he is holy, and we owe him everything. Sin. We have all broken his law, and his judgment on sin is just and real. Christ. The Son of God became man, lived without sin, died in the place of sinners, and rose bodily on the third day. Response. Repent of your sin and trust Christ alone. Everyone who comes to him he will in no wise cast out (John 6:37). The gospel page sets this out in full. Read it until you could explain it to a friend.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: How to Do It Pray for people by name. Ask God to open their hearts and to give you an opening. Live so your words are believed. Be honest at work, keep your word, and be kind. Hypocrisy closes ears. Ask questions. What do you think happens when you die? What do you think of Jesus? Then listen. Tell the bad news and the good news. Do not skip sin and judgment. Without them the cross makes no sense. Do not stop at sin either. End with Christ. Call for a response. Tell them to repent and believe, as Jesus did (Mark 1:15). Do not pressure them into a prayer or a decision. Faith is God’s gift, not something you can manufacture. Invite them to church. Bring them to hear the Word preached, and sit with them. That is God’s ordinary way of making disciples. Give them something to read. The Gospel of John, or the gospel page .

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: When They Object Answer with meekness and fear (1 Peter 3:15). You do not have to win an argument, and you do not have to know every answer. Say you will find out, and then do. The answers to objections on this site take the common ones one at a time. Remember that the deepest objection is usually not intellectual. Men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil (John 3:19). Keep coming back to the gospel.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: What to Avoid Tricks and pressure. No false urgency, no manipulation, no promises God did not make. A gospel without repentance. Christ calls sinners to turn from sin, not only to accept a gift. A gospel of health and wealth. Christ did not promise comfort in this life. He promised himself. Silence out of fear. The fear of man bringeth a snare (Proverbs 29:25). Ask God for courage, and speak.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
text: All of it is true. What reading literally means, the kinds of writing in Scripture, how to tell a figure of speech, and Christ at the center.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
text: All of It Is True All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: 2 Timothy 3:16 (KJV) Given by inspiration means breathed out by God. The Bible does not merely contain the Word of God. It is the Word of God, and Jesus said to his Father, thy word is truth (John 17:17). We believe it, the Confession says, not because a man or a church vouches for it, but because God, who is truth itself, is its Author (WCF 1.4), and his Spirit bears witness by and with the Word in our hearts (WCF 1.5). You do not sit over the Bible as its judge. You sit under it as a child before his Father. For many of us the hard part is not believing it is true. It is knowing what each part means. This page is for that.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
text: What Reading Literally Means Taking the Bible literally means taking each part as it was meant to be taken. A psalm is a song, a law is a law, and a proverb is a proverb. The meaning of a passage is the sense its author intended, and behind every human author stands God, who meant it first. That guards against two errors. A wooden reading makes the words say what no writer meant, as if the floods must grow hands because the psalm tells them to clap (Psalm 98:8). A loose reading turns plain statements into pictures whenever they become uncomfortable. The first mistakes the form. The second refuses the content. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any scripture (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly. Westminster Confession of Faith 1.9 Scripture interprets Scripture, so a hard place is read in the light of plainer ones. And the true sense of a passage is one, not many. There is a right reading, and it is worth the work of finding. Take heart. Not everything in Scripture is equally plain. But what you must know, believe, and do to be saved is set out so clearly that an ordinary reader, using ordinary means, can understand it (WCF 1.7). A hard chapter in Daniel cannot take Christ from you.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
section: Know What Kind of Writing It Is
text: Know What Kind of Writing It Is God spoke at sundry times and in divers manners (Hebrews 1:1). Each kind of writing is read by its own rules, and every one is wholly true. History tells what happened. Luke wrote that Theophilus might know the certainty of those things (Luke 1:3-4). Law commands. Thou shalt not steal (Exodus 20:15) means what it says. Israel’s ceremonial and civil laws have ended with Christ and that nation, but the moral law still binds (WCF 19.3-5). Poetry sings in pictures. The Lord is my shepherd (Psalm 23:1) is a figure, and the care it pictures is real. Proverb tells how God has ordered life to go as a rule. A soft answer turneth away wrath (Proverbs 15:1), though not every angry man softens. See Is Proverbs 22:6 a Promise? Prophecy speaks for God, often in vivid pictures. Micah named Bethlehem as the Ruler’s birthplace centuries ahead (Micah 5:2), and there Christ was born (Matthew 2:5-6). The guide to reading prophecy says more. Parable is a story Jesus told to teach. In the sower, Jesus explains that the seed is the word of God (Luke 8:11), and that lesson is true. Letter was written to a real church about real problems. Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me (1 Corinthians 7:1). Ask what the apostle was answering, then hear it as written to you. Apocalyptic vision shows heavenly things in symbols. John hears of the Lion of the tribe of Juda, turns, and sees a Lamb as it had been slain (Revelation 5:5-6). Both pictures show one real Christ, who conquered by dying.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
section: How to Tell a Figure of Speech
text: How to Tell a Figure of Speech When you are unsure, ask these questions. Would the plain sense be absurd? Jesus said, I am the door (John 10:9). He is not wood on hinges. He is the one way into God’s fold, and that is no less true for being said in a picture. Would it contradict other Scripture? Under his wings shalt thou trust (Psalm 91:4). But God is a Spirit (John 4:24), without body or parts (WCF 2.1). So the wings are a figure, and what they picture is real, his near and sheltering care. Does the Bible explain it? Jesus said, Destroy this temple, and John tells us he spake of the temple of his body (John 2:19-21). Is it overstated on purpose? When Jesus says to pluck out the offending eye (Matthew 5:29), he is not asking you to maim yourself, since sin comes from the heart (Mark 7:21). He means, deal with sin without mercy, because hell is real. When none of these applies, take the words at their plain face. And remember that a figure always points to something real. The Lamb was truly slain. A figure makes a real thing easier to see and harder to forget. The opposite error Some readers, once they learn that the Bible uses figures, begin to treat its history as myth. That does not read the author’s sense. It overrules it, and Christ himself closes that door. He grounded marriage on what God did when he which made them at the beginning made them male and female (Matthew 19:4-5). He compared his coming to the days of Noah, when the flood came, and took them all away (Matthew 24:37-39). A pretend flood is no warning of a real judgment. He set his three days in the grave beside Jonah’s three days in the fish (Matthew 12:40), and said the men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment (Matthew 12:41). Paul sets Adam beside Christ, one real man beside another (Romans 5:12-19). If Jesus read these chapters as history, his disciples may not do less. And the God who raised his Son from the dead is not strained by a great fish.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
section: Read for Christ, and With the Church
text: Read for Christ, and With the Church On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord taught his disciples to read their Bibles. Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). Later he showed them that the law, the prophets, and the psalms were all written concerning him. Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures (Luke 24:44-45). Christ is the center of the whole Book. The Passover lamb whose bones were not broken (Exodus 12:46, John 19:36) and the servant wounded for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5) lead to him. If you finish a passage and have not seen your need of him, read it again. If you have never come to him, the gospel is where to start. Context and the church Read every verse in its paragraph and its book. Most errors start with a verse torn from its setting, the way the unlearned and unstable wrest the scriptures (2 Peter 3:16). And do not read alone. How can I, except some man should guide me? the Ethiopian asked (Acts 8:31). The Confession and Catechisms are the church’s careful summary of what Scripture teaches, and they keep you from inventing a reading no faithful Christian has held. Trusted commentaries like Matthew Henry help too. Read the text first, then the help, and bring your questions to your pastor. Where faithful teachers differ On some questions godly, confessional men have differed. The Confession says God made all things of nothing, in the space of six days, and all very good (WCF 4.1). The Reformed Presbyterian Testimony adds that Genesis 1 and 2 are history, not mythology, and that man did not evolve from any lower form of life (RP Testimony 4.1, 4.4). Most have held the days to be ordinary days, while some confessional teachers have read their length another way. Faithful men differ too on the millennium of Revelation 20 (see The Thousand Years ). On questions like these, study, hold your view honestly, and hold it humbly. The secret things belong unto the Lord our God, but those things which are revealed belong unto us (Deuteronomy 29:29).

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
text: Steps for This Week Pray before you read. Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law (Psalm 119:18). Name the kind of writing before you read each passage. Work through one hard passage. Read the whole chapter, ask the four questions above, and follow the cross references in your margin. Ask where Christ is. Write one sentence on how the passage points to him. Check yourself against the church. Read Matthew Henry on it, or find where the Confession speaks to it. Sojourner puts both beside the text. Obey what is plain. Do not let a hard verse keep you from what a clear one commands today. For a plan to read the whole Bible, see How to Read the Bible .

title: How to Read Prophecy and Revelation
text: What all Reformed believers hold about the end, how prophecy works, how to read Revelation, and the thousand years.

title: How to Read Prophecy and Revelation
text: What Every Reformed Believer Holds Christians agree on more about the end than they think. Start with what is settled. God hath appointed a day wherein he will judge the world in righteousness by Jesus Christ, to whom all power and judgment is given of the Father. Westminster Confession of Faith 33.1 Christ will come again visibly and bodily. This same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven (Acts 1:11). He cometh with clouds, and every eye shall see him (Revelation 1:7). The dead will rise together, the just and the unjust. All that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth (John 5:28-29). Then comes the judgment, and after it two endings that never end, everlasting punishment for the wicked and life eternal for the righteous (Matthew 25:46). And no one knows when. Of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only (Matthew 24:36).

title: How to Read Prophecy and Revelation
text: How Prophecy Works Much of prophecy comes in pictures. Daniel saw four great beasts come up from the sea, and he was told they are four kings (Daniel 7:3, 17). John saw Christ as a Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes (Revelation 5:6). Christ is not an animal with horns, but he really was slain, and he really reigns. The picture is a sign, and what it pictures is real. Prophecy often has a nearer and a farther fulfillment. God promised David a son who would build a house for his name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever (2 Samuel 7:13). Solomon built the temple, but he died and his kingdom split. Hebrews gives the same promise to Christ (Hebrews 1:5). The near son pointed to the far one. Above all, let the New Testament show you how the Old is fulfilled. At Pentecost Peter said, But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel (Acts 2:16). Paul says the promises were made to Abraham and his seed, which is Christ (Galatians 3:16). So when you read a prophecy, ask first how it points to him.

title: How to Read Prophecy and Revelation
text: How to Read Revelation Revelation was sent and signified by an angel to John (Revelation 1:1). That means it was shown by signs. John wrote as your brother, and companion in tribulation, exiled on Patmos for the word of God (Revelation 1:9). Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand. Revelation 1:3 (KJV) These are visions given to comfort a suffering church, and their message is plain even where the details are hard. The Lion of the tribe of Juda hath prevailed, and he is the Lamb that was slain (Revelation 5:5-6). Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life (Revelation 2:10). Read the numbers and beasts as signs. The book explains some of its own figures. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches (Revelation 1:20). Like Daniel’s beasts, its beasts picture real powers that rage against Christ. They are not riddles to solve with this year’s politicians. Read it with the rest of Scripture. Its pictures come from Daniel, Ezekiel, and Zechariah. Hard places are to be known by other places that speak more clearly (WCF 1.9). Keep the main thing main. If you finish a chapter knowing more about a beast than about the Lamb, read it again.

title: How to Read Prophecy and Revelation
text: The Thousand Years Revelation 20:1-6 tells of Satan bound that he should deceive the nations no more, and of souls who lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years. Reformed teachers who agree on everything above read this in two main ways. This page does not settle between them. Amillennialism Amillennialists read the thousand years as the present age, between Christ’s first coming and his second. The number is a sign of a long and complete time, not a count of years. Satan was bound when Christ came, so the gospel now goes to the nations. Jesus asked, How can one enter into a strong man’s house, and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man? (Matthew 12:29). The souls who reign are believers who have died and now live with Christ, waiting for the resurrection. On earth this view expects Christ to gather his people out of every nation while the age stays mixed, wheat and tares growing together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). Geerhardus Vos and Louis Berkhof taught this view. Postmillennialism Postmillennialists believe the gospel will so prevail before Christ returns that the nations largely become Christian. Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance (Psalm 2:8). Yea, all kings shall fall down before him, all nations shall serve him (Psalm 72:11). The kingdom grows from a mustard seed into a tree, and works like leaven till the whole was leavened (Matthew 13:31-33). The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord , as the waters cover the sea (Habakkuk 2:14). This comes by ordinary preaching and the Spirit’s power, and Christ returns at its close. Its teachers read the details of Revelation 20 in more than one way, but they share this hope. Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, and B. B. Warfield held it. Both views hold that Christ reigns now, and he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Both expect one return, one resurrection, and one judgment. Both pray, Thy kingdom come. They differ on how much of the earth will bow before he comes, not on whether he is King. See also The Hope for the Nations . Premillennialism Many evangelicals are premillennial. They believe Christ returns before the thousand years and reigns on earth for those years, with the righteous raised at the start and the rest at the end. The view is old, and godly men have held it. Most Reformed teachers have not, because Scripture speaks of one resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust (Acts 24:15), with judgment following straight on Christ’s coming (Matthew 25:31-32). Dispensational premillennialism goes further. It treats Israel and the church as two peoples with two plans, and it teaches a secret rapture years before Christ’s visible return. The Reformed reading finds neither in Scripture. Christ hath made both one (Ephesians 2:14). And the catching up of the saints comes with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). That is hardly secret. Many who hold these views love the Bible and long for Christ. Love them as brothers, but do not mistake their charts for the Reformed faith. How It Ends says more.

title: How to Read Prophecy and Revelation
text: Do Not Set Dates Men have named the year of Christ’s return again and again, and every one has been wrong. Of that day and hour knoweth no man (Matthew 24:36). No preacher with a chart knows it either. Beware too of newspaper exegesis, reading the Bible through this week’s headlines. It shakes believers, which Paul warned against (2 Thessalonians 2:1-2). And it pulls your eyes off Christ and onto the news. Read the news in the light of Scripture, never the reverse. A teacher who sets dates has shown you not to follow him. See How to Spot a False Teacher .

title: How to Read Prophecy and Revelation
text: Watch and Be Ready As Christ would have us to be certainly persuaded that there shall be a day of judgment, both to deter all men from sin, and for the greater consolation of the godly in their adversity: so will he have that day unknown to men, that they may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful, because they know not at what hour the Lord will come; and may be ever prepared to say, Come, Lord Jesus, come quickly. Amen. Westminster Confession of Faith 33.3 God hid the day to keep you awake, not to keep you guessing. Every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure (1 John 3:3). His coming is good news only for those found in him. If you are not in Christ, the day you cannot know is the day to be ready for now. The gospel shows you how to come to him today. Read Revelation 1 to 5 and 19 to 22. Ask what each vision shows you about Christ. Learn Acts 1:11 by heart. Say it when the news frightens you. Pray Psalm 2 and Psalm 72. Ask God to give his Son the nations, whatever you think about the thousand years. Ask if you are ready. If Christ came tonight, is there a sin you would be ashamed to be found in? Put it away. See How to Examine Yourself . Turn off the prophecy charts. To go deeper, ask your elders for a sound book on the last things. Pray the Bible’s last prayer. Christ says, Surely I come quickly. Answer him every day, Even so, come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20).

title: How to Spot a False Teacher
text: Seven questions to test any teacher by Scripture, the common warning signs today, and what to do when you find one.

title: How to Spot a False Teacher
text: Christ Warned You Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. Ye shall know them by their fruits. Matthew 7:15-16 (KJV) Jesus, Paul, Peter, John, and Jude all warned that false teachers would come from inside the church, not only from outside it (Acts 20:29-30, 2 Peter 2:1, 1 John 2:19, Jude 4). They rarely announce themselves. They are often likable, gifted, and popular. So Scripture tells you to test them, not to trust them because they are famous or kind.

title: How to Spot a False Teacher
text: How to Test a Teacher Do what the Bereans did. They received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so (Acts 17:11). Then ask these questions. What does he say about Christ? Is Jesus fully God and fully man, the only Savior, crucified for sinners and bodily raised? A man who teaches otherwise, and holds to it when he is shown the truth, is not a confused brother. He is a false teacher (1 John 4:1-3, 2 John 9-10). Someone who was simply taught wrong and gladly takes correction is another case. Teach him patiently, as Aquila and Priscilla taught Apollos the way of God more perfectly (Acts 18:26). What does he say about the gospel? Is a sinner saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone? Anyone who adds works, rituals, or a church’s merit to Christ preaches another gospel (Galatians 1:6-9). What is his final authority? Scripture alone, or Scripture plus his visions, his prophecies, or his church’s tradition? God has finished speaking in his written Word, and nothing is to be added to it by new revelations of the Spirit or traditions of men (WCF 1.6). Does he handle the Bible honestly? Does he read verses in their setting, or pull them out to prove what he already wanted to say? The unlearned and unstable wrest the scriptures unto their own destruction (2 Peter 3:16). Does he call sinners to repent? A teacher who never names sin, never warns of judgment, and never calls for repentance is not preaching the gospel Christ preached (Mark 1:15, 2 Timothy 4:3-4). How does he live? Look at his fruit. Greed, sexual sin, pride, and love of money are marks Scripture names (2 Peter 2:2-3, 10, 14, 18, Titus 1:11). Who holds him to account? Is he under the oversight of a church and its elders, or does he answer to no one?

title: How to Spot a False Teacher
text: Common Warning Signs Today Health and wealth. Teaching that God promises money, health, and success to those with enough faith, or to those who give to the ministry. New revelation. Claims that God told him something new that you must believe or obey. No sin, no judgment, no hell. A message only about self-esteem, purpose, and blessing. Christ made small. Jesus presented only as a good example, a life coach, or one way among many. Celebrity without a church. A large following, a brand, merchandise, and no elders. Anger at being tested. A faithful teacher welcomes being checked against Scripture. A false one calls it attacking God’s anointed.

title: How to Spot a False Teacher
text: Be Careful in Both Directions Not every teacher who is wrong about something is a false teacher. A sound minister can be mistaken on a lesser point, or say something badly. Faithful men have differed on baptism, church government, and the millennium. Some of those differences are serious errors, but they are not heresy. Save the label for those who deny or corrupt the gospel itself. How to Spot Real Heresy sets out the difference. And do not become a man who hunts for heresy for sport. Test what you hear, hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and speak with grief, not glee. To see these questions put to work fairly on popular preachers of our day, read Teacher Reviews .

title: How to Spot a False Teacher
