text: What to Do Stop following him. Unsubscribe, stop buying, stop giving. Paul says to mark them and avoid them (Romans 16:17). Warn those you love, gently and with Scripture. If he is in your own church, go to your elders. Do not start a campaign on your own. Sit under faithful preaching. The best protection from counterfeit is to know the real thing well. See How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: How to Spot Real Heresy
text: The difference between heresy, serious error, and honest disagreement, the truths that mark the line, and how to respond.

title: How to Spot Real Heresy
text: What Heresy Is A heresy is not any teaching you disagree with. It is the denial of a truth so central that without it there is no Christian faith left. Peter called them damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them (2 Peter 2:1). It helps to sort disagreements into three kinds. Heresy. Denies the gospel or the God of the gospel. A man who holds it, and still clings to it after patient teaching and a first and second admonition, cannot be received as a brother in the faith, whatever he calls himself (Titus 3:10, 2 John 9-10). Serious error. Wrong on an important teaching, and harmful to the church, but not a denial of the gospel itself. Worth contending about. Not a reason to call someone lost. How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism shows where those two fall. Differences among the faithful. Questions on which godly, confessional Christians have disagreed for centuries, such as the millennium. Hold your view, and hold it charitably. Calling a teaching heresy is a judgment about the teaching, measured by Scripture. It is not an infallible verdict on any person’s soul. A man may be confused, badly taught, or not yet corrected, and God alone knows the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). But to reject an essential truth knowingly and to go on rejecting it is no small thing. Whosoever transgresseth, and abideth not in the doctrine of Christ, hath not God (2 John 9). The church must judge what a man professes, and the final judgment of every soul belongs to God (Romans 14:10-12).

title: How to Spot Real Heresy
section: The Truths That Mark the Line
text: The Truths That Mark the Line The early church settled these in the Apostles’, Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds and at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and the Reformation recovered the gospel itself. Denying any of them is heresy. One God in three persons. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God, the same in substance, equal in power and glory (WSC 6). Christ fully God. The eternal Son, not a created being or a lesser god (John 1:1, Colossians 2:9). Christ fully man. A true body and a reasonable soul, born of the virgin Mary (WSC 22, Hebrews 2:14-17, 1 John 4:2-3). Christ one person. Two natures, not two persons, and not a mixture of the two (WCF 8.2). His death for sinners and his bodily resurrection. If Christ be not raised, your faith is vain (1 Corinthians 15:17). Salvation by grace alone through faith alone. Any message that makes our works part of the ground of our acceptance with God is another gospel (Galatians 1:6-9, Romans 3:28). Scripture as God’s Word. A teaching that sets a new revelation or a church above Scripture cuts away the ground every other truth stands on.

title: How to Spot Real Heresy
text: Where It Shows Up Some groups that use Christian words deny these truths in their official teaching. Jehovah’s Witnesses deny the Trinity and teach that Jesus is a created being. The Latter-day Saints teach that God was once a man and that there are many gods, and they add books to Scripture. Oneness Pentecostals deny the Trinity and teach that the Father, Son, and Spirit are one person in different modes. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that justification is by God’s grace and that no one can earn the grace by which it begins. But it teaches that justification is not only the forgiveness of sins but the inward renewal of the sinner, given at baptism, that the righteousness by which a man is justified is the grace God pours into him, and that this righteousness is increased by good works done in grace. The Council of Trent, whose decrees Rome still holds, condemned anyone who says a sinner is justified by faith alone or by the imputed righteousness of Christ alone (Session 6, canons 9, 11, 24). Scripture teaches that God justifies the ungodly by counting Christ’s righteousness to him, received by faith alone (Romans 4:5-6, Philippians 3:9). To deny that is to deny the gospel the Reformers recovered (WCF 11.1). The prosperity gospel teaches that Christ died to buy health and wealth for those with enough faith, and that faith is a force men use to get what they want. That makes gain the reward of godliness and turns the gospel of grace into another gospel (1 Timothy 6:5, Galatians 1:6-9). This is about what each group officially teaches, not a verdict on every person in it. God alone knows each heart, and people inside those groups need the gospel told to them plainly and kindly.

title: How to Spot Real Heresy
text: How to Respond Know the truth well. The surest guard is a firm grasp of the Shorter Catechism and the Creeds. See Reformed doctrine . Counterfeits are spotted by those who know the real thing. Earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints (Jude 3). Do not shrug off heresy as a difference of opinion. Be gentle with the person. Paul says to instruct them in meekness, if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth (2 Timothy 2:25). Do not give a heretic a platform. John told the church not to receive one who brings another doctrine of Christ or to bid him God speed (2 John 10). Leave church discipline to the church. A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject (Titus 3:10). That is the elders’ work, not a private verdict.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: Who makes the difference when a sinner is saved? Both views set out fairly, answered from Scripture, and how to talk with a brother who disagrees.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: The One Question Underneath When a sinner is saved, who makes the difference between him and the man beside him who stays lost? Pelagianism and Arminianism give one answer. Scripture gives another. This is not a quarrel for scholars. It shapes how you pray for your children, how you tell a friend about Christ, what you trust in when you doubt, and who gets the praise on the last day. Paul put the whole question in one line. For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it? 1 Corinthians 4:7 (KJV) Paul wrote those words to humble Corinthians who were puffed up over their favorite teachers (1 Corinthians 4:6). He was not settling the debate this page is about. But the principle he lays down reaches further than Corinth. Whatever we have, we received. This page applies that principle to the greatest gift of all. This page sets out each view fairly, answers it from Scripture and the Westminster Standards, and then turns to practice. How to talk with a brother who disagrees, what not to overcorrect into, where these errors hide in churches today, and where they hide in your own heart.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: What Pelagius Taught Pelagius was a British monk who came to Rome around the year 400. He was grieved by the loose living of professing Christians, and he blamed it on teaching that made men think they could not obey. When he heard a bishop quote Augustine’s prayer, Give what thou commandest, and command what thou wilt, he could not bear it. To him that prayer made men lazy. If God commands it, he reasoned, man must be able to do it. From there he and his followers, Celestius and later Julian of Eclanum, taught these things. Adam’s sin hurt only Adam, and his children only by a bad example. No guilt and no corruption pass down to us. Every baby is born as Adam was made, innocent and able to choose good or evil. A man can keep God’s law by his own will if he will only try. Some have lived without sin. Grace means outward helps. The gift of free will, the law, the teaching and example of Christ, and the pardon of past sins. It is not a power within that changes the heart. Augustine answered him in book after book. The church condemned Pelagianism at the Council of Carthage in 418 and again at the general Council of Ephesus in 431. It is one of the oldest heresies the church has named, and it has never stayed buried.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: Answering Pelagianism We fell in Adam, not only like him Paul does not say we sin because we copy Adam. He says Adam’s one sin made us sinners. For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Romans 5:19 (KJV) Look at the two halves together. If Adam only set a bad example, then Christ only set a good one, and we are saved by copying him. Pelagius loses the gospel the moment he loses the fall. Paul also says death reigned even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression (Romans 5:14). Infants die. They have copied no one. David confessed that his sin went back further than his choices. Behold, I was shapen in iniquity (Psalm 51:5). They being the root of all mankind, the guilt of this sin was imputed; and the same death in sin, and corrupted nature, conveyed to all their posterity descending from them by ordinary generation. Westminster Confession of Faith 6.3 A dead man needs life, not an example Scripture does not say we are weak or sick. It speaks of those who were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1). Pelagius offers a drowning man a book on how to swim. Christ goes down into the water and brings up the body and breathes into it. The carnal mind is enmity against God, Paul says, for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God (Romans 8:7-8). Ought does not mean can This was Pelagius’s strongest argument, so answer it carefully. God commands every man to love him with all his heart. Does that prove every man is able? No. A man who has wasted his master’s money still owes the debt, though he cannot pay it. His inability is his own fault, so it does not cancel his duty. Our inability is not like a man with no legs who wants to walk and cannot. It is like a man who hates the road and will not walk it. Ye will not come to me, that ye might have life (John 5:40). Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil (Jeremiah 13:23). God gives the law to stop every mouth and to show us our sin, for by the law is the knowledge of sin (Romans 3:20). The law sends us to Christ. It was never a ladder. If we could, Christ died for nothing For if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain (Galatians 2:21). If a man can keep the law by trying, the cross was a tragedy and not a rescue. Augustine’s prayer was right after all. God commands what we cannot do so that we will ask him for it, and then he gives what he commands. It is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: The Halfway House After Pelagius was condemned, some monks in southern France tried a middle road. John Cassian and others taught that man is not dead in sin but badly sick. Grace is needed to finish salvation, but a sinner can often take the first step on his own. He can want to be healed, and God then helps him. Later writers called this Semi-Pelagianism. The Council of Orange in 529 rejected it. The council taught that even the beginning of faith, and the very desire to believe, is a gift of grace and not something in us by nature. Scripture agrees. No man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father (John 6:65). Flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, Jesus told Peter, but my Father which is in heaven (Matthew 16:17). Most people who have never heard the word live in this halfway house. You will hear it in sayings like these. God has done ninety nine percent and you must do the last one. God votes for you, the devil votes against you, and you cast the deciding vote. They sound humble, but they leave the hinge of salvation in the sinner’s hand.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: What Arminianism Teaches Be fair here, because many who hold this view love Christ. Jacob Arminius was a Dutch pastor and later a professor at Leiden. He had studied at Geneva under Theodore Beza, Calvin’s successor. He died in 1609. The next year his followers set out their views in five articles called the Remonstrance. Conditional election. God chose to save those he foresaw would believe in Christ and keep believing. Universal atonement. Christ died for every man, gaining forgiveness for all, though only believers actually receive it. Man needs grace. Fallen man cannot of himself think, will, or do any saving good. He must be born again by God in Christ through the Spirit. Resistible grace. Grace begins, carries on, and finishes all good in us, but a man can refuse it to the end. Uncertain perseverance. The Remonstrants first said it needed more study whether a true believer could fall away. Their followers soon said he could. A century later John Wesley taught that God gives every person a prevenient grace, a grace that goes before. It does not save anyone, but it lifts the fallen will enough that each man can accept Christ or refuse him. Arminians do not all say the same thing. Wesleyans make much of prevenient grace. Some, often called Reformed Arminians, hold that a believer can be lost only by turning from Christ in unbelief. Others hold that God chose the church as a body in Christ rather than choosing persons. Many Baptists believe in conditional election and still hold that a true believer cannot be lost. What follows answers what these views share, that the sinner’s response is what finally decides. It does not claim every one of them is built the same way. Notice the third article. Arminians are not Pelagians. Most believe in the fall, in man’s need of grace, in Christ’s death in the place of sinners, and in justification by faith. Wesley preached Christ to coal miners in the open air. Do not paint an Arminian brother as a heretic. But see where the hinge falls. In this view grace makes salvation possible for all, and the sinner’s own choice makes it actual for some. Grace is needed, but it does not decide. So when you ask why one man believed and his neighbor did not, the final answer is something in the man. That is where Paul’s principle in 1 Corinthians 4:7 presses hardest, and that is why the Reformed churches could not let it pass.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: How the Church Answered The Dutch churches called the Synod of Dort, which met in 1618 and 1619, with delegates from Britain, Germany, and Switzerland. It answered the five articles of the Remonstrance point by point. Those answers are what people now call the five points of Calvinism. They were never meant to be the whole Reformed faith. They are a reply to five errors about how God saves. A generation later the Westminster Confession taught the same things in its own words. Here they are, answered from Scripture, in the order the Remonstrants raised them. God chose freely, not by foreseen faith According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, Ephesians 1:4-5 (KJV) He chose us that we should be holy, not because he saw we would be. And the cause is the good pleasure of his will. Paul says the same of Jacob and Esau, chosen before they were born, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth (Romans 9:11). So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Romans 9:16). If election hung on foreseen faith, Paul would have said so here. It would have answered every objection he raises in Romans 9 in one sentence. Luke gives the order plainly. As many as were ordained to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48). He does not say as many as believed were ordained. Arminians point to Romans 8:29, For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate. But notice the word whom. God foreknew persons, not their choices. In Scripture to know often means to set your love on someone. God said to Israel, You only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). He knew about every nation. He had chosen only one. And if God only looked ahead and saw who would believe, then he did not really choose anyone. He only noticed. Those of mankind that are predestinated unto life, God, before the foundation of the world was laid, according to His eternal and immutable purpose, and the secret counsel and good pleasure of His will, hath chosen, in Christ, unto everlasting glory, out of His mere free grace and love, without any foresight of faith, or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving Him thereunto; and all to the praise of His glorious grace. Westminster Confession of Faith 3.5 Faith itself is a gift The Arminian says God chose those who would believe. But where does the believing come from? For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake (Philippians 1:29). Faith is given. If God gives the faith, he cannot have chosen us because of the faith he planned to give. Christ died to save, not to make salvation possible The angel did not say Jesus would make salvation available. He said, he shall save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). Christ said, I lay down my life for the sheep (John 10:15), and then he told some who stood there, ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep (John 10:26). On the night before he died he said, I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me (John 17:9). That verse is about his prayer that night, so do not lean on it alone. But dying and praying are two parts of one priestly work. The high priest offered the sacrifice and then carried the names of the tribes in before God. Christ by his own blood entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12), and he ever liveth to make intercession for them that come unto God by him (Hebrews 7:25). He died that they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance (Hebrews 9:15). So it is a fair question, drawn from his whole work as priest. Would he shed his blood for those he would not bring by name before the Father? Paul builds assurance on this very point. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died (Romans 8:34). If Christ died for every man, and many men are condemned, that argument falls apart. If Christ paid for the sins of a man who is in hell, then God punishes the same sins twice. If you answer that the man is punished for his unbelief, then ask whether Christ paid for that sin too. The Arminian cross makes salvation possible for everyone and certain for no one. The Reformed churches have never said Christ’s death is too small. It is of infinite worth, enough for the whole world. And Christ is to be freely offered to every sinner who hears. The question is not how much his blood is worth. It is what he meant to do when he shed it, and whether he did it. The Spirit’s call raises the dead Men do resist the Holy Ghost. Stephen said so (Acts 7:51). Every sinner resists the outward call of the gospel for as long as he is left to himself. But God promised more than an offer. A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them. Ezekiel 36:26-27 (KJV) Read the verbs. I will give, I will take away, I will put, and cause you to walk. There is no perhaps in it. Jesus said the same. No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day. John 6:44 (KJV) Everyone who is drawn in that verse is raised up at the end. So the drawing is not a grace given to all that many refuse. It brings the sinner all the way home. Arminians answer with John 12:32, I will draw all men unto me. Read the verses before it. Greeks had just come asking to see Jesus (John 12:20-21). He says the cross will draw not only Jews but men of every nation. And Scripture never describes Wesley’s prevenient grace, a grace that lifts every man halfway and leaves the last step to him. It shows us Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul (Acts 16:14). This is not God dragging a man against his will. It is God giving him a new will. Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power (Psalm 110:3). All those whom God hath predestinated unto life, and those only, He is pleased, in His appointed and accepted time, effectually to call, by His Word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation, by Jesus Christ; enlightening their minds spiritually and savingly to understand the things of God, taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and, by His almighty power, determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ: yet so, as they come most freely, being made willing by His grace. Westminster Confession of Faith 10.1 Those he saves, he keeps If salvation hung on my will at the start, it would hang on my will to the end, and I would fall. But Christ says of his sheep, they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand (John 10:28). He that hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). Believers are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation (1 Peter 1:5). Paul’s golden chain has no missing links. Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. Romans 8:30 (KJV) No one drops out between called and glorified. The warnings in Hebrews are real, and they are one of the means God uses to keep his people running. They are not a sign that he will let go. See Kept to the End .

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: What Free Will Really Is The Reformed faith does not say man has no will, or that he is a puppet. Every man chooses what he most wants. Nothing outside him forces him. The trouble is inside. His wants are bent away from God, so he will not choose God. Man, by his fall into a state of sin, hath wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation: so as, a natural man, being altogether averse from that good, and dead in sin, is not able, by his own strength, to convert himself, or to prepare himself thereunto. Westminster Confession of Faith 9.3 The Confession traces the will through four estates. Adam in innocence was free to do good and able to fall. Fallen man still makes real choices, and he can do things that are outwardly good. He can love his children, keep his word, and serve his town. But apart from God’s grace he cannot choose any spiritual good that goes with salvation. Even his best deeds do not come from a heart made clean by faith, so they cannot please God or earn his favor (WCF 16.7). The converted man is freed to do good, though sin still clings to him. The saint in glory will be free to do good alone and never fall again (WCF 9.2-5). Notice that the freest will of all, in heaven, cannot choose evil. Freedom in Scripture is not standing in the middle of the road with equal power to go either way. It is being made what you were meant to be. Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed (John 8:34, 36).

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: The “All” and “World” Verses Arminians lean on a handful of verses with the word all or world in them. Take them seriously. Every word in them is true. The question is what each word means where it stands, and you settle that the way you settle any word, by its context. This is not a question of literal or figurative. It is the plain meaning in its own setting. How to Read the Bible Rightly says more. World does not always mean every person. When the Pharisees said, behold, the world is gone after him (John 12:19), they did not mean every human being. That only shows the word can be used more than one way. It does not settle what it means in a given verse. For that, look at the verses themselves. Read John 3:16 with Nicodemus. Jesus was speaking to a teacher of Israel, and the Jews of that day looked for God’s mercy to rest on Israel. God so loved the world tells him it reaches past Israel to sinners of every people. The wonder is also in what the world is, a world in rebellion against its Maker. And the very next verses divide that world into two. He that believeth on him is not condemned, Jesus says, but he that believeth not is condemned already (John 3:18). Reformed teachers read this verse as God’s love for the world in its sin and in its breadth, and as a sincere call to whosoever believeth. Read 1 John 2:2 with John 11. John says Christ is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. John used almost the same words once before. Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation, And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad (John 11:51-52). There the whole world beyond Israel means God’s children scattered among the nations. Ask what propitiation means. A propitiation does not merely make it possible for God’s wrath to be turned away. It actually turns it away. If Christ was in that sense the propitiation for every person who ever lived, then wrath is turned away from people who will still bear it. Read the way John 11 suggests, the verse holds together. Christ’s death turns away God’s wrath from his people in every nation, not from John’s first readers only. Look at who is addressed. 2 Peter 3:9 says God is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish. Peter wrote to them that have obtained like precious faith (2 Peter 1:1). God delays the end so that all his people will be brought in. Look at the verses around it. 1 Timothy 2:4 says God will have all men to be saved. Paul had just told Timothy that prayers be made for all men, and then he named some of them. For kings, and for all that are in authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2). He means men of every rank, even the rulers who persecute the church. Hold God’s sincere call as well. As I live, saith the Lord God , I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). Reformed teachers have always held that God’s plea to sinners is real, and that he takes no delight in their ruin. His command and his plea go out to all. His secret decree is his own (Deuteronomy 29:29). Do not let a system make you mute where Scripture pleads.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: Questions People Ask Doesn’t that make us robots? No. A robot does not want anything. A believer comes to Christ wanting to come, more willingly than he ever did anything. God does not go around the will. He changes it. Paul tells you to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, and in the same breath says it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do (Philippians 2:12-13). Both are true at once. Isn’t it unfair? Fairness would send us all to hell. No one in hell will be there for want of being chosen. He will be there for sins he loved. God wrongs no one by showing mercy to some. I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy (Romans 9:15). If God Chooses, Is He Fair? takes up this question at length. Then why evangelize? Because God saves through preaching. How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? (Romans 10:14). When Paul was afraid in Corinth, the Lord told him to keep speaking, for I have much people in this city (Acts 18:10). Election was the reason he stayed. If salvation hung on how persuasive you are, you would be crushed. Since it hangs on God, you can speak boldly and leave the result to him. Then why pray? Listen to an Arminian pray for his lost son. He does not ask God to make salvation possible for the boy. He asks God to save him, to open his eyes and change his heart. On his knees he prays like a Calvinist. Keep praying exactly that way. God has bound himself to work through the prayers of his people.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: Is an Arminian My Brother? How to Spot Real Heresy sorts disagreements into heresy, serious error, and differences among the faithful. Here is where these views fall. Pelagianism is heresy. It denies original sin and our need of inward grace, and it makes Christ an example instead of a Savior. The church has condemned it for sixteen centuries. A man who teaches it, knowingly, after patient correction, is not preaching the gospel. Semi-Pelagianism was condemned at Orange, because it puts the start of salvation in man. It is a deep error that leans hard toward the first. Arminianism is a serious error. It touches the doctrine of grace itself, so it weighs more than a difference over church government. The Synod of Dort removed Remonstrant ministers from their pulpits, and the Westminster Confession denies its points one by one. But an Arminian who rests on Christ alone for his justification has not denied the gospel. He is inconsistent, and happily so. His heart and his prayers are often better than his system. Some who began as Arminians have gone further. Open theism teaches that God does not know what men will freely choose tomorrow. That is no longer a question about grace. It is a different God from the one who declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10). Do not lump an ordinary Arminian believer in with that. Remember the history. George Whitefield and John Wesley quarreled sharply over these very doctrines, and Whitefield did not back down. Yet he asked that Wesley preach his funeral sermon, and Wesley did. Charles Spurgeon could say Calvinism is the gospel and nothing else, and still honor Wesley’s holiness and count many Arminians as dear children of God.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
section: How to Talk With an Arminian Friend
text: How to Talk With an Arminian Friend In 1784 a young Charles Simeon met the aged John Wesley. Simeon asked him whether he felt himself so depraved that he would never have turned to God if God had not first put it into his heart. Wesley said yes. Whether he looked for salvation only through the blood and righteousness of Christ. Yes, solely through Christ. Whether he was to save himself afterward by his own works. No, he must be saved by Christ from first to last. Whether he was upheld every moment by God, as an infant in its mother’s arms. Yes, altogether. Then Simeon said, in effect, that this was all his Calvinism, and that they should rejoice in what they shared. Simeon did not give up the doctrine. He showed Wesley that his heart already held it. That is the best way to begin. Find out what he means. Many Christians say free will and mean only that they really chose and were not forced. You agree. Ask before you argue. Start with what you share. Christ’s deity, his death in our place, his rising, justification by faith. Say it out loud. It changes the temperature. Ask Simeon’s questions. Would you have come to God if he had not first moved your heart? Will you keep yourself to the end, or must he keep you? Ask how he prays. Do you thank God for your faith? If you supplied it, why thank him? When you pray for a lost friend, what exactly do you ask God to do? Ask the hard question gently. You and your friend heard the same gospel. You believed and he did not. Why? Were you wiser, humbler, or more willing than he? Most believers will not say yes. That refusal is the doctrine of grace in seed form. Open one passage together. John 6:35-65 is the best place to start. Read it slowly and ask what each verse says about who comes and why. Be patient. Many Reformed believers were Arminians first, and it took them years. The servant of the Lord must not strive, Paul says, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient (2 Timothy 2:24). He corrects in hope, if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth (2 Timothy 2:25). If you believe God opens hearts, you have no need to force one open. Do not lead with it to an unbeliever. A lost man needs Christ crucified, not the five points. Tell him to come, and tell him Christ will not cast him out. How to Disagree With Another Christian has more on doing this well.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: Do Not Overcorrect There is a ditch on the other side of the road. Hyper-Calvinism says we must not call every sinner to repent and believe, or that a man needs some sign he is chosen before he may come. That is not the Reformed faith. The Confession says God freely offereth unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ (WCF 7.3). God now commandeth all men every where to repent (Acts 17:30). Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth (Isaiah 45:22). Spurgeon fought the hyper-Calvinists of his day as hard as he fought the Arminians. There is another ditch, the proud Calvinist. Some men learn the doctrines of grace and become the least gracious men in the church. That is a sad contradiction. If you really believe you added nothing to your salvation, you have nothing to sneer about. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1 Corinthians 8:1). A man who boasts in sovereign grace has not yet understood it.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: Where It Hides Today Few churches today would call themselves Pelagian, but its ideas are everywhere. Moralism. God helps those who help themselves. Good people go to heaven. Be a better person and God will be pleased. That first saying is not in the Bible. God is the one that justifieth the ungodly (Romans 4:5). Revival by technique. Charles Finney, the great revivalist of the 1800s, denied that we inherit a sinful nature from Adam. He preached a sermon titled Sinners Bound to Change Their Own Hearts, and he taught that a revival is a purely philosophical result of the right use of the constituted means. In plain words, use the right methods and you will get converts. Many of the methods he spread are still used, and so is the belief behind them. Decisionism. Calling sinners to come to Christ now is right. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). But telling a man he is saved because he walked an aisle or repeated a prayer puts his assurance in his act, not in Christ. Point him to Christ, and let the fruit show over time. Pressure. Pleading is biblical. We pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20). Working on people’s feelings with music and repetition until hands go up is not. If the Spirit gives new birth, you do not need to manufacture it. Half truths. God has done all he can, and now it is up to you. Jesus is a gentleman and will not force himself on anyone. There is a grain of truth here, since God does not drag the unwilling. But he can make the unwilling willing, and he does. When you hear these things, do not storm out. Test them by Scripture, speak to your elders, and remember that the people saying them often mean well. See How to Spot a False Teacher for when the problem goes deeper.

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
section: The Pelagian in Your Own Heart
text: The Pelagian in Your Own Heart Pelagianism is a system of doctrine, and no baby is born holding a system. But the fallen heart naturally wants to take credit for its own righteousness. Its religion is always do and live. Even a man who confesses sovereign grace can fall into Pelagian ways of thinking, and he can live as if his standing with God rose and fell with his performance. Watch for these signs in yourself. Your assurance goes up on good days and down on bad ones. Then you are resting on yourself, not on Christ. You look down on weaker believers. The Pharisee thanked God that I am not as other men are (Luke 18:11), and went home unjustified. You secretly think you were wiser to believe. Go back to 1 Corinthians 4:7. You pray little. A man who thinks he can manage does not cry for help. You despair after a fall. If your salvation rested on you, despair would make sense. It does not, so get up and go to Christ again. The cure is not to try less. It is to know where your strength comes from. Paul worked harder than all the apostles, and then he caught himself. But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. 1 Corinthians 15:10 (KJV)

title: How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism
text: Salvation Is of the Lord Jonah learned it in the belly of a fish. Salvation is of the Lord (Jonah 2:9). Not mostly of the Lord with a little help. Of the Lord. That is why the doctrines of grace are not cold. They mean the Father chose you, the Son died for you by name, and the Spirit raised you when you were dead. They mean you will be kept, because the one who began the work does not quit. And they mean every crown in heaven gets thrown at his feet. Charles Wesley, John’s brother and an Arminian too, could not help singing it. In his hymn And Can It Be, his spirit lay “fast bound in sin and nature’s night” until God’s eye shone into the cell. “I woke, the dungeon flamed with light.” Then “my chains fell off, my heart was free.” That is not a man who decided. That is a prisoner God set loose. If you are not sure you are chosen, do not start there. Start with Christ’s open door. All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. John 6:37 (KJV) No one ever came to him and found the door shut. The gospel tells you how to come today, and How God Saves Sinners sets out the doctrines of grace in brief.

title: How to Weigh “God Told Me”
text: God has spoken in his Son. How God guides you now, how to test a claimed word, and how to answer a friend kindly.

title: How to Weigh “God Told Me”
section: God Has Spoken in His Son
text: God Has Spoken in His Son God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds; Hebrews 1:1-2 (KJV) God once spoke by dreams, visions, and prophets. Then he spoke last and fullest by his Son. The Confession says God committed his word wholly unto writing, those former ways of God’s revealing his will unto his people being now ceased (WCF 1.1). That written Word is enough. It makes the man of God perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works (2 Timothy 3:16-17). It is the faith which was once delivered unto the saints (Jude 3), once for all. The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man’s salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men. Westminster Confession of Faith 1.6 The Bible closes with a warning against anyone who shall add unto the words of the prophecy of this book (Revelation 22:18-19). Read fairly, it guards the book of Revelation itself. But it echoes what God said through Moses, Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you (Deuteronomy 4:2). No man may add to what God has said. And see who that last Word is. The Son, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3). You need no fresh message to know God’s heart toward sinners. If you have never come to Christ, start with the gospel .

title: How to Weigh “God Told Me”
text: Prophecy, Tongues, and Miracles Reformed churches hold that prophecy and tongues, as gifts that brought new words from God, have ceased. They belonged to the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone (Ephesians 2:20). A foundation is laid once. The wonders of that time confirmed the apostles’ word (Hebrews 2:3-4), and Paul calls them the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). Some evangelicals differ. They believe these gifts continue, and most say any prophecy today can be mistaken and must be tested by the Bible. Many of them love Christ, and this is not a line between the saved and the lost. But a word that may be wrong is not what the prophets meant by Thus saith the Lord . Call an impression an impression. God has not stopped working. He still heals in answer to prayer (James 5:14-16), and he is free to work without, above, and against means (WCF 5.3). But an answered prayer is providence, not new revelation, and it makes no one an apostle. False prophets also shall shew signs and wonders (Mark 13:22). A wonder never proves a message.

title: How to Weigh “God Told Me”
text: How God Guides You Now Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path (Psalm 119:105). The picture is a lamp carried at night, enough for the next step, and what it pictures is real. His Word. Most choices are already answered. Be honest, keep yourself pure, honor your parents, and marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39). His providence. A man’s heart deviseth his way, but the Lord directeth his steps (Proverbs 16:9). Wisdom. Where Scripture leaves you free, ask. If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God (James 1:5). Counsel. In the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Proverbs 11:14). The Spirit in the Word. The Confession says the inward illumination of the Spirit is necessary to understand what is revealed in the Word (WCF 1.6). The Spirit opens your eyes to what is written. He does not whisper what is not. So may you say the Lord led you? Yes. Looking back on a closed door, you may thankfully say so. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths (Proverbs 3:6). That confesses providence and claims no message. “I believe the Lord has led me here” is humble. “God told me, so you must accept it” claims a prophet’s authority.

title: How to Weigh “God Told Me”
text: Test Every Claimed Word Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. 1 John 4:1 (KJV) Moses gave Israel two tests. A prophet whose sign came true but who said, Let us go after other gods, was not to be heard (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). A word can come true and still be false. And when a word spoken in the Lord ’s name did not come to pass, he had not spoken it. Thou shalt not be afraid of him (Deuteronomy 18:21-22). The Bereans checked even Paul against the scriptures (Acts 17:11). Does it contradict Scripture? Refuse it, even from an angel from heaven (Galatians 1:8). Does it add to Scripture? Refuse a new doctrine, duty, or rule for others too (WCF 1.6). Does it agree with Scripture? Then obey the Scripture. The claim adds nothing. Did it fail? Then God did not speak it. Do not fear it. Dreams, Impressions, and Feelings A dream now is a dream. Jeremiah set a dream beside God’s word and asked, What is the chaff to the wheat? (Jeremiah 23:28). A strong feeling or a sense of peace may be God stirring you toward a duty he already commanded. It may also be your own wishes or fears. The heart is deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9). So these things cannot bind your conscience or anyone else’s. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and he binds it by his Word (WCF 20.2). Weigh impressions by Scripture, never Scripture by impressions.

title: How to Weigh “God Told Me”
section: When a Friend Says “God Told Me”
text: When a Friend Says “God Told Me” Most who say it are not false prophets. They usually mean they prayed and came away with a strong sense. Be kind. Do not mock, and do not pounce. Ask what he means. “How did God tell you?” Often it was an impression in prayer. Agree with what Scripture says. If he says God wants him to forgive his brother, say amen and show him the verse. Point him to the surer word. Peter heard the Father’s voice on the holy mount, yet he wrote, We have also a more sure word of prophecy (2 Peter 1:16-19). Leave room on lesser choices. If he says God told him to take a job, you need not argue. Encourage him to hold it as his judgment under God. Be firmer when a word is used to control. If someone says God told him you must marry him, give him money, keep quiet about how he treats you, or obey him without question, he is laying a yoke God never laid. To require absolute and blind obedience is to destroy liberty of conscience (WCF 20.2). You may say no. Tell your elders. If a leader does this, read How to Spot a False Teacher . If someone is hurting you, read If You Are Not Safe .

title: How to Weigh “God Told Me”
text: This Week Read Hebrews 1 and 2 Peter 1. Notice what God calls sure. Take one decision in front of you. Write down what Scripture says about it, pray for wisdom, and ask a wise believer. Watch your words. Instead of “God told me,” say what happened. “I prayed and have come to believe this,” or “This verse convicted me.” Lay down a false burden. If a word frightens or binds you, weigh it by Scripture with an elder. Rest in the Son. God’s last Word to you is Christ, and he is enough.

title: How to Test Books, Music, and Preachers Online
text: Testing teaching online, your own elders, worship music, books and films, and your time and attention.

title: How to Test Books, Music, and Preachers Online
text: Every Believer Must Discern Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. 1 John 4:1 (KJV) John wrote that to ordinary church members. The Bereans searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so, and they did it with an apostle (Acts 17:11). Paul told a young church to prove all things and hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Discernment is a skill that grows with use. Hebrews speaks of those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil (Hebrews 5:14). The writer pictures a man whose senses are trained by practice, and that training is real. A Christian who never tests what he hears stays a child. And the voices now reach you in your pocket all day long.

title: How to Test Books, Music, and Preachers Online
text: Testing Teaching Online A book, a podcast, a video, or a sermon from another church is tested the same way as a preacher in a pulpit. Hold it up to Scripture, and use the Westminster Standards as a faithful summary of what Scripture teaches. The Larger Catechism tells hearers to examine what they hear by the Scriptures (WLC 160). Use the seven questions in How to Spot a False Teacher . The last of them, who holds him to account, matters most online, where anyone with a camera can build a following. Your Own Elders Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you. Hebrews 13:17 (KJV) A teacher you have never met cannot watch for your soul. He does not know your name, and he will not give account for you. Christ gave pastors and teachers to his church for the perfecting of the saints (Ephesians 4:11-12), and he gives them through a local church. A sound teacher online can help. When he becomes the voice you trust over your own elders, something has gone wrong. Let the sermon you hear on the Lord’s Day be the main meal of your week, and the rest a side dish. What the Feed Feeds You The apps that serve you videos are built to keep you watching. They learn what stirs you, and they bring you more of it. If outrage or flattery keeps you watching, you will get more of it. Paul warned of people who, after their own lusts, heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears (2 Timothy 4:3). A feed can do the heaping for you. Choose what you listen to on purpose. Do not let a machine choose it for you.

title: How to Test Books, Music, and Preachers Online
text: Worship Music and Other Songs In the public worship of God, he decides what is sung. This site holds, with the Reformed Presbyterian churches, that God gave the Psalms to be sung in worship, without instruments. How God Wants to Be Worshiped explains why. Listening at home or in the car is a different matter, and many in Reformed churches listen to songs about God outside of worship. Some hold that any singing of praise to God is worship and keep to the Psalms in private as well. Either way, test what you take in. Are the words true? Read the lyrics on their own, without the music. Would they stand if a minister said them from the pulpit? Is there theology in them? Do they say who God is, what Christ has done, and what sin is? Or could you sing them to a girlfriend by changing one word? What does it stir? Music moves the feelings. That is a gift. Ask whether it stirs love for Christ and hatred of sin, or only a mood you mistake for God’s presence.

title: How to Test Books, Music, and Preachers Online
text: Books, Music, Films, and Games Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things. Philippians 4:8 (KJV) Not all culture is evil. Paul quoted the pagan poets to the Athenians (Acts 17:28). Good stories, honest history, and beautiful music can be enjoyed with thanks. God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF 20.2), and no one may bind you with rules Scripture does not give. But liberty is not license. They who, upon pretense of Christian liberty, do practice any sin, or cherish any lust, do thereby destroy the end of Christian liberty (WCF 20.3). David said, I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psalm 101:3). Paul said to have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, for it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret (Ephesians 5:11-12). Scripture itself tells of wicked deeds, so a story may show sin. The question is whether it shows sin to be hated or serves it up to be enjoyed. The Larger Catechism names lascivious songs, books, pictures, and stage plays among the sins of the seventh commandment (WLC 139). Nudity and sex on a screen are not a matter of taste. What does it make me love? Does it make evil look good, or good look foolish? Does it rule me? All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any (1 Corinthians 6:12). Can I do it in faith? Whatsoever is not of faith is sin (Romans 14:23). If your conscience is uneasy, leave it. Films that portray Christ raise a further question. The Larger Catechism counts any representation of any of the three persons of God a sin against the second commandment (WLC 109), and an actor playing Jesus is such a representation.

title: How to Test Books, Music, and Preachers Online
text: Your Time and Your Attention See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Ephesians 5:15-16 (KJV) Your hours belong to God. A show can be clean and still steal an evening that was owed to prayer, to your wife, or to your children. The Larger Catechism calls for a sober use of recreations and counts their immoderate use a sin (WLC 135, 136). Many believers do not lack time to pray. They spend it on a screen a few minutes at a time. If you find that you cannot put the phone down, that is not a small thing. It has brought you under its power. Confess it, and take steps. If the screen has led you into pornography, read the part on the eyes . Guiding Children and Teens Parents must guide what their children watch, hear, and read, and teach them to test it themselves. Watch with them and ask afterward what the story made them admire. Go first. Children learn more from what you scroll than from what you say. See Phones and Screens in the parenting guide.

title: How to Test Books, Music, and Preachers Online
text: This Week List your voices. Write down every teacher and channel you follow. Run each through the seven questions. Ask your elders. Tell your pastor who you listen to and ask what he thinks. Let him be the teacher you hear most. Read the lyrics. Take the songs you play most and read the words alone. Keep what is true. Check your screen time. Compare last week’s hours on the phone with your hours in prayer and the Word. Then keep it off at the table and at bedtime. Bring it to Christ. Where you have fed on what grieves him, confess it. The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin (1 John 1:7). If you have never come to him, start with the gospel .

title: How to Disagree With Another Christian
text: Three kinds of difference, Romans 14 in practice, how to disagree well, and when to let it go.

title: How to Disagree With Another Christian
text: Three Kinds of Difference Christians will disagree until Christ comes. First know what kind of disagreement you are in, because Scripture does not treat them all alike. Matters of the faith. Who God is, who Christ is, and how a sinner is saved. To deny these is heresy, and you must earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints (Jude 3). How to Spot Real Heresy sets out where that line runs. Serious error. A brother is wrong on something Scripture teaches and that matters, such as baptism, worship, or the government of the church, but he does not deny the gospel. Hold your ground, and still own him as a brother in Christ. Some questions of interpretation, such as the thousand years of Revelation 20, sit near here, and faithful Reformed men have read them differently (see Prophecy ). Matters of conscience and wisdom. Things Scripture neither commands nor forbids. Here God has left believers free. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.2 To tell which you are in, ask two questions. Does this touch the gospel itself? Does Scripture command or forbid this, either in plain words or by good and necessary consequence (WCF 1.6)? If not, it is a matter of liberty, like whether to drink wine ( Alcohol ). Some questions sit where faithful believers weigh Scripture’s principles differently, such as tattoos ( Tattoos ) or the spacing of children ( Birth Control ). Wisdom still applies, but leave room where God leaves room. Treat your opinions as gospel and you become a Pharisee. Treat the gospel as opinion and you have nothing left to stand on.

title: How to Disagree With Another Christian
text: Romans 14 in Practice Rome was divided over food and holy days, and Paul told both sides how to treat each other. Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him. Romans 14:3 (KJV) The strong brother knows the thing is lawful, and his temptation is to despise the tender conscience. The weak brother thinks a lawful thing is sin, and his temptation is to judge the other as worldly. Paul forbids both. Each will answer to his own master (Romans 14:4, 10-12). Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind (Romans 14:5). Settle it before God, and never push a brother to act against his conscience, for whatsoever is not of faith is sin (Romans 14:23). And love sets limits on liberty. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died (Romans 14:15). If your freedom would lead a brother to sin against his conscience, lay it down (1 Corinthians 8:9-13). Christ laid down far more for you. Yet bearing with a weaker brother is not the same as letting any man make his scruple a law for the church. Paul would not have believers bound by Touch not, taste not, handle not, after the commandments and doctrines of men (Colossians 2:20-22).

title: How to Disagree With Another Christian
text: How to Disagree Well Listen first. Be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19). State his view so fairly that he would agree with it. Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). Both halves. Truth without love is a club. Love without truth leaves him in his error. Do not fight to win. Aim at his good and God’s truth. And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth; 2 Timothy 2:24-25 (KJV) Assume the best. Charity believeth all things, hopeth all things (1 Corinthians 13:7). The Larger Catechism counts misconstructing intentions, words, and actions as a sin against the ninth commandment (Q&A 145). Read him in the kindest way his words honestly bear. Argue the point, not the man. No mocking, no labels, no guessing at motives. And remember you may be the one who is wrong (Matthew 7:3-5).

title: How to Disagree With Another Christian
text: Two Quarrels in Scripture Paul and Barnabas Paul and Barnabas could not agree whether to take John Mark again, since he had left them before. And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other (Acts 15:39). It was a matter of wisdom, not doctrine, and Scripture does not say who was right. But later Paul names Barnabas as a fellow worker (1 Corinthians 9:6) and tells the Colossians to receive Mark (Colossians 4:10). From prison near the end of his life he writes, Take Mark, and bring him with thee (2 Timothy 4:11). Good men may part ways. They must not stay enemies. Paul and Peter At Antioch Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers out of fear of men. Paul writes, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11). He did it before them all, because the wrong was public and they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:14). If Gentiles had to live as Jews to sit at the table, then Christ alone was not enough. When the gospel is at stake, love speaks up, even to an apostle. Yet this quarrel did not end in hatred. Peter later calls him our beloved brother Paul (2 Peter 3:15).

title: How to Disagree With Another Christian
section: Online, in the Church, and Letting Go
text: Online, in the Church, and Letting Go Online All of this applies online, and more so. You cannot see his face, and an audience tempts you to perform. In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin (Proverbs 10:19). Before you post, ask whether you would say it at his table, and whether you are writing to help him or to be seen winning. Often the faithful answer is a phone call, or silence. In the Church If a brother has wronged you, go to him alone first (Matthew 18:15). If you differ with your church’s teaching or a decision of the session, take it to your elders humbly and in person. They watch for your souls, as they that must give account (Hebrews 13:17). Do not take it to the parking lot or the group chat. Gathering a party is how churches split, and God hates him that soweth discord among brethren (Proverbs 6:19). When to Let It Go The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression. Proverbs 19:11 (KJV) Not every slight needs answering, and not every mistaken opinion needs correcting by you. Charity shall cover the multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). Let small things go, and let them go for good. But do not let go of the gospel, or keep silent about sin that is harming someone. Take those to the elders.

title: How to Disagree With Another Christian
text: This Week Name one disagreement you are in. Decide honestly which kind it is. If it is a matter of liberty, confess any despising or judging to God, and to your brother if he knows of it. Pray for him by name, then write out his view in a few sentences he would agree with. If you cannot, you are not ready to answer it. Walk away from one online argument. If you have been talking behind his back, stop. Go to him, or to your elders. If you parted from a brother like Paul and Barnabas, call or write. First be reconciled to thy brother (Matthew 5:24). Remember how you were received. Receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God (Romans 15:7). If you have never come to him, start with the gospel .

title: How to Tell a True Church From a False One
text: The marks of a true church, what makes a church false and why, the warning signs, and what to do.

title: How to Tell a True Church From a False One
section: Impure Is Not the Same as False
text: Impure Is Not the Same as False Every church on earth has sin and error in it. The Confession says plainly that churches are more or less pure, and that the purest churches under heaven are subject both to mixture and error (WCF 25.4-5). So the question is not whether a church is perfect. It is whether it is a church of Christ at all, and how faithful it is. The purest churches under heaven are subject both to mixture and error; and some have so degenerated, as to become no churches of Christ, but synagogues of Satan. Nevertheless, there shall be always a church on earth, to worship God according to his will. Westminster Confession of Faith 25.5

title: How to Tell a True Church From a False One
section: The Marks of a True Church
text: The Marks of a True Church The Reformed churches have named three marks. The Belgic Confession sets them out (Article 29), and the Westminster Standards teach the same things. The pure preaching of the gospel. The Word of God is preached as the final authority, and Christ is held out as the only Savior of sinners by grace alone, through faith alone. The right use of the sacraments. Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are given as Christ gave them, no more and no fewer, as signs and seals of his promises and not as acts that save by their own power. Church discipline. The elders watch over the members, teach, warn, and correct, and when needed bar the unrepentant from the Lord’s Table, in order to bring them back (Matthew 18:15-17).

title: How to Tell a True Church From a False One
text: What Makes a Church False A church becomes false when it gives up one of those marks at its root, not when it falls short in practice. These are the things that do it, and why. It denies the gospel. If it teaches that sinners are saved by their works, their rituals, or the church itself, it has another gospel, and Paul says such a gospel is no gospel at all (Galatians 1:6-9). It denies the God of the gospel. If it denies the Trinity, the deity of Christ, or his bodily resurrection, it is not worshiping the God of Scripture. See How to Spot Real Heresy . It puts itself above Scripture. If its tradition, its leader, or its new prophecies bind the conscience where Scripture does not, it has taken Christ’s place as head of the church (WCF 20.2, 25.6). It corrupts the sacraments. If it adds sacraments, teaches that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood, or offers the Supper as a sacrifice for sins, it has turned a sign of Christ’s finished work into a work of its own (WCF 27.4, 29.2, 29.6). It has abandoned discipline entirely. If it blesses open, unrepentant sin and calls it good, it no longer guards the Table or the flock.

title: How to Tell a True Church From a False One
text: Warning Signs in a Church These do not make a church false by themselves. They are reasons to look closer and to talk with the elders. The sermons rarely open a passage of Scripture and explain it. Sin, judgment, and repentance are seldom or never mentioned. The church will not say plainly what it believes, or has no confession of faith. Worship is built around entertainment rather than what God has commanded (WCF 21.1). See How God Wants to Be Worshiped . There are no elders, or the elders do not know or shepherd the members. The pastor answers to no one. The church ordains women as pastors or ruling elders, which Scripture does not permit (1 Timothy 2:12, 3:2), or approves what Scripture calls sin.

title: How to Tell a True Church From a False One
text: What to Do If your church is impure but true, the ordinary course is to stay and serve, pray for it, and raise your concerns with the elders in the proper way. Do not leave over preferences or small things. No congregation on earth is without mixture and error (WCF 25.5). Serious corruption can be a reason to leave even a church that keeps the marks. False teaching the elders will not correct, open sin the session will not discipline over a long time, abuse that is covered up, or a real threat to your safety or your children’s are such reasons. If you are in danger, get safe first, and read If You Are Not Safe . Use the church’s own courts before you go, where you safely can. Speak to the elders, and if they will not hear, a Presbyterian church gives you the right to bring the matter to the presbytery (Matthew 18:15-17, WCF 31.3). Ask faithful elders elsewhere for counsel. Where abuse or danger is involved, you do not have to wait on that process to protect yourself or others. Abuse and other crimes belong with the police, and harm to a child must be reported to them or to child protective services. Church discipline is never a substitute for civil justice (Romans 13:4). If it has departed from the gospel, you must leave. Do it openly and kindly, telling the elders why. Leaving a congregation is not leaving the church. Christ’s visible church is larger than one congregation, and out of it there is no ordinary possibility of salvation (WCF 25.2). Do not stay home. Find a faithful church and join it. See How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: How to Leave a Church Well
text: Membership is a covenant. Good and bad reasons to leave, how to leave well, discipline, and when a church has hurt you.

title: How to Leave a Church Well
text: Membership Is a Covenant When you joined a church, you made promises before God and his people, among them to submit in the Lord to its elders. The elders in turn took on the charge of your soul. Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you. Hebrews 13:17 (KJV) God tells his people to consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together (Hebrews 10:24-25). That is a body, not a club. Leaving is not a sin in itself, and sometimes it is a duty. But it is serious, and it should be done slowly and in the open.

title: How to Leave a Church Well
section: Good and Bad Reasons to Leave
text: Good and Bad Reasons to Leave Reasons That Are Not Enough Preferences and programs. The length of the sermon, the size of the church, the manner of the pastor, a busier calendar somewhere else. They are not reasons to break a covenant. Your soul is fed by the Word, the sacraments, and prayer, under elders who know you. An offense you have not taken to the person. Go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone (Matthew 18:15). Leaving without a word is not peace. It is avoidance. Avoiding discipline. Leaving does not end the matter. See If You Are Under Discipline . Church-hopping. Paul warns of those who heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears (2 Timothy 4:3). A believer who keeps moving is never known, corrected, or shepherded. Reasons That Can Be Enough The church has abandoned the gospel. Then you must leave. See What Makes a Church False . Serious error the elders will not correct. False teaching on a weighty matter, worship God has not commanded, or open sin left undisciplined for years. Raise it first, as below. If nothing changes, you may go. You cannot worship there in good conscience. God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF 20.2), and whatsoever is not of faith is sin (Romans 14:23). If the church requires what you believe Scripture forbids, and patient talks with the elders have not settled it, you may go. Be sure it is conscience and not a preference dressed up as one. A move or a providential call. A new job, a marriage, the care of a parent, or a call to help plant a church. Seek your elders’ counsel, and go with their blessing.

title: How to Leave a Church Well
text: How to Leave Well Pray, and do not hurry. Search me, O God, and know my heart (Psalm 139:23). Talk with the elders first. They should hear it from you, not from others. Tell them plainly what troubles you, and give them time to answer. Use the proper courts where it is safe. If someone has sinned against you, follow Christ’s order, alone, then with one or two witnesses, then to the church (Matthew 18:15-17). If the elders will not hear a serious matter, a Presbyterian church lets you bring it to the presbytery, as What to Do explains. Ask for a letter of transfer. When Apollos went to Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him (Acts 18:27). A letter keeps you under care and helps your new elders know you. Guard your mouth on the way out. Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth (Ephesians 4:29). The Larger Catechism counts backbiting and tale bearing as sins against the ninth commandment, but it also forbids undue silence in a just cause (Q&A 145). Real abuse should be told plainly to those who must know. Keep the friendships you can. Do not make anyone choose sides. Be kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you (Ephesians 4:32). Join a faithful church soon. Do not drift. A few weeks of rest can become years at home. See How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: How to Leave a Church Well
text: If You Are Under Discipline If your elders have admonished you or kept you from the Lord’s Table, leaving will not take you out from under it. Church censures are for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren (WCF 30.3). They are Christ’s medicine for your good. A faithful church will not receive you while the matter stands. The way out is repentance, not a new address. Go back, confess what is true, and let them restore you in the spirit of meekness (Galatians 6:1). If you believe the discipline is unjust, appeal to the presbytery rather than walking away. And if you are being disciplined for reporting abuse or for fleeing danger, that is not Christ’s discipline. Get safe, and tell the presbytery or another faithful pastor.

title: How to Leave a Church Well
section: When a Church Has Hurt You
text: When a Church Has Hurt You Some of the deepest wounds come from God’s own people. David wrote, It was not an enemy that reproached me, but it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company (Psalm 55:12-14). Your grief is real, and you may pour it out to God as David did. The temptation then is to give up on the church altogether. Please do not. God is against shepherds who harm his flock, and he says of his sheep, I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken (Ezekiel 34:16). He does that through faithful shepherds in faithful churches. Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. Ephesians 5:25-27 (KJV) Paul pictures a bride washed and made ready, and what the picture shows is real. Christ loves his church, he died for her, and he is cleansing her by his Word. He will remove every spot you have seen. He has not given up on his church, or on you. If you are not sure you are his, start with the gospel . Then find a faithful church, and let its elders earn your trust over time.

title: How to Leave a Church Well
text: This Week If you are in danger, get safe today and call the police. Read If You Are Not Safe . Write down why you want to leave. Hold each reason up to Scripture, and cross out the preferences. Ask to meet with your pastor or an elder, and go privately to anyone who has sinned against you, if it is safe. If you go, ask for a letter of transfer, and thank the elders for what was good. Be in worship this Lord’s Day, in your own church or a faithful one you are visiting. Pray by name for the church you are leaving.

title: How to Find a Faithful Church
text: How to find a Reformed Presbyterian congregation, what to expect when you visit, what to do if none is near, and the questions to ask any church.

title: How to Find a Faithful Church
text: Why You Need One Christ did not save you to follow him alone. He gave his Word, the sacraments, and prayer to his church, and he set elders over his flock to watch for their souls (Hebrews 13:17). Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together is a command (Hebrews 10:25). A livestream, a podcast, or this website cannot baptize you, feed you at the Lord’s Table, or shepherd you.

title: How to Find a Faithful Church
text: Finding a Reformed Presbyterian Church This site is written from within the Reformed Presbyterian tradition. The Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America, the RPCNA, holds the Westminster Confession and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms as its standards, along with its own Testimony, a further statement of what it believes and practices. Its congregations sing the Psalms only, without instruments. Search the directory. Go to reformedpresbyterian.org/congregations and choose your state on the map or from the list. Each congregation belongs to one of seven presbyteries, regional bodies of elders, one of them in Japan. Outside North America, look for the sister Reformed Presbyterian churches in Scotland, Ireland, and Australia. Call or write the pastor first. Say you are looking for a church and would like to visit. Ask the service times. Many congregations worship in the morning and again in the afternoon or evening. Visit on the Lord’s Day. If the congregation worships more than once that day, try to be at each service, so you see the whole of its life together. Ask about the Lord’s Supper before you come to it. Reformed Presbyterian elders guard the Table and will want to speak with visitors first. That is care, not coldness. Stay for the meal or the fellowship. Many congregations eat together after worship. Meet the elders and their families.

title: How to Find a Faithful Church
section: If There Is None Near You
text: If There Is None Near You Do not stay home. Look for the nearest church that holds the Westminster Standards in earnest and practices what they teach. Then go through the questions below with it. Ask the RPCNA for help. Write to the nearest congregation or presbytery and ask whether there is a mission work or a family nearby, or what they would counsel. Consider whether to move. Many Christians have moved to be near a faithful church. Pray about it and seek counsel. Do not settle for no church. An imperfect faithful church is far better than none.

title: How to Find a Faithful Church
text: Questions to Ask Any Church What do you believe? Does it have a written confession, and does it actually hold to it? Is the gospel clear? Salvation by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, preached plainly. See How to Tell a True Church From a False One . Is the Word preached? Do the sermons open a passage of Scripture, explain it, and apply it? Is worship ordered by Scripture? Is it made of what God has commanded, Scripture read and preached, prayer, singing of psalms, and the sacraments (WCF 21.1, 21.5)? See How God Wants to Be Worshiped . Are there elders who shepherd? Do they know the members, visit them, and exercise loving discipline? How do I join? A faithful church will ask about your faith and your life before receiving you as a member. Expect that, and welcome it.

title: How to Find a Faithful Church
text: Then Join It Visiting is not belonging. Once you have found a faithful church, ask to become a member, put yourself under its elders, and stay. Serve, give, pray for it, and be there every Lord’s Day. If you are not sure where to start, write to me and I will help you look.

title: What the Bible Says About Marriage
text: God made marriage before sin entered the world. What it is, what it pictures, what husbands and wives owe each other, and when it may end.

title: What the Bible Says About Marriage
text: God Made Marriage Marriage was not invented by the church or the state. God made it in the garden, before there was any sin in the world. And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him. Genesis 2:18 (KJV) This was the first thing in creation God called not good. Adam had no sin and walked with God, and still he should not be alone. So God made the woman from the man’s own side and brought her to him. Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh. Genesis 2:24 (KJV) This is history, not a fable. Jesus pointed back to it as something that happened. He which made them at the beginning made them male and female, he said. Then he added, What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder (Matthew 19:4-6). In a wedding it is God who joins. Marriage is to be between one man and one woman: neither is it lawful for any man to have more than one wife, nor for any woman to have more than one husband at the same time. Westminster Confession of Faith 24.1 Some patriarchs and kings took more than one wife, and the grief in the homes of Jacob and David shows what came of it. Of such things Jesus said, from the beginning it was not so (Matthew 19:8). One man and one woman, for as long as they both live, is God’s design. For the same reason, the union of two men or two women is not a marriage, whatever a law may call it. That is taken up with care in What the Bible Says About Homosexuality and Gender . Why God Gave It Marriage was ordained for the mutual help of husband and wife; for the increase of mankind with a legitimate issue, and of the Church with an holy seed; and for preventing of uncleanness. Westminster Confession of Faith 24.2 The first purpose is help. A help meet is a helper fit for him. Help is no small word, for God uses it of himself. He is our help and our shield (Psalm 33:20).
