Parents owe their children love, prayer, teaching, correction, and a life worth following (WLC 129). The commandment runs both ways. Even its promise of long life is given as far as it shall serve for God’s glory and their own good (WLC 133). Some obedient children die young. Hold on to that for the part on Proverbs below. Discipline Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child (Proverbs 22:15), as it is in ours, and a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame (Proverbs 29:15). Eli was judged because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not (1 Samuel 3:13). Correct calmly and consistently, never in a rage and never to shame. Aim at the heart, and end with the child restored and held. The full treatment is in What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline .

title: What the Bible Says About Raising Children
text: Is Proverbs 22:6 a Promise? Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it. Proverbs 22:6 (KJV) Many parents read this verse as a guarantee. Then a son walks away from the faith at nineteen, and the verse becomes an accusation. Either God broke his word, or the parents broke the formula. Neither is true. The way out is to read the verse as the kind of writing it is. Taking the Bible literally means taking each part as it was meant to be taken. A psalm is a song, a law is a law, and a proverb is a proverb. Proverbs are wholly true, because they are God’s Word. But a proverb is a short saying that tells how God has ordered life to go as a rule. It does not stop to list the exceptions. The book of Proverbs shows this itself. Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit. Proverbs 26:4-5 (KJV) Both are true, and no one can follow both at once. Wisdom knows which fits the fool in front of you. Or take the hand of the diligent maketh rich (Proverbs 10:4). That is how life usually goes, and a lazy man should hear it. Yet the same Bible says the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong (Ecclesiastes 9:11). The fear of the Lord prolongeth days (Proverbs 10:27), and yet righteous Abel’s days were cut short by his brother (Genesis 4:8, Matthew 23:35). None of these sayings is false. Each is a general truth of wisdom, and the rest of Scripture shows where it bends. So it is with Proverbs 22:6. It is a real encouragement, and parents should lean on it. God ordinarily uses faithful teaching in the home to bring children to himself, and many wanderers have come home late, carried back by words they heard at their mother’s table. Train your children with hope. But the verse is not a contract that makes a child’s salvation the wage of a parent’s work. It cannot be, because salvation is of the Lord. And Scripture shows it is not. Hezekiah did right though his father Ahaz did not, and his own son Manasseh did evil (2 Kings 16:2, 18:3, 21:2). God himself said, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me (Isaiah 1:2). That was no failure in his fathering. Reading the verse rightly guards against two sins. If your children walk with God, do not take the credit. It was grace, and other parents did as much as you and are weeping tonight. If your child has wandered, do not decide that God has broken his word, and do not carry your child’s sin as your own (Ezekiel 18:20). Confess where you did wrong, and keep praying. When Your Child Walks Away From the Lord is written for you.

title: What the Bible Says About Raising Children
text: The Teen Years The first chapters of Proverbs are mostly a father talking to a son on the edge of manhood. My son, he says, again and again. He warns him about friends who will entice him into violence for quick money (Proverbs 1:10-19), and about the strange woman, whose lips drop as an honeycomb (Proverbs 5:3). That is the Bible’s picture of raising a teenager, long and honest talk about what the world is about to press on him. The aim shifts in these years. You still require obedience while he lives under your roof, but now you are reaching for the heart. My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways (Proverbs 23:26). Obedience without the heart rarely survives the day he leaves. It may comfort you that Mary and Joseph did not understand their son at twelve, and he was without sin. He went home and was subject unto them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart (Luke 2:48-51). Not understanding your teenager for a season is not always a sign that something is wrong. Talking and Listening Be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19). He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him (Proverbs 18:13). If you jump to the lecture the moment your daughter tells you something hard, she will stop telling you. Teens often open up late at night, or side by side in the car. Moses already named those times, when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down. Stay up for it. Phones and Screens A phone with the open internet puts the whole world in a child’s pocket, its foulest parts included. Scripture gives no age for a first phone, and Christian families draw the lines in different places. But David said, I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psalm 101:3). The Larger Catechism counts among the sins of parents careless exposing, or leaving them to wrong, temptation, and danger (WLC 130). An unfiltered phone behind a closed bedroom door is exactly that. Keep screens out of bedrooms at night. Use filters, and tell your children why. Then go first. A father who scrolls through supper cannot tell his son to put the phone down. If your child is already caught in pornography, do not explode. Help him fight it, and read the part on pornography together. Tell your children that if anyone online pressures them for pictures or threatens them, they can come to you without shame. That is a crime against them, and you should report it . Friends He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed. Proverbs 13:20 (KJV) Teenagers become like the friends they keep. Know their friends by name. Open your home and feed them, so your house is where they gather. Do not only forbid bad company. Help them find good. Letting Go The goal is not a child who needs you forever. It is a grown man or woman who fears God when you are not in the room. A man shall leave his father and his mother (Genesis 2:24), and the arrow was made to fly. Hannah brought Samuel to the house of the Lord when the child was young, and said, I have lent him to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:24-28). Every parent must give his children up to God in his own way. Hand over responsibility a little at a time while they are still at home, and move from command toward counsel. When they set up their own homes, the obedience of a child under your roof gives way, but the duty to honor never ends (Mark 7:10-12). You become a counselor, not a ruler. That is not losing them. It is what you were raising them for. Praying for Them Job’s children were grown and keeping their own houses, and still he rose up early in the morning and offered for every one of them. For Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts (Job 1:5). You do not know their hearts either. Pray for each by name every day, for their souls first, and then for their purity and their future homes. Pray as Christ prayed for his own, not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil (John 17:15). Your prayers go where you cannot.

title: What the Bible Says About Raising Children
text: Single Parents, Step-Parents, and Grandparents Single parents. God is a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows (Psalm 68:5). Timothy knew the holy scriptures from a child, taught by his mother and grandmother, and Scripture says only that his father was a Greek (Acts 16:1, 2 Timothy 1:5, 3:15). Ask your church to stand with you, and let godly men and women into your children’s lives. Step-parents. Joseph raised a son who was not his by blood, and Mary still said to Jesus, thy father and I (Luke 2:48). Your authority will grow with trust. At first, let the child’s own parent lead in correction while you win the child’s heart, and never speak against the other parent in his hearing. Grandparents. Children’s children are the crown of old men (Proverbs 17:6). Tell your grandchildren what God has done, as Moses told Israel to teach thy sons, and thy sons’ sons (Deuteronomy 4:9). Pray for them, and stand behind their parents even where you would have done things differently.

title: What the Bible Says About Raising Children
text: Parenting Under a Patient Father Every honest parent knows how often he has failed. There was the angry word at bedtime, and the promise forgotten. You need more than better methods. You need a Father yourself. Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust. Psalm 103:13-14 (KJV) God disciplines his children, but always for their good and with great patience. For they verily for a few days chastened us after their own pleasure; but he for our profit, that we might be partakers of his holiness. Hebrews 12:10 (KJV) After their own pleasure means as seemed best to them. Our fathers did what they thought right, and sometimes they got it wrong. God never does (Hebrews 12:5-11). Because he is that kind of Father to you, you can correct your children as he corrects you, patiently and for their good, never to get even. But how does a sinner become one of God’s children? Not by growing up in a Christian home, and not by trying harder. The Son of God bore the wrath that sinners deserved on the cross, and on the third day he rose from the dead. All who turn from their sin and trust in him are forgiven and adopted, and receive the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father (Romans 8:15). If you are not sure you are his, read the gospel and come to him today. Then let your children see grace at work in you. When you sin against them, say so plainly and ask their forgiveness. Few things teach a child the gospel like a parent who repents. Grace never excuses sin, yours or theirs, but it means your home does not have to run on fear. Your children’s deepest need is not perfect parents. It is the Savior their imperfect parents point to.

title: What the Bible Says About Raising Children
text: What to Do This Week Begin family worship, or begin again. Tonight after supper, read a short passage, sing a psalm, and pray. Ten minutes is enough. Learn one catechism question together. Say it at meals all week. Spend time alone with each child. With a teenager, ask one real question and then listen far more than you talk. Look hard at the screens in your home. Start with your own. Settle a rule, explain it, and keep it yourself first. Confess one sin to your children. If you have been harsh or absent or unfair, tell them so, and ask their forgiveness. Pray for each child by name every morning. Write down what you ask, so in time you can see what God has done. Ask for help. Talk to your elders, or to an older couple whose children are grown. You were never meant to do this alone.

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
text: What the rod in Proverbs means, how to correct a child in love and never in anger, and where discipline ends and abuse begins.

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
section: Why God Commands Parents to Discipline
text: Why God Commands Parents to Discipline God does not leave children to raise themselves. He places them under a father and a mother, and he tells those parents to correct them. That is not because God is harsh. It is because he is a Father himself, and he loves. My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord ; neither be weary of his correction: For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth. Proverbs 3:11-12 (KJV) The Lord ’s correction is a mark of his delight. A father who never corrects is not kind. He has stopped minding where his child is going. So Proverbs says it bluntly. He that spareth his rod hateth his son, but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes (Proverbs 13:24). Betimes means early, while the child is young and the habit is still soft. Hebrews quotes Proverbs 3 to suffering Christians and reasons from the home to heaven. We gave our earthly fathers reverence when they corrected us, so we should much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live (Hebrews 12:9). For they verily for a few days chastened us after their own pleasure; but he for our profit, that we might be partakers of his holiness. Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. Hebrews 12:10-11 (KJV) Earthly fathers corrected after their own pleasure, as seemed best to them, and did not always get it right. God never errs. Hold the rod with that humility. You are a father under the Father, and you will give account to him for how you used the authority he lent you. The Larger Catechism sums up what God requires of everyone set over others, parents first of all. to love, pray for, and bless their inferiors; to instruct, counsel, and admonish them; countenancing, commending, and rewarding such as do well; and discountenancing, reproving, and chastising such as do ill Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 129 Love comes first in that list, and chastising comes near the end. That is the right order. Correction grows out of love, and it is only one part of it.

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
text: The Rod in Proverbs Proverbs speaks of the rod in the correcting of a child in 13:24, 22:15, 23:13-14, and 29:15, and in 29:17 it names the fruit. Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest. Many honest parents struggle to know how much of this to read literally. The question deserves a careful answer. Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him. Proverbs 22:15 (KJV) The rod was real The rod in these verses was a real stick, used to strike. Proverbs lays the same rod on the back of a fool (Proverbs 10:13, 26:3), and the law of Moses speaks of a master striking a servant with one (Exodus 21:20). It is not merely a figure of speech. These proverbs teach that measured physical correction of a child is a right and loving thing. You may not read the rod out of them. The rod also stands for more than itself. The rod and reproof give wisdom (Proverbs 29:15), blows and words together. Foolishness here is not childishness. It is a heart bent on its own way against God and parents. The rod pictures the whole work of correcting that bent, and what it pictures is real. But the picture never empties out the thing. The stick was real, and so is the folly. A proverb, not a rulebook Proverbs are sayings of wisdom. They teach a principle and its normal means, and they trust the reader to apply them with judgment. Answer not a fool according to his folly, the book says, and in the next verse, Answer a fool according to his folly (Proverbs 26:4-5). Both are true, and wisdom knows which fits the hour. So the rod proverbs do not tell you what age to begin or end, what instrument to use, or how many strokes. Anyone who hands you a fixed method and calls it God’s is saying more than God said. Nor are the promises machines. Only the Spirit gives a new heart. A child who has been made to behave is not yet a child who has been born again. He shall not die Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die. Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell. Proverbs 23:13-14 (KJV) In the English of 1611, beat simply means strike, not what we now call a beating. The verse speaks to a parent who holds back out of soft fear, as though a measured stroke would ruin the child. It will not, Solomon says. He is not drawing the line at death, as if anything short of it were allowed. God’s law limited even a guilty man’s punishment to forty stripes, lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee (Deuteronomy 25:3). A master who struck out his servant’s eye or tooth had to set him free (Exodus 21:26-27). If God’s law set bounds for the correction of a criminal and a servant, it sets them far more for a little child. Hell in verse 14 is the Hebrew word for the grave and the world of the dead. Folly left alone leads down to death, and many Reformed teachers add, to eternal ruin. Correction is one of God’s means to turn a child from that road. A spanking does not save a soul. Only Christ saves. Where faithful parents differ Godly Reformed parents who believe all of this still differ in practice. Some use a small rod or a wooden spoon, so that the hand stays for comfort, and others use only an open hand. Some spank often while children are very small. Others keep it for open defiance and use it rarely, or stop by six or seven. Some, for a particular child or under a promise they have made, hardly use it at all. These are matters of wisdom, and no parent should bind another’s conscience where Scripture has not. What none may do is call the rod cruel, when God calls it love, or make it the whole of raising a child, when God never does.

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
text: Discipline Is More Than Spanking And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. Ephesians 6:4 (KJV) Nurture is training, and admonition is warning with words. Most discipline in a godly home happens with no rod in sight. Teaching. Talk of God’s ways when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way (Deuteronomy 6:7). Gather them for family worship and teach them the catechism. Warning. Tell the child plainly what is wrong and what will follow, before it happens. A rule he never knew is a trap, not a rule. Consequences. A lost privilege, an early bed, paying for what was broken. These often teach better than a smack, and as a child grows they take its place. Example. Children learn more from how you handle your own sin than from how you handle theirs. When you wrong them, ask their forgiveness. Praise. The Catechism counts commending such as do well as part of the duty. Catch your children doing right, and tell them.

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
text: The Guardrails Scripture Sets The same catechism that requires parents to chastise also names the sins of those in authority. correcting them unduly; careless exposing, or leaving them to wrong, temptation, and danger; provoking them to wrath Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 130 A parent can sin by never correcting, and a parent can sin by correcting wrongly. Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. James 1:19-20 (KJV) Never in anger. If you are angry, wait. Send the child to his room and go pray. A wise man keepeth it in till afterwards (Proverbs 29:11). If you cannot become calm, do not spank today. A stroke in temper only teaches that the bigger person wins. Never to injure. Correction should sting for a moment and then be over. If it leaves a bruise, a welt, or any mark at all, it has gone too far, whatever you meant. Never on the face or the head. Only on the seat. Never shake a child, never use a fist, and never strike anywhere that can be hurt. Mostly for young children. It fits the years before a child can be fully reasoned with. As he grows, words and consequences take over, and a spanked teenager is usually shamed rather than corrected. Children differ too. A tender child may need only a word. God knoweth our frame (Psalm 103:14), and you should know your child’s. Private, not humiliating. Never in front of brothers, sisters, or friends, and never with mockery. God would not let even a criminal be made vile in his brother’s eyes (Deuteronomy 25:3). For sin, not for childishness. Spilled milk is not rebellion, and a tired toddler is not a fool. It is the glory of a man to pass over a transgression (Proverbs 19:11). Keep the rod for willful defiance, and pass over much else. Explained before, and restored after. Tell the child calmly what he did and why it is wrong. Afterward, hold him, pray with him, and tell him you love him. Then it is finished, and you do not bring it up again. Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged (Colossians 3:21). A child corrected too often, too hard, or without warmth does not grow wise. He loses heart. If your children flinch when you come near, stop and examine yourself before God.

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
text: When Correction Becomes Abuse Abuse is not discipline. Striking in rage, leaving bruises, hitting the face or head, shaking a baby, choking, kicking, using a belt or a cord, threatening, terrifying, or shaming a child is a sin against the sixth commandment, which forbids striking and wounding (Larger Catechism Q&A 136). It is also a crime. To call it biblical discipline is to put God’s name on what God forbids. If you have crossed that line, here is what to do. Stop today. Put the rod away, and do not take it up again unless your elders, knowing everything, agree. For some parents that will mean never. Tell your pastor. Do not soften the story. If you are afraid you will hurt your child, leave the house now. If a child is in danger, call 911 . Let it be reported. Harm to a child must be reported to the police or to child protective services. Do not ask your child, or anyone in the family, to keep quiet. Accept what the law does, for pardon with God does not cancel earthly justice (Romans 13:4). Get help for your anger. Read My anger frightens my family , and do what it says. Christ turns away no one who comes to him in true repentance. But he that doeth truth cometh to the light (John 3:21), and hiding it is not repentance. If you see a child being hurt, in your church or anywhere else, do not wait for someone else to act. Read If a child is being hurt , and report it. And if you were beaten as a child by someone who said God required it, that was not God’s discipline. He saw it, and he does not ask you to call it love. Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him (Psalm 103:13).

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
section: What the Law of the Land Says
text: What the Law of the Land Says Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers (Romans 13:1). Know the law where you live. In most of the United States a parent may still use reasonable physical correction, but what counts as reasonable differs by state, and a mark can bring an investigation. Foster parents are almost always forbidden by their license to spank a child placed with them, and many adoption agencies ask the same promise. If you gave it, keep it, as one that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not (Psalm 15:4). Many of these children have already been hurt by adults, and a stroke may teach them fear rather than wisdom. A number of countries forbid all physical correction of children, Sweden and Scotland among them. If you live under such a law, obey it. Scripture commends the rod as a normal means, but it does not make that one means the only way to keep God’s command to correct your child. Use the others. Do not decide alone that the law may be broken. Take the question to your elders, for in the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Proverbs 11:14).

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
text: Discipline Under the Cross But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. Isaiah 53:5 (KJV) The chastisement of our peace is the punishment that made peace between sinners and God, and it fell on Christ. He bore it in full for his people, and he rose on the third day because the debt was paid. Christ bare our sins in his own body on the tree, by whose stripes ye were healed (1 Peter 2:24). If you do not yet know him, read The Gospel before anything else on this page. So if you are in Christ, God’s discipline of you is never payment for your sin. That was paid once, on the cross. The Confession says God’s adopted children are pitied, protected, provided for, and chastened by him as by a father; yet never cast off Westminster Confession of Faith 12.1 A sinning believer may fall under God’s fatherly displeasure (Westminster Confession 11.5), but it is a Father’s displeasure, not a Judge’s sentence (Romans 8:1). And so you correct your child as one who has been forgiven. You are not making him pay for his sin. No child can pay that debt, and only Christ could. You correct to turn him from folly and to point him to the Savior who bore the stripes. When it is over, tell him of Christ. A parent who remembers how much he has been forgiven will not correct with contempt. Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you (Ephesians 4:32).

title: What the Bible Says About Spanking and Discipline
text: What to Do This Week Settle your own heart first. Read Hebrews 12:5-11 and Psalm 103:8-14. Ask God to make you toward your children what he is toward you, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. Agree with your husband or wife. Write a few plain house rules and what follows when each is broken. Then, in a calm hour, explain them to the children. Make a rule for yourself. If you are angry, you will not spank. You will wait, and pray, and come back when you are quiet. Spend time with each child that has nothing to do with correction. Correction from a parent who delights in a child lands very differently. Ask for counsel. Talk with your elders, and with an older couple whose grown children walk with the Lord. If you have gone too far, stop and tell your pastor today. See When Correction Becomes Abuse . Pray for their souls by name. Ask God to give each child a new heart. Your rod can restrain folly for a season, but only Christ can make a child his own. The King your children most need to know is the one who shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom (Isaiah 40:11). Correct them in such a way that they can believe it.

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
text: The unborn child bears the image of God. What Scripture says, the hard cases, help for a mother who is afraid, and mercy for the guilty.

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
section: What God Says About the Unborn
text: What God Says About the Unborn Every human being bears the image of God, and that is why taking an innocent life is so great a wrong. Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man. Genesis 9:6 (KJV) The only question, then, is whether the child in the womb is a man in that sense, a human being. Scripture speaks of him that way again and again. For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother’s womb. I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well. Psalm 139:13-14 (KJV) Psalm 139 is poetry. Covered pictures God knitting a body together, and the reins are the inward parts. But the person in the picture is real. David does not say God made some tissue that later became David. He says God covered me. The one praising God in the psalm is the same one who was in the womb. Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations. Jeremiah 1:5 (KJV) God set Jeremiah apart for his work before he was born. Sanctified here means set apart. God deals with the unborn as persons with names and callings. When Mary came to her cousin Elisabeth, the babe leaped in Elisabeth’s womb for joy (Luke 1:41, 44). Luke uses the same Greek word for that unborn John that he uses for the newborn Jesus lying in the manger (Luke 2:12) and for the infants brought to Jesus (Luke 18:15). To the Holy Spirit, a baby is a baby, inside the womb or out. Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me. Psalm 51:5 (KJV) David traces his own sin back to his conception. Only a person can be a sinner. So Scripture counts a human being as one of Adam’s fallen race from the very start. The law of Moses guarded the unborn too. If men fought and struck a woman with child, so that her fruit departed, and no harm followed, the man paid a fine. But if harm followed, then thou shalt give life for life (Exodus 21:22-23). The words for her fruit departing are the plain Hebrew words for children going out, which is how the Bible speaks of birth. Many Reformed teachers read it as a child born early. If mother and child were unharmed, a fine was paid. If either one was harmed or killed, the same justice applied as for any other person. Some read the passage another way, but no reading of it makes the child nothing.

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
section: The Son of God in the Womb
text: The Son of God in the Womb The strongest word on this is the incarnation itself. The eternal Son of God did not come into the world as a grown man. He was conceived. And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS. Luke 1:31 (KJV) The Shorter Catechism says Christ became man by taking to himself a true body and a reasonable soul, being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the Virgin Mary (WSC 22). From that moment he was God and man in one person. He passed through every stage of life that we pass through, from the womb on, so that he could redeem people at every stage of it. Christ has been a child in the womb. Every unborn child is that small and that hidden, and none of them is beneath his notice.

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
text: What People Say It is only a clump of cells. So are you, and so am I. From conception the child is a living human being with his own body and his own genetic code, distinct from his mother. He is growing as fast as he ever will. Size, development, and where he lives do not decide whether he is human. A newborn is smaller and weaker than a toddler, and no one thinks he matters less. It is my body. The child lives in his mother’s body but is not part of it. He often has a different blood type, and half of what he is came from his father. And Scripture says something deeper. Ye are not your own, for ye are bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). No one owns his body in a way that gives him the right to end someone else’s life. The child cannot live outside the womb yet. Needing someone to survive does not make anyone less of a person. A newborn cannot live a day without care. Neither can a man on a ventilator. God puts the weak in our care so that we will protect them, not so that we may decide whether they live. It would be cruel to bring a child into poverty or a hard home. A hard life is still a life, and the answer to a hard situation is help, not death. That is where the church is meant to stand (James 1:27). Many children born into hard places have grown up to know Christ. The child will be disabled. And the Lord said unto him, Who hath made man’s mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the Lord ? (Exodus 4:11). A child with a disability bears God’s image as fully as any other. Jesus said of a man born blind that his blindness was so the works of God should be made manifest in him (John 9:3). Christians should not push their morality on others. Every law pushes someone’s morality on someone. The only question is whose. God gave rulers the sword to punish evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:3-4). Protecting the weakest people in a land is one of the plainest things a ruler is for.

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
text: The Hardest Cases These are real, and the people in them deserve patience, not slogans. When a child is conceived by rape. Rape is a monstrous evil, and the woman bears no guilt for it. Under the law of Moses, a man who forced a betrothed woman was put to death, and the woman was counted innocent (Deuteronomy 22:25-26). But the child did not commit that crime. The law says every man shall be put to death for his own sin, and not children for their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). Ending the child’s life does not undo the first wrong. It adds a second victim. A woman in this place needs her church to surround her, to carry her and her child, and to see that justice is sought against the man. If she cannot raise the child, adoption is a good and loving choice. When the mother’s life is in danger. Sometimes, as in an ectopic pregnancy, a child grows where he cannot survive, and if nothing is done both mother and child will die. Treating the mother to save the one life that can be saved is not the same as abortion. The aim is to save life, and the child’s death is grieved, not sought. Such cases are rare, and modern medicine can often save both. When you face one, take it to your elders and to a doctor who honors life, and decide it before God with care. When the baby has already died. A doctor’s care to remove a baby who has already died is not an abortion. It is care for the mother after a death. If that is your sorrow, read If your baby died before birth .

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
section: If You Are Pregnant and Afraid
text: If You Are Pregnant and Afraid Maybe you did not plan this. Maybe you are young, or alone, or out of money, or someone is telling you that this child will ruin everything. The fear is real, and God sees it. Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord : and the fruit of the womb is his reward. Psalm 127:3 (KJV) However this child came, God calls him a gift, and he does not give gifts and then walk away from the one who receives them. You do not have to see the whole road tonight. You only have to keep from the one step that cannot be taken back. Tell someone who will help. Call your pastor or a Christian friend today. If you have no church, the people at Option Line, 1-800-712-4357 , answer at any hour and can put you in touch with a free pregnancy help center near you. Many of those centers give free ultrasounds, baby supplies, and help with housing and work. Do not let anyone rush you. If someone is pressuring you, threatening you, or hurting you, get safe first . No one has the right to force this choice on you. Remember adoption. If you cannot raise this child, there are families waiting and praying for one. Giving your child life and a home is an act of love, not of failure. Pray. Tell God plainly that you are afraid. Casting all your care upon him, for he careth for you (1 Peter 5:7).

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
section: If You Have Had an Abortion
text: If You Have Had an Abortion Maybe it was years ago, and you have never told anyone. Maybe you were the father who drove her there, or the parent who insisted, or the one who paid for it. Maybe you worked in a clinic. The guilt you feel is not your imagination, and this page will not tell you it was nothing. A child died, and that is why you need a Savior and not just a reassurance. But hear this as clearly as you have ever heard anything. Your sin is not beyond the blood of Christ. As there is no sin so small but it deserves damnation, so there is no sin so great that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent. Westminster Confession of Faith 15.4 King David took a man’s wife and then had the man killed. When the prophet showed him his sin, he did not excuse it, and God did not destroy him. Psalm 51 is the prayer he prayed afterward. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness. Psalm 51:14 (KJV) Bloodguiltiness is the guilt of having blood on your hands. That is the prayer for you. The apostle Paul once voted for Christians to be put to death (Acts 26:10), and he later wrote that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom he counted himself the chief (1 Timothy 1:15). If Christ saved the chief, he can save you. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord : though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool. Isaiah 1:18 (KJV) Christ bore the wrath of God for every sin of everyone who trusts in him, this one included. He rose from the dead, and he says, Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out (John 6:37). Come to him as you are. Confess the sin by name, and do not dress it up. Then believe what he says, that he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). If you are already in Christ and this was before you knew him, or even after, it is not hanging over you. There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). You may still grieve your child, and you should. Forgiven grief is different from guilty grief. It weeps, but it does not hide from God. Tell your pastor. Many churches have women and men who have walked this same road and found mercy. You were never meant to carry this in secret. If the old guilt keeps coming back after you have confessed it, read What I did is too great to forgive .

title: What the Bible Says About Abortion
text: What Christians Should Do The Larger Catechism says the sixth commandment requires all lawful efforts to preserve the life of ourselves and others, and to protect and defend the innocent (WLC 135). Opposing abortion is not a hobby for a few believers. It is part of keeping the law of God. Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Proverbs 31:8 (KJV) Pray. Pray for mothers in fear, for fathers who have walked away, for the unborn, for those who work in abortion clinics, and for rulers. Pray that God would turn hearts. Speak the truth. Say plainly that the unborn child is a person and that abortion takes his life. Say it with tears, not with contempt, and never without the gospel. Help mothers. Give money, time, diapers, meals, a spare room. Support a pregnancy help center. A church that says no to abortion must say yes to the mother and her child. Consider adoption and foster care. God set the solitary in families (Psalm 68:6). Christians have been taking in unwanted children since the earliest days of the church. Vote and call on rulers to protect life. Laws do not change hearts, but they do restrain evil and protect the weak, which is what God gave them for. Welcome the guilty. There are people in your church who have had abortions. Let them hear from your mouth that Christ forgives, so that they never have to wonder whether there is room for them at his table.

title: What the Bible Says About Work
text: God gave work before the fall. Working as to the Lord, a hard boss, laziness and overwork, providing for a family, and resting in Christ.

title: What the Bible Says About Work
section: Work Before the Fall and After It
text: Work Before the Fall and After It Work is not part of the curse. God himself worked six days and rested the seventh (Genesis 2:2). Then, before there was any sin in the world, he gave the man a job. And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it. Genesis 2:15 (KJV) This was a real garden, and Adam was to tend it and guard it. To make, keep, and mend things is part of bearing the image of the God who works (John 5:17). Then Adam sinned, and God spoke to him about his work. And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field; In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return. Genesis 3:17-19 (KJV) The thorns were real thorns in a real field, but the curse reaches past farming. The creature, meaning the whole creation, was made subject to vanity (Romans 8:20). That is why the floor you mopped is tracked with mud an hour later, why the part you fixed breaks again, and why the body that does the work wears out and returns to the ground (Genesis 3:19). The curse did not make work evil. It made work hard, and every ache after a long shift points to the One who was made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

title: What the Bible Says About Work
section: The Carpenter and Every Lawful Calling
text: The Carpenter and Every Lawful Calling When Jesus taught in the synagogue at Nazareth, his neighbors could not get past what he used to do for a living. Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us? And they were offended at him. Mark 6:3 (KJV) The eternal Son of God spent most of his years on earth working with his hands. No one wrote down a single job he did, and those years were not wasted. When they ended, the Father said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Matthew 3:17). And on the night before he died, he took a towel, and girded himself, and washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:4-5). That was a slave’s work, and no one who scrubs, hauls, or cleans up after others is doing work beneath the Son of God. Some work is seen and some is not. Think of those who clean the halls after the building empties, haul out the trash, and fix the broken door before anyone comes. Done well, it goes unnoticed. People notice only when it is not done. God notices. He is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love (Hebrews 6:10). The psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness (Psalm 84:10). Keeping a door was humble work, and he counted it an honor. Before the Reformation, many spoke as if priests, monks, and nuns had a calling from God and everyone else merely had jobs. The Reformers taught from Scripture that every lawful calling is service to God. Calvin likened each man’s calling to a post the Lord has set him to keep, and said no task is so lowly that it will not shine before God when done in obedience to that calling (Institutes 3.10.6). Paul said, Let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God (1 Corinthians 7:24). That does not forbid changing work, for Paul told a slave who could gain his freedom to take it (7:21). It means you serve God where you are. Whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ. Colossians 3:23-24 (KJV) Those words were first written to slaves. If they could serve the Lord Christ, so can a janitor, a nurse, or a mother at home. The Larger Catechism says the eighth commandment requires a lawful calling, and diligence in it (WLC 141), and forbids unlawful callings (WLC 142). Work that is itself sin cannot be done to God’s glory. All other honest work can.

title: What the Bible Says About Work
section: Servants and Masters, Workers and Bosses
text: Servants and Masters, Workers and Bosses Paul wrote to servants and masters in a world full of slavery, and we should be honest about it. Scripture’s words to slaves are not approval of man-stealing, which it condemns. God’s law put to death the man who stole a man and sold him (Exodus 21:16), and Paul lists menstealers beside murderers (1 Timothy 1:9-10). The trade that seized men and women in Africa and sold them in America was man-stealing, and God’s Word stands against it. Most of us are not slaves. We agreed to our work, we are paid for it, and we may leave it. So these words bind us with more force, not less. Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ; Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart; With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men: Ephesians 6:5-7 (KJV) Eyeservice is working hard only while the boss is watching. Singleness of heart is being the same worker when no one is. A Christian employee does his job as if Christ were his supervisor, because he is. Such faithfulness adorns the doctrine of God our Saviour (Titus 2:10). Bosses are not let off. Paul tells masters to do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening, knowing that your Master also is in heaven (Ephesians 6:9). Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven. Colossians 4:1 (KJV) The Larger Catechism places employers under the fifth commandment (WLC 124). They are to care for those under them, and not seek their own ease and profit at their workers’ cost (WLC 129-130). God’s law told employers to pay the hired man before nightfall (Deuteronomy 24:15), and James warns that wages kept back by fraud cry out to the Lord of sabaoth (James 5:4). When the Boss Is Hard Peter wrote to servants who worked for harsh men. Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward. For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully. 1 Peter 2:18-19 (KJV) Froward means crooked and hard to deal with. Peter points you to Christ, who suffered for us, leaving us an example (1 Peter 2:21). When he was reviled, he reviled not again, and he committed himself to him that judgeth righteously (2:23). He did not call the wrong right. He handed it to his Father. So work well under a hard boss, and leave the reckoning to God. But patience is not doing wrong when told to. You owe willing obedience to lawful commands (WLC 127). If you are told to lie, cheat, or cover up a crime, answer as the apostles did, We ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). You may report wrongdoing, seek what you are owed, and look for other work. If you are being threatened or hurt, get safe first , and tell your elders.

title: What the Bible Says About Work
section: Diligence, Honesty, and Providing for Your Own
text: Diligence, Honesty, and Providing for Your Own Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest. Proverbs 6:6-8 (KJV) Solomon means a real ant. No one stands over her, and the work still gets done. The sluggard always means to start after a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands, and poverty comes on him like an armed man (Proverbs 6:10-11). Paul told the idle in Thessalonica, If any would not work, neither should he eat, and commanded them to work quietly and eat their own bread (2 Thessalonians 3:10-12). Notice would not. That word is for the unwilling, not the unable. Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth. Ephesians 4:28 (KJV) Thou shalt not steal is also a command to labor (see the commandments in plain words ). The Larger Catechism says it requires truth, faithfulness, and justice in our dealings, and paying back what we have wrongly kept. It forbids fraud, unfaithfulness in matters of trust, and idleness (WLC 141-142). At work that means honest hours, leaving the company’s supplies where they belong, and not calling in sick when you are well. But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. 1 Timothy 5:8 (KJV) Paul wrote this about caring for widowed mothers, and it reaches every household duty. It does not demand a large wage. It demands what you honestly can. A modest paycheck faithfully earned and brought home is a holy thing.

title: What the Bible Says About Work
text: When Work Becomes an Idol Work can become a god, and so can the money it brings. Jesus said, Ye cannot serve God and mammon (Matthew 6:24). Mammon is wealth, pictured as a master that wants your whole heart. Then Jesus turns straight to anxiety, because worry is one way mammon rules us. Your Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, and you are worth more than they (Matthew 6:26-30). Take therefore no thought for the morrow (Matthew 6:34). It forbids anxious worry, not planning. Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain. It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep. Psalm 127:1-2 (KJV) The psalm does not tell the builders and the watchman to stop working. It tells them the outcome is in God’s hand. The man who works past midnight because everything depends on him is eating the bread of sorrows. Going to bed can be an act of trust. Ecclesiastes sees the worker whose heart taketh not rest in the night, and calls such toil vanity (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Yet it also says a man should make his soul enjoy good in his labour, for that is from the hand of God (2:24). God also built rest into the week. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work (Exodus 20:9), and the seventh is his, for the servant as well as the master. Since Christ rose, that day is the Lord’s Day. Laying your work down for a whole day confesses that God, not your job, holds your life. Read How to Keep the Lord’s Day .

title: What the Bible Says About Work
text: When You Cannot Work Maybe you were laid off, or your body has given out, or a disability keeps you from the work others do. Maybe you are old, and your work has gone to someone younger. It can feel as if you no longer count. Your worth was never in what you produced. You bear God’s image whether you work or not. Paul’s word about the man who will not work does not touch the man who cannot. For him the church is told to support the weak (1 Thessalonians 5:14), and Paul worked with his own hands to do just that (Acts 20:35). Receiving that help is not shameful. It is Christ’s body doing what he made it to do. If you have lost your job, read My work or my home is gone . If illness has gone on for years, read When it has gone on for years . To the old, God says, Even to hoar hairs will I carry you (Isaiah 46:4). Of the righteous the psalm says, They shall still bring forth fruit in old age (Psalm 92:12-14). The tree is a picture, and the fruit it pictures is real. Prayer, counsel, and telling the next generation of God’s strength (Psalm 71:18) are work too. So is bearing weakness without bitterness. His strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). If losing your work has made you think others would be better off without you, that thought is a lie. Call 988 or text 988 , and tell someone near you today.

title: What the Bible Says About Work
text: Christ’s Finished Work and Ours Here is the most important thing to say about work. It cannot save you. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. Ephesians 2:8-10 (KJV) Christ kept the law we broke, and he bore the curse we earned. On the cross he said, It is finished (John 19:30), and on the third day he rose. There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God (Hebrews 4:9). He that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his (Hebrews 4:10). The believer has stopped working to be saved. If you have been trying to earn God’s favor by being a good worker, stop. Turn from your sin and trust the work Christ finished. If you do not know him yet, read the gospel . Then you will work gladly. A saved man does not work to be accepted. He works because he has been accepted, and God receives his weak work for Christ’s sake. Yet notwithstanding, the persons of believers being accepted through Christ, their good works also are accepted in him, not as though they were in this life wholly unblamable and unreprovable in God’s sight; but that he, looking upon them in his Son, is pleased to accept and reward that which is sincere, although accompanied with many weaknesses and imperfections. Westminster Confession of Faith 16.6 That takes in a floor mopped well for Christ’s sake and a meal made for tired children. Your labour is not in vain in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15:58). Scripture tells us a little of what lies ahead, and we should not say more than it says. Those who die in the Lord rest from their labours, and their works do follow them (Revelation 14:13). In the city to come there shall be no more curse, and his servants shall serve him (Revelation 22:3). Isaiah speaks of new heavens and a new earth where God’s people shall not labour in vain (Isaiah 65:17, 23), and faithful Reformed teachers read that prophecy in more than one way. So hold any picture of work in glory loosely. What is sure is that the curse which made work bitter will be gone.

title: What the Bible Says About Work
text: What to Do This Week Give your work to God each morning. Pray Moses’ prayer, Establish thou the work of our hands upon us (Psalm 90:17). Do the unseen part well. Pick one thing no one will check, and do it as to the Lord. Set right what is crooked. If you have padded hours or taken what was not yours, confess it to God, and pay it back where you can (WLC 141). If you are over others, check your wages and your words. Pay what is just, and pay it on time. Speak without threats. Honor plain work. Thank the person who cleans your church or your child’s school. Lay the work down on the Lord’s Day. Finish what you can on Saturday, then trust God with what is left. Give from what you earn. Set something aside for the church and for someone in need (Ephesians 4:28). If someone in your church is out of work, tell the deacons and help.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: God owns it all. Contentment, giving, the tithe, borrowing and debt, cosigning, saving, taxes, and help when debt has you under.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: The Earth Is the Lord’s First ask whose money it is. The earth is the Lord ’s, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. Psalm 24:1 (KJV) God says it again through Haggai, The silver is mine, and the gold is mine (Haggai 2:8). That takes in the paycheck, the truck, and the change in the jar. So we are not owners. We are stewards, managing what belongs to another, and one day we will give an account. Jesus said, He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10). Then he called money the unrighteous mammon, and that which is another man’s (16:11-12). Mammon is money and worldly goods, and it is lent to us. That is good news for a family with little. God measures faithfulness not by the size of the account but by what you do with what is in it. Forty dollars handled honestly before him is not a small thing.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
section: Contentment and the Love of Money
text: Contentment and the Love of Money But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out. And having food and raiment let us be therewith content. But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. 1 Timothy 6:6-10 (KJV) Paul does not say money is the root of all evil. He says the love of it is a root from which every kind of evil grows. They that will be rich means those who want to be, and a man can love money with almost none of it. It shows in envy and in the lottery ticket. The snare is a hunter’s trap, and the ruin it pictures is real. Jesus said, Take heed, and beware of covetousness (Luke 12:15). Then he told of a rich man who planned bigger barns and said to his soul, take thine ease. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee (Luke 12:19-20). The man in the story is made up, but that night is real, and it comes for each of us. So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God (12:21). Paul knew hunger, and he wrote, I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content (Philippians 4:11). It had to be learned. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me (4:13) was written about that very lesson. It is not a promise of a raise. It is a promise of strength to live without one. Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. Hebrews 13:5 (KJV) Conversation means your whole way of life. The ground of contentment is not your budget but God’s promise. Paul also charged the rich to trust not in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy, and to be ready to distribute (1 Timothy 6:17-19). If you have a warm house and food in the cupboard, do not be quick to think that charge is only for someone else. The Prosperity Gospel Some preachers teach that God wants every believer rich and healthy, and that enough faith, or a large gift to their ministry, will unlock it. Paul warned of men supposing that gain is godliness (1 Timothy 6:5). That teaching crushes the poor saint by telling him his want proves weak faith. Yet Christ was poor. It is not a different emphasis but another gospel. See Where Heresy Shows Up .

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Honoring God With Your Substance Honour the Lord with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: Proverbs 3:9 (KJV) The firstfruits were the first of the harvest, brought to God before the farmer knew how the rest would turn out. Faithful giving still has that shape. It comes off the top, not out of what is left. The best picture of giving comes from the poor churches of Macedonia, whose deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality (2 Corinthians 8:2). They first gave their own selves to the Lord (8:5), and the money followed. Then Paul gives the root of all giving. For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. 2 Corinthians 8:9 (KJV) The Son of God left heaven’s glory, was laid in a manger, and gave himself on the cross. We do not give to earn his love. We give because we have it. So give regularly and in proportion. Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give gladly, for God loveth a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). And give in trust. He which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully (9:6). Sowing is a picture of seed thrown into the dirt in hope. The harvest is real, though not always paid in money, for God is able to make all grace abound toward you (9:8). If your gift seems too small, remember the widow and her two mites. Jesus said she gave more than all the rich, for she gave of her want (Mark 12:41-44). Does the Tithe Still Bind? Faithful Reformed teachers differ here. Some hold that the tithe, a tenth, binds Christians still. Abraham gave tithes long before Moses (Genesis 14:20), and Jesus told the Pharisees not to leave it undone (Matthew 23:23). Others answer that the tithe supported Israel’s Levites and temple, which Christ fulfilled, and that the New Testament names no percentage. Both sides agree on far more. Giving should be regular, generous, proportionate, and first. The church that feeds you with the Word should be supported by you (Galatians 6:6). Many who do not hold it binding still start with a tenth, as a floor and not a ceiling. If a tenth feels impossible right now, do not give nothing. Set an amount, give it first, and ask God to grow it.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Borrowing and Debt The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. Proverbs 22:7 (KJV) When you owe, part of next month’s paycheck is spent before you earn it. Debt promises freedom and delivers a kind of servitude. Scripture is just as plain about failing to pay. The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again (Psalm 37:21). A debt is a promise, and a Christian keeps it even when it costs him. Owe No Man Any Thing Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law. Romans 13:8 (KJV) Some read this as a ban on every loan. Many Reformed teachers read it with the verse before, Render therefore to all their dues (13:7), as a command to pay what is due when it is due and not to stay in debt. The same Bible that warns about debt regulates lending. God forbade charging interest to a poor brother (Exodus 22:25), and Jesus said, from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away (Matthew 5:42). He would not command his people to lend if every loan were sin. Other faithful Christians hold that a believer should avoid borrowing almost entirely, and they deserve respect. Both agree that debt is dangerous, that a promised payment must be made, and that the one debt never paid off is love. Cards, Payday Loans, and Car Notes Credit cards. A card paid in full every month is a tool. A balance carried over grows while you sleep. If you cannot stop carrying one, cut the card up. Payday and title loans. The Larger Catechism names usury and extortion as sins (WLC 142). Calvin and many after him allowed fair interest in trade, but lending that preys on the desperate is what Scripture condemns. Go to your deacons first. Buy now, pay later. Several small payments at once can quietly eat a paycheck. If you could not buy it today, ask whether you should buy it at all. Car loans. A working man needs a car that runs. A plain used car you can afford beats a new one you will pay on for years. Cosigning The old word for cosigning is surety, promising to pay another man’s debt if he does not. Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts. If thou hast nothing to pay, why should he take away thy bed from under thee? (Proverbs 22:26-27). If you have already done it, Solomon says to go humbly and press the man to release you. Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids (Proverbs 6:3-4). He pictures a roe and a bird slipping out of a trap (6:5), and the trap is real. When a son or friend needs help, it is often kinder to give what you can afford to lose than to sign for what you cannot (WLC 141).

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Thou Shalt Not Steal The eighth commandment reaches much further than shoplifting. The eighth commandment requireth the lawful procuring and furthering the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 74 The Larger Catechism fills it out (WLC 141-142). It requires honest dealing, paying each his due, restoring what we wrongly kept, and giving and lending freely as we are able. It requires a lawful calling worked hard, careful provision, and frugality. It forbids theft, fraud, extortion, and usury, and also covetousness, anxious care, envy, idleness, waste, and wasteful gaming (see What the Bible Says About Gambling ). It even forbids robbing yourself and your family of the right use and comfort of what God gave. No one keeps that list. It should send us all to Christ. Working and Saving God’s first plan for a family’s needs is work. If any provide not for his own, he hath denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). A modest wage faithfully earned is a holy thing. See Diligence, Honesty, and Providing for Your Own . Solomon sends the sluggard to the ant, who gathers her food in the harvest (Proverbs 6:6-8). There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man spendeth it up (Proverbs 21:20). Jesus asked which man would build a tower without first sitting down to count the cost (Luke 14:28). A budget is just counting the cost. Yet the rich fool saved too. Saving for the broken water heater or the lean months is faithfulness. Saving so that you will never need to trust God is hoarding. Plan, and then sleep. Paying Taxes Taxes are part of what is due. For for this cause pay ye tribute also, Paul wrote, for they are God’s ministers (Romans 13:6). He wrote under Nero. Jesus said, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s (Matthew 22:21). That holds when taxes are high and rulers waste them (WCF 23.4). It means an honest return, cash jobs included. Do not cheat. See What the Bible Says About Government . Remembering the Poor He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord ; and that which he hath given will he pay him again. Proverbs 19:17 (KJV) Here is a loan Scripture urges on you, and it is made to God. The apostles asked Paul for one thing, that we should remember the poor (Galatians 2:10). John asks, whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? (1 John 3:17). Bowels was the old word for the deep inward feelings. Christ gave his church an office for this work. When widows were neglected, the church chose seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, to see to it (Acts 6:1-3). Reformed churches see the deacon’s office there. Give to the deacons’ fund, tell them when you see a need, and if the need is yours, let them help. Saints are bound to relieve each other in outward things, according to their several abilities and necessities (WCF 26.2).

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: When Debt Has You Under Maybe the bills are stacked on the counter unopened, and you have hidden them from your husband or wife, or from your church, because the shame is heavy. Maybe it is your own fault, or partly, or it came through sickness or a layoff. Hear this. Your worth is not your credit score, and God has not turned his face away. Scripture tells of a widow whose husband had feared the Lord and still left debts. The creditor was coming to take her two sons as bondmen. God filled her empty vessels with oil, and Elisha told her, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest (2 Kings 4:1-7). That happened. God did not shame her. He provided so that she could pay. He may not fill your jars that way, but his ordinary way of helping is through his people. Tell the truth. If you are married, tell your spouse all of it, if it is safe to. Then tell your deacons. Stop digging. No new debt, even if it means hard cuts for a season. Write it all down. Every debt, its amount, rate, and due date. Talk to those you owe. Many will work out a plan with an honest debtor. Beware anyone who promises to make debt vanish for a fee. Pay something, faithfully. A small payment kept every month is the righteous man of Psalm 37 at work. If you are weighing bankruptcy, do not decide it alone. Talk with your elders. The law may release a debt that love would still move you to repay if God later prospers you. If some of this is sin, the overspending, the hiding, the envy, confess it plainly. Jesus taught us to pray, forgive us our debts (Matthew 6:12). Debt there is a picture of sin, and the debt it pictures is real and far larger than any bill. Christ paid it, blotting out the handwriting that was against us, nailing it to his cross (Colossians 2:14). If he paid the debt you never could, he will not leave you alone with the one you can.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Christ Our Treasure Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. Matthew 6:19-21 (KJV) Moths in the closet and rust on the truck are real, and everything you can hold will wear out or be taken. Treasure in heaven is just as real, and nothing touches it. The true treasure is Christ himself. He was sold for thirty pieces of silver, and he died under God’s wrath for sinners who loved money more than God. On the third day he rose. Now he offers himself freely. He that hath no money, come ye, buy, and eat (Isaiah 55:1). If you have loved money, or feared its lack more than you trusted God, turn from that and trust Christ alone. If you do not know him yet, read the gospel . Whoever has him is rich, whatever the bank says.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: What to Do This Week Give thanks. Name ten things God has given you, starting with the plain ones. Count the cost. With your spouse if you are married, write what comes in and goes out this month, and pray over it. Set your giving first. Decide what you will give on the Lord’s Day, and set it aside before anything else is paid. Start a small reserve. Put by a few dollars a week for the breakdown you know will come. Make things right. If you owe money you have been avoiding, or kept what is not yours, begin to pay it back (WLC 141). Remember the poor. Give to your deacons’ fund, or meet one need you know of. Pray for daily bread. Ask for a competent portion, enough, as God’s fatherly wisdom sees best (WLC 193). Then rest. He hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: No verse says thou shalt not gamble. What the commandments do say, about lotteries, betting apps, lots, and the way out.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: Where Scripture Speaks and Where It Is Silent
text: Where Scripture Speaks and Where It Is Silent We should be honest from the start. No verse in the Bible says, Thou shalt not gamble. Anyone who tells you otherwise is saying more than God said. But Scripture is not silent about money, about the heart that craves it, or about the neighbor whose loss becomes our gain. The Confession says the whole counsel of God is either expressly set down in Scripture or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from it (WCF 1.6). So we answer this question the way we answer most questions of daily life. We ask what the commandments require and forbid, and we apply them with care. The Larger Catechism did exactly that. In its long list of sins against the eighth commandment, Thou shalt not steal, it names gaming among them. covetousness; inordinate prizing and affecting worldly goods; distrustful and distracting cares and studies in getting, keeping, and using them; envying at the prosperity of others; as likewise idleness, prodigality, wasteful gaming; and all other ways whereby we do unduly prejudice our own outward estate, and defrauding ourselves of the due use and comfort of that estate which God hath given us. Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 142 Notice the word wasteful. The Catechism does not say every game is a sin. It sets wasteful gaming beside idleness and prodigality, which means throwing money away, and it counts them as ways of robbing ourselves and our households of what God gave us. That is a theft too, even if no one else’s wallet is touched. For the whole commandment in plain words, see the Ten Commandments .

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: The Heart That Hastes to Be Rich
text: The Heart That Hastes to Be Rich The tenth commandment goes beneath our hands to our desires. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s. Exodus 20:17 (KJV) Gambling feeds on the wish to have much without waiting and without working. Solomon warned against that wish. A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent. Proverbs 28:20 (KJV) He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him (Proverbs 28:22). Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished, but he that gathereth by labour shall increase (Proverbs 13:11). Vanity there means emptiness, gain that comes from nothing. God’s way is slower, and it runs through labor. But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. 1 Timothy 6:9-10 (KJV) A snare is a hunter’s trap, set with bait. The picture is a figure, and the trap it pictures is real. Men are drowned by it, and their families with them. What Is in Your Hand Is God’s The earth is the Lord ’s, and the fulness thereof (Psalm 24:1). Your paycheck is his, and you hold it as a steward, and it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2). He gives it to feed your family, to pay what you owe, and to give to him that needeth (Ephesians 4:28). Staking it on a roll or a game hands what belongs to him over to chance. For more, read What the Bible Says About Money and Debt . Gain From Your Neighbor’s Loss God’s law knows a few honest ways for goods to pass from one man to another. You may work for them, trade something of worth for them, or receive them as a gift. Gambling is none of these. The winner does no work and gives nothing in exchange. In a lottery, the prize is simply the other players’ losses gathered up. It comes to him only because others lost, and he wanted them to. Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. Romans 13:10 (KJV) To hope another man loses his rent so that you can have it is not love, even if he played freely. The Catechism asks us to further the wealth and outward estate of others, as well as our own (WLC 141). Gambling turns that upside down.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: Lotteries, Apps, and the House Most gambling today is not a game between friends. It is a business. Every casino, lottery, and betting site sets its odds so that, over time, the players as a whole lose more than they win. That is not bad luck. It is the design. Look at who buys lottery tickets, and anyone can see it. The lottery draws hardest on those who have the least, because it sells the hope of a way out to people who feel they have none. A government that lives off that hope is feeding on its weakest citizens. Rob not the poor, because he is poor (Proverbs 22:22). He that oppresseth the poor to increase his riches shall surely come to want (Proverbs 22:16). Sports betting apps and online casinos never close. They live in your pocket. They offer free bets to start, so you learn the habit before you spend your own money. They make losing feel like nearly winning. They send offers during the game and at midnight. They are not built to entertain you. They are built to keep you.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: Lots, Raffles, and Friendly Bets Casting Lots in Scripture Some say the Bible approves of gambling because God’s people cast lots. But look at what they were doing. The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord . Proverbs 16:33 (KJV) The lot was a way of asking God to decide what men could not settle. When the apostles needed a man to take Judas’s place, they prayed, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen, and the lot fell upon Matthias (Acts 1:24-26). Even the heathen sailors in Jonah’s ship cast lots to learn who had brought the storm (Jonah 1:7). No one staked money. They were seeking an answer, not a prize, so the lot is no defense of gambling. Scripture does show one group casting lots for gain. At the foot of the cross the soldiers gambled for the coat of the dying Christ (John 19:23-24). They wanted a prize. He was giving his life. The Larger Catechism says lots are to be used holily and reverently, and it lists sinful lots among the sins of the third commandment (WLC 112-113). Some Puritans warned that to play at lots is to treat God’s providence lightly. Others, such as Thomas Gataker, who later sat in the Westminster Assembly, held that a lot used in play is no such appeal to God. Faithful men differed on that point. Small Bets and Raffles What about a dollar bet with a friend on a ballgame, or a raffle ticket at a school fundraiser? Here we must not invent rules that God has not given. Rolling dice in a board game where nothing changes hands is not gambling at all. Beyond that, faithful Christians differ. Some will stake nothing, however small, because they see the same root in a dollar as in a thousand. Others think a friendly wager, with no one hurt and nothing coveted, is not the wasteful gaming the Catechism means. Some churches will not hold raffles, wanting gifts to be given freely and not bought with a chance to win. Others see a raffle as a gift with a small token attached. Where Scripture is not plain, ask honest questions before God. Am I hoping to get something for nothing? Would I be glad to see my friend lose? Could this be a first step for someone weaker, or for me? Whatsoever is not of faith is sin (Romans 14:23). Paul said, All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any (1 Corinthians 6:12). If even a small bet stirs a hunger you cannot easily put down, leave it alone entirely.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: When Gambling Has Hold of You
text: When Gambling Has Hold of You For some, gambling is not a question of liberty. It is a chain. You tell yourself one more bet will win it back. You hide the statements. You borrow, then lie about why. Maybe the rent is gone, or the savings. This is real, and it ruins families. Trust breaks, and honest men become liars. Christ came for people exactly where you are. God is faithful, Paul says, and with the temptation he will also make a way to escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). But you will not get out alone, or by trying harder in secret. Confess it. He that covereth his sins shall not prosper, but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy (Proverbs 28:13). Tell God, then your husband or wife and your pastor or an elder, the whole truth, including how much. Cut off access. Jesus said, If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out (Matthew 5:29). The eye is a figure, and what it pictures is real, a costly cutting off of whatever leads you into sin. Delete the apps today and close the accounts. Many states and betting sites let you ban yourself. Ask your bank whether it can block gambling payments. Give someone else control of the money.
