Hand your cards and accounts to your spouse or a trusted brother for a season. This is not shame. It is wisdom. Find accountability. Ask a few believers to ask you plainly and often whether you have gambled. Mortify lets you link with brethren from your church and fight covetousness and the love of money together. For the long fight itself, read Struggling With Sin . See a doctor. God works through means. A doctor can treat the depression and anxiety that so often come with this, and can point you to further help. Lean on the church. Tell the deacons if your family needs help with food or rent. Let the elders help you make a plan for your debts, and read When Debt Has You Under . Do not borrow to chase what you lost. If the debts and the shame have you thinking your family would be better off without you, that is a lie. They would not. Call 988 or text 988 now, and tell someone near you tonight.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: Pardon for What You Lost Maybe what you lost was not yours. It was the family’s savings, or money from an employer, a client, or a church. The guilt is heavy because the wrong is real, and this page will not tell you it was nothing. But your sin is not bigger than the blood of Christ. Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot: 1 Peter 1:18-19 (KJV) You could never buy back your soul with money, and you do not have to. Christ paid with his own blood, and he rose again on the third day. Turn from your sin to him. Let him return unto the Lord , and he will have mercy upon him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon (Isaiah 55:7). If you do not yet know him, read the gospel , and come. Pardon from God does not end your duty to those you wronged. When Zacchaeus met Jesus, he said, If I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold (Luke 19:8). He did not pay to be forgiven. He paid back because he had been. God’s law required the guilty man to restore what he took and add a fifth part (Numbers 5:7), and the Catechism names restitution among the duties of the eighth commandment (WLC 141). If you took from an employer, confess it, even if it costs you the job. Make a plan with your elders to repay, little by little if you must. Some of what was lost may never be repaid. God knows that, and his pardon is no less full.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: Contentment and the Treasure No Wager Can Buy
text: Contentment and the Treasure No Wager Can Buy The cure for the gambler’s hunger is not a smaller hunger. It is a better treasure. Paul wrote from prison. Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. Philippians 4:11-13 (KJV) Contentment is learned. It does not come in a jackpot. It rests on a promise. Your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things. Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you (Matthew 6:32-33). The gambler is always trying to secure tomorrow by luck. The believer has a Father who has already promised it, and who has said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee (Hebrews 13:5). Jesus told of a man who found treasure hid in a field. For joy thereof he goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field (Matthew 13:44). The treasure in the story is a picture, and what it pictures is real. Christ and his kingdom are worth more than everything you own. Yet no wager can win him, and no money can buy him, because he gives himself freely. Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money (Isaiah 55:1). Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Whoever has him has already gained what the whole world cannot give.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: What to Do This Week Look honestly at your own money. Add up what went to tickets, apps, and bets in the last year, and bring the number to God. If it has a hold on you, act today. Follow the steps above . Do not wait for Monday. Pray for contentment. Pray Agur’s prayer, Give me neither poverty nor riches, feed me with food convenient for me (Proverbs 30:8). Give. Put something in the offering this Lord’s Day, or into a needy hand. Giving loosens money’s grip on the heart. A word to husbands and wives. If your spouse gambles, it is not your fault, and covering for it will not fix it. Do not quietly pay the debts and keep the secret. Protect what your household needs to live on, in a separate account if you must. Go to your elders together, or alone if he will not come. If the lying has turned to threats or violence, get safe first . Love him enough to let him face what he has done. A word to parents. Your children are being taught to bet before they can drive. The ads come with every game, and some video games sell paid chances at prizes that work much the same way. Talk about it plainly, and show them how the house wins. Let them see you content with what God gives, and see you give. For more, read What the Bible Says About Raising Children . In the church, welcome the one who is fighting. Someone near you may be hiding this. Let him hear that there is mercy in Christ and help in his people.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: Wine is a gift and drunkenness is sin. Christian liberty, the weaker brother, when to abstain, drugs, and help when drink has hold.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: A Good Gift From God Scripture does not begin with wine as an enemy. It names wine among the good things God brings out of the earth. He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth; And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man’s heart. Psalm 104:14-15 (KJV) The psalm praises God the Creator, and the gladness it names is real. The Preacher says the same. Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart (Ecclesiastes 9:7). The Wine at Cana and at the Table The Lord Jesus did his first sign at a wedding in Cana when the wine ran out (John 2:1-11). He had six stone waterpots filled to the brim, and the water became wine, well over a hundred gallons of it. And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now. This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him. John 2:10-11 (KJV) The wine was real, and so was the joy he gave that couple. The sign also pointed past itself. Isaiah foretold a feast of wines on the lees well refined that God would spread for all people (Isaiah 25:6). Christ is the Bridegroom who brings that feast, and he has kept the good wine until now. On the night he was betrayed, he took the cup and said, Drink ye all of it, for this is my blood of the new testament (Matthew 26:27-28). He called what was in it this fruit of the vine (26:29), and the Confession speaks of the elements of bread and wine (WCF 29.3). Reformed churches today differ in what they pour. Many use wine, many use grape juice, and some offer both so that no one who must abstain is kept from the table. Was It Only Grape Juice? Some sincere Christians, having seen what drink did to the homes around them, have taught that the good wine of the Bible was unfermented juice. But the case does not hold. Noah drank of the wine, and was drunken (Genesis 9:21). Paul says, be not drunk with wine, and no one needs that warning about juice. At Corinth some left the Lord’s Supper drunken (1 Corinthians 11:21). Jesus was slandered as a winebibber because he drank wine where John the Baptist did not (Luke 7:33-34). Juice that would keep without turning to wine came only in the 1800s. The wine of Scripture was wine, which is why the Bible both praises it and warns about it.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: Drunkenness Is Sin The Bible that calls wine a gift calls drunkenness a sin. And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; Ephesians 5:18 (KJV) Excess means a wasted, unruly life. Paul sets two fillings side by side. The drunkard lets something outside him take over his mind and lift his heart for a few hours. God fills his people with his own Spirit, and the fruit is singing and thanksgiving (5:19-20). Many drink to feel brave or to bear the night. The Spirit gives what the bottle only promises, and he leaves no ruin in the morning. Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging, and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise (Proverbs 20:1). It mocks the one who trusts it. Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes? They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine. Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder. Proverbs 23:29-32 (KJV) The serpent is a picture, and the harm it pictures is real. The drunk man says what he never would sober, his world reels like a ship’s mast, and he wakes up beaten without having felt it (23:33-35). Then the saddest line of all. When shall I awake? I will seek it yet again. That is bondage. Drunkenness is not only falling down in the street. It is drinking until your judgment is dulled and you are no longer master of yourself. Paul lists it among the works of the flesh, and says that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:21). Drunkards stand beside thieves and adulterers in 1 Corinthians 6:10. Scripture also pronounces a woe on him that makes his neighbour drunken (Habakkuk 2:15). The host who keeps pouring for a friend who has had enough shares the sin.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
section: Free to Drink, Free to Abstain
text: Free to Drink, Free to Abstain Since Scripture allows wine and forbids drunkenness, a believer may drink in moderation with thanks, or he may abstain, and either may do it to the Lord. No man and no church may add a rule to God’s Word and bind a conscience with it. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.2 Beside it means added to it. But the Confession guards the other side just as firmly. They who, upon pretense of Christian liberty, do practice any sin, or cherish any lust, do thereby destroy the end of Christian liberty; which is, that, being delivered out of the hands of our enemies, we might serve the Lord without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.3 Upon pretense means using liberty as an excuse. Christ did not free you from sin so that you could drink your way back into it. Paul’s word about food fits the cup as well. Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him. Romans 14:3 (KJV) The one who drinks must not despise the one who abstains as narrow. The one who abstains must not judge the one who drinks as worldly. Both give God thanks, and both do it to the Lord (14:6). Faithful Reformed people have differed here. In the 1800s many Presbyterian ministers, having watched drink ruin families, urged total abstinence on every Christian. Others held moderate drinking free. A church may wisely counsel abstinence in a hard age, but it may not call wine itself a sin, because God does not. The Reformed Presbyterian Church once required total abstinence of every member and officer. In the 1980s its Synod ruled that the Testimony strongly recommends abstinence but does not demand it, and in 1998 the promise to abstain was taken out of the vows of its officers. The Testimony still teaches that, to avoid harming our neighbor and to help one another live a disciplined life, it is altogether wise and right for Christians to abstain from the use, sale, and making of alcoholic drinks (RP Testimony 26.6). If you belong to a Reformed Presbyterian congregation, give that counsel real weight, and talk with your elders. For the Sake of Your Brother It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak. Romans 14:21 (KJV) The weaker brother is not merely someone who disapproves. He is one whom your example may lead against his conscience, or back into a sin that once ruled him. Take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak, Paul says. To wound such a conscience is to sin against Christ, who died for that brother (1 Corinthians 8:9-13). If a friend at your table is fighting to stay sober, leave the bottle in the cupboard. Liberty is never the last word. Love is.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
section: When It Is Wise to Abstain
text: When It Is Wise to Abstain A Christian who may drink is not bound to, and Scripture honors some who did not. He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried. Numbers 6:3 (KJV) The Nazarite vow was taken freely by one who wished to be set apart to the Lord for a season (Numbers 6:2). The Rechabites drank no wine for generations at their father’s charge, and God held up their faithfulness as a rebuke to Judah, which would not keep his word (Jeremiah 35:6, 14). The lesson there was obedience. God never made either path a law for all his people. They are examples for those who choose to abstain, and some have good reason to. A family history of addiction. If drink ruined a parent or grandparent, you may be wise to leave it alone. All things are lawful unto me, Paul said, but I will not be brought under the power of any (1 Corinthians 6:12). Recovery. If drink once ruled you, the cup is a door back into the old bondage. Keep it shut, and let no one shame you for it. A calling. Kings were warned against wine lest they forget the law (Proverbs 31:4-5). A pastor, or anyone who works among those who struggle, may abstain so that nothing he does becomes their excuse. An unsettled conscience. Whatsoever is not of faith is sin (Romans 14:23). If you are not sure before God that you may, do not.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
section: The Law of the Land and the Life of Your Neighbor
text: The Law of the Land and the Life of Your Neighbor Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Romans 13:1 (KJV) Where the law sets an age for drinking, a Christian under that age keeps it, because God set that ruler over him. A teenager who drinks behind his parents’ backs disobeys both. An adult who buys drink for other people’s children sins with them. For more, read What the Bible Says About Government . Drunk Driving Thou shalt not kill reaches further than murder. The Larger Catechism says the sixth commandment forbids the immoderate use of drink, and whatever else tends to destroy anyone’s life (WLC 136). Driving after drinking gambles with your neighbor’s life. Moses’ law made a man build a wall around his flat roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence (Deuteronomy 22:8). God holds a man guilty for the danger he could have prevented. Do not drive when you have been drinking, and do not ride with anyone who has. Marijuana and Other Drugs Scripture does not name marijuana or pills, but it says plainly what a Christian’s mind is to be. Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: 1 Peter 5:8 (KJV) The lion is a picture, and the enemy it pictures is real. To be sober is to keep a clear and watchful mind, for they that be drunken are drunken in the night, and we are of the day (1 Thessalonians 5:6-8). A man can drink a glass of wine with supper and keep his head, but a drug taken to get high is taken for the altered mind itself. That is drunkenness by another road. Where the law now allows it, the call to be sober has not changed. Medicine prescribed by a doctor is a different thing. The Larger Catechism counts a sober use of physic, the old word for medicine, among the duties of the sixth commandment (WLC 135). Pain medicine after surgery, or medicine for anxiety or depression, taken as directed, is a lawful means of preserving life. Scripture even says, Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish (Proverbs 31:6). Taking more than you were told, or taking it for the feeling, is another matter.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
section: If Drink Has Hold of You
text: If Drink Has Hold of You Perhaps you hide how much you drink, or have promised to cut back and could not. Then you are in bondage, and you need a deliverer. First, hear this. If you drink heavily every day, do not stop all at once on your own. Stopping suddenly can bring seizures and can kill. See a doctor this week, tell him the whole truth about how much you drink, and let someone go with you. The same is true of daily pills like Xanax or Valium. God works through means, and a doctor and treatment are among them. Then tell your pastor or an elder. You were not meant to fight this in secret. Read Drink or drugs have hold of me , and for the daily fight, Mortify . Get the bottles out of the house, and stay away from the friends who pull you back. Make not provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14). You are not only giving something up. You are being filled with the Spirit, whose joy does not end in shame. If you love someone who drinks, his choices are not your fault, and you cannot stop him by your own effort. Pray, speak the truth in love, and lean on your church. If he is a danger to you or your children, your safety comes first.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: Washed and Justified Paul wrote this to a church that had drunkards in it. Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God. And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. 1 Corinthians 6:10-11 (KJV) They had been drunkards, and now they were washed, set apart for God, and declared righteous. That pardon is held out to you. Look at the Lord Jesus on the cross. They gave him to drink wine mingled with myrrh, and he received it not (Mark 15:23). Many take it to have been a drink to dull the pain. In the garden he had prayed about another cup, the cup of his Father’s wrath against sin (Matthew 26:39). He drank that one to the bottom with a clear mind, for drunkards and for all who come to him, and he rose again. If you have never come to him, read The Gospel , and come today. Confess the sin by name, and the things you did while drunk. Make right what you can. If someone was hurt or killed because of your drinking, Christ forgives that too, but pardon with God does not cancel earthly justice. If you fall again, do not hide from him. If old guilt keeps returning after you have confessed it, read What I did is too great to forgive .

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: What to Do This Week If you drink, give thanks. Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Ask yourself whether you could go a month without it, gladly. If not, put it down and talk to someone. If you abstain, keep it free of pride. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost (Romans 14:17). If you host, host with love. Have something good for those who do not drink, and never press a glass on anyone. If You Are a Parent In Proverbs 23 a father says, My son, give me thine heart (23:26), and a few verses later he warns his son about the wine that bites like a serpent. Talk to your teens about drink before the world does. Teach both halves. Show them that wine is God’s gift and drunkenness is sin. Tell them the family history. If addiction runs in your family, say so plainly and early. Teach them to keep the law. Underage drinking is not a rite of passage. It is disobedience to rulers God set over them, and to you. Let your example speak. If you drink, let them never see you drunk or see you need it. If you abstain, do not teach them that Christians who drink are lesser Christians. Give them a way out. Tell them that if they ever need to leave a place where there is drink, or the driver has been drinking, they can call you and you will come. Get them home safe first, and talk the next day. For more, read The Teen Years .

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What Leviticus 19:28 meant, how Old Testament laws bind now, Christian liberty, and a word for those who already have them.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What Leviticus 19:28 Says One verse in the Bible speaks to marks on the skin. Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the Lord . Leviticus 19:28 (KJV) A verse must be read where God put it. Just before it, Israel is told not to use enchantment or observe times, and not to round the corners of the head or mar the corners of the beard (Leviticus 19:26-27). These were the ways of the nations around Israel, in their sorcery and in their grief. Moses gives the reason in Deuteronomy. Ye are the children of the Lord your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead. For thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God, and the Lord hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself, above all the nations that are upon the earth. Deuteronomy 14:1-2 (KJV) The heathen cut themselves for their dead, and the prophets of Baal cut themselves till the blood gushed out upon them (1 Kings 18:28). Israel was not to grieve or worship like that. The word translated marks is found nowhere else in the Old Testament, so its exact sense is not certain, and whether for the dead reaches to the marks as well as the cuttings is debated. What is plain is the reason God gives. I am the Lord . Israel belonged to him, and was not to carry the signs of other gods or of hopeless grief.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
section: Which Kind of Law Is It?
text: Which Kind of Law Is It? Leviticus 19 holds very different laws side by side. It says, thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (19:18), and a line later forbids a garment mingled of linen and woollen (19:19). No one thinks those bind us in the same way. The Confession says the moral law, summed up in the ten commandments, binds all men forever (WCF 19.5). Then it names two other kinds. Beside this law, commonly called moral, God was pleased to give to the people of Israel, as a Church under age, ceremonial laws, containing several typical ordinances, partly of worship, prefiguring Christ, his graces, actions, sufferings, and benefits; and partly holding forth divers instructions of moral duties. All which ceremonial laws are now abrogated under the New Testament. Westminster Confession of Faith 19.3 Israel’s judicial laws, the civil laws of her nation, expired with that state, and bind others now only as far as their general equity requires (WCF 19.4). So which is Leviticus 19:28? Reformed teachers ask whether a law is rooted in creation and the ten commandments, or whether its reason lies in Israel’s being set apart from the nations as a picture of the holiness Christ would bring. Many answer that this law belongs with the beard and the mingled cloth. It marked Israel off from her neighbors, and that wall came down in Christ. But they see a moral duty folded inside it. Do not take on the marks of false gods. Do not sorrow as others which have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). God’s people are still a peculiar people (1 Peter 2:9), but now by holiness of life and not by the cut of the beard. Other faithful teachers hold that the ban on marks still binds, as a moral law guarding the body God made, and they counsel every Christian never to be tattooed. Still others call it ceremonial but think its general equity weighs so heavily against tattoos that a believer should not get one. These are godly men, and they do not all land in the same place. This page will not settle more than Scripture settles. No one may bind you where God’s Word has not, or loosen you where it has. The questions below bind every believer, whichever view he holds. Pictures Are Not Permits Some say God approves of tattoos because he said, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands (Isaiah 49:16). That is a picture. God is saying he cannot forget his people, any more than a man could forget what is cut into his own palm. What it shows is real and very sweet, but it is not a ruling on tattoos. When Paul says, I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus (Galatians 6:17), he means the scars of his beatings for Christ (2 Corinthians 11:24-25). Reading a figure as a permit is as careless as reading Leviticus 19:28 without its setting.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: Your Body Belongs to God What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s. 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 (KJV) Paul wrote this about sexual sin, but it reaches every use of the body. The temple is a picture, and what it pictures is real. The Holy Spirit dwells in every believer, and Christ paid for your body with his blood. You are a steward, not an owner, and no Christian may say, It is my body, so it is my business. But the verse does not by itself forbid every change to the body. Christians cut their hair and have surgery, and the verse does not say which changes honor God. It does not hand you the answer. It tells you whom you must ask, and that the answer matters.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: Christian Liberty and Its Limits God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.2 Where Scripture has not forbidden a thing, the church may not make a new law and lay it on your neck. But the Confession says at once that those who, under pretense of liberty, practice any sin or cherish any lust destroy the very end of liberty, which is to serve the Lord in holiness and righteousness (WCF 20.3). Paul said, Ye have been called unto liberty, only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another (Galatians 5:13). All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not. 1 Corinthians 10:23 (KJV) Expedient means helpful. Whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). And whatsoever is not of faith is sin (Romans 14:23). If you cannot get a tattoo with a clear conscience, you must not get one. Questions to Ask First Why do I want it? To be admired, or to fit in? Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain (Proverbs 31:30). Is it rebellion? If part of the pleasure is that it will upset your parents, the motive is already sin. Will I want it when I am old? What seems deep at twenty may shame you at sixty. Where will it go? A mark placed to draw eyes to what should be covered is immodest (WLC 139). What does it say? Nothing occult, obscene, cruel, or mocking of holy things belongs on a Christian (Philippians 4:8). What does it tie me to? A believer may not wear the badge of a gang, a false religion, or a sinful way of life. What will it say to others? Think of your witness and of the weaker believer (1 Corinthians 8:9). Love sometimes gives up what liberty allows.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
section: If You Are Young and Living at Home
text: If You Are Young and Living at Home Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right. Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;) That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth. Ephesians 6:1-3 (KJV) In the Lord means in all things lawful. A parent who says no to a tattoo is not commanding sin. Children owe willing obedience to their parents’ lawful commands and counsels (WLC 127). While you live under your parents’ roof, their decision is your answer, even if the law of the land would let you go ahead. Getting one in secret breaks the fifth commandment. A tattoo will still be possible in five years. Broken trust is harder to mend. Parents, give your reasons, and be honest about which are God’s law and which are your own judgment. Provoke not your children to wrath (Ephesians 6:4). See also The Teen Years .

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What About Piercings? Abraham’s servant put the earring upon Rebekah’s face as a gift for a bride (Genesis 24:47). When God pictures his rich grace to Jerusalem, he says he put earrings in her ears (Ezekiel 16:12), and he would hardly use what is wicked in itself to picture his own kindness. But earrings were also bound up with idols. Jacob’s household buried theirs with their strange gods (Genesis 35:4). So jewelry is not sin in itself. Ask the same questions of it. A plain earring and a face full of metal meant to shock do not say the same thing. Some piercings leave lasting marks and deserve the same care as a tattoo. Young people at home should again honor their parents’ decision.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: If You Already Have Tattoos Maybe you got them before you knew Christ, or as a believer and now wish you had not. Hear this plainly. You are not a second-class Christian. Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV) The ink is still in your skin, but you are not who you were. Whatever your old life held, such were some of you, but ye are washed (1 Corinthians 6:11). The blood of Christ purges the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Ink cannot reach where that blood has washed. If your tattoo was a matter of liberty, there is nothing to repent of. If you got it in sin, out of rebellion or vanity, confess that sin to God by name. The sin was in the heart, and the heart is what Christ forgives. If you do not yet know him, read The Gospel . He receives sinners as they are. If a tattoo shows something sinful or obscene, love for God and your neighbor will want it out of sight. Cover it with clothing, or have an artist work it into something clean, or have it removed if you are able. But removal is never a condition of grace. Christ does not wait for clear skin before he receives you, and no church should either. If you are unsure, talk with your pastor.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
section: How the Church Should Receive Them
text: How the Church Should Receive Them James warns the church that seats the man with a gold ring in a good place and tells the poor man in vile raiment to stand. Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? (James 2:1-4). Skin is no different from clothing here. Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). The tattooed man who walks into your church may be a new believer, or a sinner God is drawing, or a brother of forty years in Christ. You cannot tell by looking. Do not stare or lecture. Learn his name and sit with him. Many have known years of scorn from Christians. Let your church be where that ends.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What to Do If you want a tattoo, wait. Give it a long season, and pray through the questions above. Ask the right people. If you live at home, abide by your parents’ answer. If you are married, decide it with your husband or wife. Keep your conviction without binding others. If you think tattoos are forbidden, do not treat believers who differ as rebels. If you think they are allowed, do not press your liberty on the weak or the young. Deal honestly with what you have. If a tattoo you have is sinful in its message, cover it this week. Then stop carrying shame that Christ has already carried. Welcome the stranger. Next Lord’s Day, look for the person who looks least like your church, and greet him first. One risen body still bore marks. Thomas said he would not believe unless he saw in his hands the print of the nails (John 20:25), and the risen Christ showed him. He was wounded for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5). Every mark of shame we carry, on the skin or in the conscience, he carried to the cross. And he will finish his work in our bodies too. Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself. Philippians 3:21 (KJV) Vile here means lowly and weak. Whatever your skin carries today, if you are his, he will raise your body and make it glorious, to stand with him forever.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Rulers are ordained of God and owe allegiance to his Son. Obeying, praying, paying taxes, and when to obey God rather than men.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Government Is God’s Ordinance Government was not invented by kings or voted into being by the people. God made it. Paul wrote this to Christians living under Rome, a pagan empire that would later put many of them to death. Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation. Romans 13:1-2 (KJV) God, the Supreme Lord and King of all the world, hath ordained civil magistrates to be under him, over the people, for his own glory and the public good, and to this end hath armed them with the power of the sword, for the defense and encouragement of them that are good, and for the punishment of evil-doers. Westminster Confession of Faith 23.1 Rulers are over the people, and they are under God. The proudest king on earth had to learn that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men (Daniel 4:17). The Minister of God With the Sword Peter says governors are sent for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well (1 Peter 2:14). Paul says it more sharply. For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. Romans 13:4 (KJV) Minister means servant. The magistrate serves God as truly as a pastor does, though in a different work. The sword is a picture, and what it pictures is real. It is the power to use force and to punish, even with death. God gave it after the flood. Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for in the image of God made he man (Genesis 9:6). Private men may not avenge themselves (Romans 12:19). God repays by the hand of the ruler. So a Christian may hold the sword. The Confession teaches that Christians may accept the office of a magistrate when called to it, and that rulers may wage war upon just and necessary occasion (WCF 23.2). John the Baptist did not tell soldiers to leave the army. He told them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely (Luke 3:14). Cornelius was a centurion who feared God with all his house (Acts 10:1-2). A believer may serve as a judge, a soldier, or a police officer to the glory of God. If You Have Borne the Sword Some who read this have used force in war or in the line of duty, and some have taken a life. Lawful force used for justice and in defense of others is not murder. Yet many carry it for years. That weight is not always guilt. Often it is grief over what sin does to the world. If there was real sin in it, cruelty or rage or harm to the innocent, Christ’s blood is enough for that too. Confess it to him plainly, and tell your pastor. If the weight has brought you to thoughts of ending your life, call 988 or text 988 now, and read the page on getting safe .

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Christ Is King of Kings Above every ruler stands a King. In the second psalm the nations rage against the Lord and his anointed, and God laughs, for he has set his King on his holy hill (Psalm 2:1-6). Then he speaks to the rulers. Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him. Psalm 2:10-12 (KJV) A subject kissed his king as a sign of homage, and a worshiper kissed his idol (1 Kings 19:18). The kiss is the picture. What it pictures is real submission. God commands kings and judges, as kings and judges, to bow to his Son. That Son is Jesus Christ. After he rose he said, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth (Matthew 28:18). As the eternal Son he always ruled with the Father. This is power given to him as Mediator, the God-man who died and rose again, crowned and set over everything for his people’s sake. Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come: And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Ephesians 1:20-22 (KJV) Under his feet is a picture of a conquering king, and the rule it pictures is real. Every court and congress is beneath him now. John calls him the prince of the kings of the earth (Revelation 1:5). In John’s vision he rides out with a name written on his robe, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS (Revelation 19:16). The vision is full of pictures, but that name is the plain truth about him. So a nation is not neutral ground. Its rulers owe Christ their allegiance, and its laws ought to honor his law. The Reformed Presbyterian Church has long borne witness that nations owe allegiance to Christ. If you are a member, ask your elders how the church’s Testimony applies to you. The Hope for the Nations Scripture promises, Yea, all kings shall fall down before him, all nations shall serve him (Psalm 72:11). Reformed believers differ on how much of that we will see before Christ returns. Some believe the gospel will so prevail in this age that nations as nations will confess Christ before he comes, as the leaven worked till the whole was leavened (Matthew 13:33), and the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord (Habakkuk 2:14). Others believe Christ gathers his people out of every nation while this age stays mixed, wheat and tares growing together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30), with the church often small and suffering, and that every knee will bow on the day he appears (Philippians 2:10-11). Both hold that Christ reigns now, that the nations owe him obedience now, and that he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Both pray, Thy kingdom come. We see not yet all things put under him. But we see Jesus (Hebrews 2:8-9).

title: What the Bible Says About Government
section: What the State May Not Do
text: What the State May Not Do Because rulers are under Christ, their power has edges. It may not rule the church. When King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense, the priests withstood him and said, It appertaineth not unto thee (2 Chronicles 26:18). A king had a real office, but not that one. The civil magistrate may not assume to himself the administration of the Word and Sacraments, or the power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven Westminster Confession of Faith 23.3 No ruler may preach, keep the Lord’s Table, or tell the church how to worship. Nor may he bind the conscience. The state may tell you how fast to drive. It may not tell you what to believe about God. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.2 Jesus drew the line with a coin. Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s (Matthew 22:21). The coin bore Caesar’s image, so it could go to Caesar. You bear God’s image, so you belong to God. Caesar gets taxes and honor. He never gets the soul. And the state is not a savior. Its sword can restrain evil, but it cannot make anyone new.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Honor, Pray, Pay, and Obey The fifth commandment reaches to all who are over us by God’s ordinance, whether in family, church, or commonwealth (WLC 124). It is the duty of people to pray for magistrates, to honor their persons, to pay them tribute and other dues, to obey their lawful commands, and to be subject to their authority, for conscience’ sake. Infidelity or difference in religion doth not make void the magistrate’s just and legal authority, nor free the people from their due obedience to him Westminster Confession of Faith 23.4 A ruler who does not believe, or believes falsely, is still a ruler. Peter wrote under a pagan emperor, Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king (1 Peter 2:17). I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. 1 Timothy 2:1-2 (KJV) First of all. Before we complain about rulers, we pray for them, and even give thanks. If a ruler seems foolish or wicked, pray for him anyway. Ask God to give him wisdom and to save his soul. Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon, the city that had burned Jerusalem, and pray unto the Lord for it (Jeremiah 29:7). Render therefore to all their dues, tribute to whom tribute is due (Romans 13:7). Cheating on taxes is stealing, even when the money will be spent badly. Obey the laws, not only for fear of being caught but for conscience sake (Romans 13:5). And Paul says to speak evil of no man (Titus 3:2). That includes the man in office you did not vote for.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
section: When We Must Obey God Rather Than Men
text: When We Must Obey God Rather Than Men Our obedience to rulers has a limit, and the limit is God. When the council commanded the apostles to stop preaching Jesus, Peter and John answered, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard (Acts 4:19-20). Brought in again, they answered more shortly. Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. Acts 5:29 (KJV) The Hebrew midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive (Exodus 1:17), and God dealt well with them. Daniel kept praying three times a day, as he did aforetime, after a law forbade it (Daniel 6:10). And three young men would not bow to a golden image. If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. Daniel 3:17-18 (KJV) Look at how they disobeyed. They refused only what would have been sin, and they did it openly. Daniel still said, O king, live for ever (Daniel 6:21). They took up no sword, and they left the outcome with God. If a ruler commands you to deny Christ, to worship falsely, or to take part in killing the innocent, you must refuse. Refuse humbly, and refuse firmly. What about rulers who become tyrants? Calvin, at the close of his Institutes, taught that private persons are not to rise up against their rulers on their own, but that lesser magistrates, those who also hold lawful office, ought to restrain a ruler who oppresses the people. The Reformed tradition after him has held that resistance to tyranny belongs first to such lawful authorities and to lawful means. Paul, denied justice, used the law and said, I appeal unto Caesar (Acts 25:11). Bring hard questions of this kind to your elders before you act.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: The Christian Citizen Most of us are citizens, not rulers. Where the law gives us a voice, a Christian may vote, write to his rulers, and speak in public as a servant of Christ. He should do it with a conscience shaped by God’s Word, asking what honors Christ and protects the weak, not only what helps himself. The Reformed Presbyterian Testimony speaks plainly here. Where it involves no disloyalty to Christ, a Christian should help choose rulers who fear God, love truth and justice, and hate evil (Exodus 18:21). He should vote only for men publicly committed to the Scriptural principles of civil government. He may not take an oath that compromises his supreme loyalty to Christ, and he may not vote for an officer who must take an oath he could not take himself in good conscience, because a vote makes the voter answerable for what the office requires (RP Testimony 23.15-16, 29). Weigh every ballot by that, not by habit or by party, and ask your elders when you are unsure. Righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people (Proverbs 14:34). It is right to ask rulers to protect life and punish evil. See What Christians Should Do about abortion for one plain case. Put Not Your Trust in Princes Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish. Psalm 146:3-4 (KJV) Every leader you hope in will die. If your peace rises and falls with an election, your trust is in a prince. Ask yourself. Do I feel more joy when my side wins than when a sinner repents? Do I despise the people who vote the other way? The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God (James 1:20). Rage at the news and contempt for opponents are sins, not zeal. Your political opponent is a neighbor made in God’s image, and perhaps a brother in Christ. Love him. Keep the church above party. She must preach the whole Word, including what God says to rulers, and the Confession keeps her assemblies from meddling in civil affairs beyond humble petition and advice (WCF 31.5). Her message is, Be ye reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20). When she becomes the chaplain of a party, she trades it for a smaller one.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: The Throne That Matters Most On the morning of the day he died, Jesus stood before a Roman governor who asked whether he was a king. Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence. John 18:36 (KJV) Not of this world means his kingdom does not come from here. It is not won by votes or held by soldiers, but spreads by the Word and the Spirit. Yet he rules over all. He told Pilate, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above (John 19:11). Then the soldiers crowned him with thorns and mocked him, Hail, King of the Jews (Matthew 27:29). Pilate put a title on the cross, THE KING OF THE JEWS (John 19:19). They meant it as a joke, but it was true. The King was lifted up on a cross, bearing the wrath of God for rebels. He won his kingdom not by taking his enemies’ lives but by giving his own for them. On the third day he rose, and now he sits at the right hand of God. Every one of us has been a rebel against this King. The command to kiss the Son is spoken to you before any president. Turn from your sin and trust him. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him (Psalm 2:12). He is the prince of the kings of the earth, and in the same breath John says he loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood (Revelation 1:5). If you do not know him yet, read the gospel . The throne that matters most is not in any capital. It is the one Christ sits on now, where he gathers and defends his church, subdues her enemies, and makes intercession for his people (WLC 54). He removeth kings, and setteth up kings (Daniel 2:21). But of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end (Isaiah 9:7). We have received a kingdom which cannot be moved (Hebrews 12:28).

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: What Christians Should Do Kiss the Son yourself. Before you ask anything of your rulers, bow to Christ. Confess where politics has ruled your heart more than he has. Pray for your rulers by name. Pray this week for the president, your governor, and one local official, and give thanks for them. See How to Pray . Pay and obey with a clean conscience. If you have cheated on taxes or broken a just law, confess it and set it right. Watch your mouth. Speak of officials with respect, even in disagreement. Stop passing on what mocks or slanders. Take part with care. Vote, write, and speak as a servant of Christ, with the counsel of your elders. Know your line. Settle now what you will not do, whatever a ruler commands. Ask God for Daniel’s courage and Daniel’s respect. Turn off the noise. If the news feeds fear or rage, put it down and read Psalm 2 instead.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: Death is an enemy Christ has beaten. What happens when we die, the resurrection, burial and cremation, and the end of life.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: What Death Is People often call death natural, a part of life, even a friend. Scripture never does. God made man to live. He warned Adam about the forbidden tree, In the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die (Genesis 2:17). Adam ate, and God said, Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return (Genesis 3:19). By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin, and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned (Romans 5:12). For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Romans 6:23 (KJV) Wages are what a man has earned, and death is what sin has earned. It was not part of God’s first creation. That is why it feels so wrong to us. It is wrong. So the Bible calls death an enemy, the last enemy that shall be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). Jesus stood at his friend’s grave and groaned in the spirit (John 11:33). Yet death is not loose in the world on its own. God says, I kill, and I make alive (Deuteronomy 32:39). No one dies outside his hand. And for those in Christ the enemy is already beaten. The sting is gone, though the wound is still felt.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: What Happens When We Die At death body and soul are torn apart for a time. The body goes to the grave, and the soul goes on, awake, to God. The bodies of men, after death, return to dust, and see corruption; but their souls (which neither die nor sleep), having an immortal subsistence, immediately return to God who gave them. The souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies: and the souls of the wicked are cast into hell, where they remain in torments and utter darkness, reserved to the judgment of the great day. Besides these two places for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none. Westminster Confession of Faith 32.1 So the soul does not sleep until the last day, and there is no purgatory where believers pay what Christ left unpaid. The Shorter Catechism gives the believer’s part. Their souls are made perfect in holiness and immediately pass into glory, and their bodies, still united to Christ, rest in their graves till the resurrection (WSC 37). The Believer Goes to Be with Christ For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Philippians 1:21 (KJV) Paul had a desire to depart, and to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). He was willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). And Jesus told the dying thief, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Paradise was a word for a garden, and it calls Eden to mind. It is a picture, and what it pictures is real. The thief was with Christ that very day. The Unbeliever Is Kept for Judgment This must be said soberly, and never with pleasure. Jesus told of a rich man who lived for himself and died. In hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments (Luke 16:23). Jesus speaks of his tongue and of a flame, though the man’s body lay in its grave. Those words picture the torment of a soul without its body, and the torment is real. Between that place and Abraham’s side there is a great gulf fixed (16:26). It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment (Hebrews 9:27). No one repents after death, which is why the gospel always says today. Yet we may not pronounce on any particular person who has died, for we do not know what passed between a soul and God at the end. If that fear presses on you, read When You Fear They Did Not Know Christ . But it is our place to warn the living, ourselves first.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: The Resurrection of the Body God made us body and soul, and he will not leave half his work in the dust. Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation. John 5:28-29 (KJV) All will rise, the just and the unjust, each in the same body that was laid down. At the last day, such as are found alive shall not die, but be changed; and all the dead shall be raised up with the self-same bodies, and none other, although with different qualities, which shall be united again to their souls forever. Westminster Confession of Faith 32.2 Job knew it long before Christ came. Though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God (Job 19:26). The pattern is Christ’s own body. After he rose he said, Handle me, and see, for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have (Luke 24:39). The risen body is not a new creature in place of the old one. It is the old one made new. The Confession adds that the bodies of the unjust are raised by Christ’s power to dishonor, and the bodies of the just by his Spirit to honor, made like his own glorious body (WCF 32.3). He shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). Vile here means lowly and weak.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: Burial in Scripture Because the body will rise, God’s people have always honored it in death. In Scripture burial is often an act of faith. I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight. Genesis 23:4 (KJV) When Sarah died, Abraham owned no land in Canaan. God had promised him all of it, but he still lived in tents. The first piece of the promised land he ever owned was a grave, bought at full price (Genesis 23:16-20). He laid his wife in the promised land because he believed the promise. Joseph died a ruler in Egypt, but he made his brothers swear to carry his bones up out of it (Genesis 50:24-25). Centuries later Moses carried that coffin out in the exodus, and Israel buried it at Shechem (Exodus 13:19, Joshua 24:32). The Holy Spirit counts the request among the great acts of faith. By faith Joseph, when he died, gave commandment concerning his bones (Hebrews 11:22). Most of all, Christ himself was buried. Paul counts it part of the gospel, that Christ died for our sins, and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Faithful hands wound his body in linen with spices and laid it in a new tomb in a garden (John 19:40-41). Because he lay in a grave, the grave of a believer is no longer a prison. Their bodies rest in their graves as in their beds (WLC 86). So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 (KJV) Paul pictures burial as sowing. A farmer drops a seed into the ground, and it rots there and seems lost. Then up comes a living plant, far more glorious than the bare grain, yet grown from that very seed (15:36-38). The body laid in the grave is the seed. The sowing is the picture. The rising is not a picture. It is as real as the resurrection of Jesus, and the same God promises it. A spiritual body does not mean a body made of spirit. Christ’s risen body had flesh and bones. It means a body wholly ruled and filled by the Holy Spirit, never again weak or dying or able to sin. A Christian standing at a grave is standing in a field God has sown, waiting for the harvest.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: What About Cremation Christians have historically buried their dead, as a testimony that the body will rise, and many Reformed teachers still counsel burial today. Burial says with the body what the creed says with the mouth. In Scripture the burning of a body is mostly tied to judgment. Achan was stoned and then burned for his sin (Joshua 7:25). And God judged Moab for an act of contempt toward the dead. Thus saith the Lord ; For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime: Amos 2:1 (KJV) There is one case to weigh honestly. When the Philistines killed King Saul, they cut off his head and fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan (1 Samuel 31:9-10). The men of Jabeshgilead went all night, took down the bodies of Saul and his sons, and burnt them. Then they took their bones, and buried them under a tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days (31:12-13). David blessed them for this kindness (2 Samuel 2:5). So burning was not always contempt. Here it seems meant to spare bodies already shamed by enemies, and even then they buried the bones. It was a hard measure in a hard hour, not a new custom. But hear this just as plainly. Cremation does not hinder God from raising anyone. Every body returns to dust in the end, whether in a grave or a fire or the sea, and the sea gave up the dead which were in it (Revelation 20:13). Many martyrs were burned and their ashes scattered, and they will rise in glory. Scripture gives no direct command about how the dead must be laid to rest. So faithful Christians differ. Some believe cremation should never be chosen. Many more hold that it is not forbidden, but that burial is the clearer testimony, and they counsel it whenever it can be done. God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF 20.2), and no church may bind where Scripture has not. Where cremation is chosen, many counsel burying the ashes under a stone with a name, rather than scattering them. If someone you love was cremated, hear this gently. You did not shut them out of the resurrection. If they were in Christ, their body is still united to him, whatever has become of it, and he will raise it. If you must choose cremation because of cost, you are not sinning against your loved one or against God. Before you decide, tell your pastor or your deacons, since the church may be able to help with a simple burial. But if cremation is the only way you can bear the cost, choose it without shame, and trust God with the last day.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
section: Choices at the End of Life
text: Choices at the End of Life Thou shalt not kill (Exodus 20:13). The Larger Catechism says the sixth commandment forbids taking away our own life or anyone else’s, except in public justice, lawful war, or necessary defense, and it forbids neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of keeping life (WLC 136). That rules out euthanasia and assisted suicide, whatever kinder name the law gives them. It is still killing when a doctor does it, and when the dying man asks for it. Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s (Romans 14:8). Life is his to give and his to take. But not every possible treatment must be used until the last breath. A patient may refuse or stop a treatment that is a heavy burden and can no longer heal him, but only stretch out his dying. That is not killing. The difference lies in the aim. Ending a life is one thing. Ceasing to fight a death that has already come is another. Ordinary care, such as keeping someone clean and warm and offering food and water while the body can take them, should never be withheld to bring death sooner. It is right to relieve pain, even with strong medicine that may shorten life. Scripture says, Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish (Proverbs 31:6). The aim must be to ease suffering, never to kill. God sees the aim of the heart, even when two doses look alike on paper. Do not make these choices alone. Take them to your elders, and seek a doctor who honors life as God’s gift. Hospice, rightly given, eases pain without hastening death. If long nights of caregiving bring a dark thought of ending it, for the one you love or for yourself, tell someone today, and call 988 or text 988 . Organ Donation Giving an organ to save another is a matter of Christian liberty, and it can be a fine act of love. No one is bound to do it. The one caution is grave. Death must be truly confirmed before anything is taken, and no one may be hastened toward death for another’s sake. Christians differ on some of the medical tests for death, so talk with your elders and a doctor you trust before you sign.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: Preparing to Die Death is not the master of the Christian. Christ is. I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death. Revelation 1:18 (KJV) Keys picture authority. The authority they picture is real. Christ went down into death and came out holding the keys. He took part of flesh and blood, that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage (Hebrews 2:14-15). None of his people will die an hour before his time. So the first and greatest preparation for death is to be found in Christ (Philippians 3:9). If you have never come to Christ, or are not sure you have, read the gospel today. He died for sinners and rose again, and he turns away none who come. Then get ready in plain, earthly ways too. When King Hezekiah was sick, God sent the prophet to tell him to set his house in order, for he would die (2 Kings 20:1, Isaiah 38:1). God gave Hezekiah fifteen more years, but the word still stands for us. Setting your house in order is not a lack of faith. It is love for those you will leave. Pray with Moses, So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom (Psalm 90:12). Make sure of Christ. Confess your sins and rest on him alone. How to Examine Yourself can help. Make a will. If any provide not for his own, he hath denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Name guardians who will raise your children in the Lord. Do it this year. Write down your wishes for care. Choose someone who honors life to speak for you if you cannot. Tell them you want no one to hasten your death, and no burdensome treatment that only prolongs dying. Plan a funeral that preaches Christ. Ask for Scripture, psalms, prayer, and a plain word of the gospel. A funeral is a sermon to the living, who lay death to heart that day (Ecclesiastes 7:2). Say whether you wish to be buried, and settle the cost ahead if you can. Be reconciled. If anyone has something against you, go to them now (Matthew 5:23-24). Ask forgiveness, and give it. Tell your family where your hope is. Jacob blessed his sons before he was gathered to his people (Genesis 49). Say it aloud, and write it down. And remember the dying in your church. Visit them, and help with the funeral bill. On the last day the One who holds the keys will open every grave of his people, and death will be swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54).

title: Teacher Reviews
text: Careful reports on popular preachers, each weighed by Scripture and the Westminster Standards from the man’s own words, with what he gets right told as plainly as what he gets wrong.

title: Teacher Reviews
text: Why This Page Is Here For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them. Acts 20:29-30 (KJV) Paul wept as he said those words to the elders at Ephesus. He knew the danger would not always come from outside the church. It would rise up from inside it, from men who stand in pulpits and draw crowds. That is still true, and today a preacher can reach millions of young believers through a phone before any elder in their own church has heard his name. This page gathers careful reports on popular teachers. Each one weighs what a man teaches by the Word of God, so that believers can tell a faithful shepherd from a dangerous one, and so that parents, pastors, and friends have something sound to hand to someone they love. More reports will be added over time.

title: Teacher Reviews
text: How Each Teacher Is Weighed He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him. Proverbs 18:17 (KJV) A report here is meant to be fair before it is anything else. Every one of them is held to the same rules. Scripture is the standard. Holy Scripture alone binds the conscience. The Westminster Confession of Faith and its catechisms are used as the church’s faithful summary of what Scripture teaches. His own words come first. The evidence is drawn first from the teacher’s own sermons, books, interviews, and his church’s written beliefs. Where a quotation carries great weight, the report names the sermon and about where in it the words come, so any believer can listen for himself. Critics are leads, not proof. What critics say is read for leads but never treated as evidence. A charge that cannot be traced to the man’s own words or to reliable reporting is left out, and a report says so plainly when a common charge does not hold up. What he gets right is told too. A man should be judged by the whole of what he teaches. Truth is still truth when it comes from a man with errors, and the report says so. Each finding is given its weight. A grave finding touches the foundation of the faith. A serious finding departs from clear Reformed teaching in a way that harms hearers. A caution marks a weakness believers should watch for. Sound and credit mark what is right and good. Each ends in a plain answer. Is he safe to sit under? A green check means yes. A red cross means no, he should not be anyone’s steady teacher. The answer stands at the top of every report and beside every name below, so no one has to read the whole report to find it. Each report can also be downloaded in full as a PDF, sources and all, to print or pass along. The reports themselves quote the English Standard Version. On this site the same verses are given in the King James Version, like every other page here.

title: Teacher Reviews
text: The Reports Not safe Philip Anthony Mitchell Pastor of 2819 Church in Atlanta and founder of the ACCESS prayer gatherings. Many true things, and errors that reach the person of Christ. 42 min read

title: Teacher Reviews
section: In What Spirit to Use These
text: In What Spirit to Use These Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (KJV) Not every teacher named here is called a wolf. Some are badly wrong at the root, and some are brothers whose errors are serious enough that they should not be anyone’s steady teacher. A report says which, and why, and it leaves the judging of hearts to God. So when you use them, quote the man’s own words, not rumors about him. Do not mock him, and do not repeat charges the record does not support. Pray for him, because God can still humble a proud preacher and set a confused one straight. And if a teacher is troubling your own church, go to your elders rather than starting a campaign of your own. The surest guard against the counterfeit is to know the true thing well. Sit under faithful preaching in a church where the elders know your name. For more help in testing a teacher yourself, read How to Spot a False Teacher , How to Spot Real Heresy , and How to Weigh “God Told Me” .

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Pastor of 2819 Church in Atlanta and founder of the ACCESS prayer gatherings. Many true things, and errors that reach the person of Christ.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: The Short Answer Philip Anthony Mitchell preaches many true things with real force. He calls sinners to repent. He says plainly that no one can earn acceptance with God. He warns against the prosperity gospel and against sexual sin, and he presses the return of Christ on the conscience of a young generation. Believers should be glad whenever Christ is truly preached. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice. Philippians 1:18 (KJV) Even so, he is not a safe teacher to sit under. His own published sermons teach that the Son of God emptied himself “of some of his divine nature.” He speaks often of God charging him and telling him things directly. He taught his church to make an arena “a portal from earth to heaven” and to “put a demand” on God. He told a congregation that fasting can “move God” and that “your bodies are going to be healed.” On perseverance he hangs final salvation on the believer staying in God’s will, which leaves weak believers without the anchor Scripture gives them. His Lord’s Day services and stadium events are built as produced experiences that lift the preacher, and signs of idolizing him are plain to see. Verdict. Not a safe teacher. Don’t sit under his teaching or recommend it to other believers. So the counsel of this report is simple. Don’t make him your teacher, and don’t hand his sermons to new or struggling believers. If a brother or sister already listens to him, don’t mock the man or slander him. Show them his own words, show them where those words depart from Scripture, and point them to sounder shepherds, beginning with the elders of their own church.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: How This Report Was Made The standard used here is Holy Scripture, which alone binds the conscience. The Westminster Confession of Faith and its catechisms are used as the church’s faithful summary of what Scripture teaches. The evidence comes first from Mitchell’s own words. That means sermon transcripts published from the 2819 Church podcast feed, the church’s statement of beliefs, his personal website, and his long interviews. Reporting from the Associated Press, Christianity Today, Premier Christianity, Charisma, and others was used for the facts of his life and ministry. Critics were read for leads but never treated as proof. A charge that could not be traced to his own words or to a reliable report was left out. The sermon transcripts are made by machine from the church’s audio, so small slips in spelling appear in them. Where a quotation carries great weight, this report names the sermon and about what minute it comes at, so any believer can listen for himself. That’s the Berean way. These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. Acts 17:11 (KJV) The full report. This page follows the written report of October 2026. The PDF holds every part of it, with each claim tied by number to its source. It quotes Scripture in the ESV, where this page gives the same verses in the KJV. Download the full report (PDF)

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Who He Is Philip Anthony Mitchell was born and raised in Queens, New York, to parents who came from the Caribbean. He grew up in a Christian home, but by his own account he was dealing drugs by age twelve and carrying a gun in his early twenties. He has spoken often of time at Rikers Island, of paying for abortions, and of a dark season around 2003 that brought him near to taking his own life. That crisis turned him back to Christ. He says he sensed a call to preach while reading Proverbs 3:5-6, and that he ran from that call for four years before he gave in. He is an honors graduate of North Carolina Central University. He also holds a degree in Pastoral and Church Leadership from Valor Christian College in Columbus, Ohio, the school the Pentecostal preacher Rod Parsley founded at World Harvest Church. In one sermon he held up the Bible his college gave him, inscribed “Valedictorian of Valor Christian College, May 15, 2010.” He has been married to his wife Lena since August 2004, and they have two sons and two daughters. For about ten years he pastored a small Atlanta congregation called Victory Church. Looking back on those years, he has said he wanted to be rich and famous. The congregation was scattered during COVID. In December 2018 he traveled to Israel and, by his own account, had an encounter with God there that changed the direction of his ministry. In January 2023 he relaunched the work as 2819 Church, named for Matthew 28:19, with 183 people. The growth since then has been very large. The church reports about 6,000 people in person each week and about 75,000 more watching online, and its YouTube channel is near two million subscribers. He preached through Matthew for about three years and has since moved through Acts and into Ephesians. He appears on TBN, co-hosts a touring podcast called Street Preachers with Florida pastor Tim Timberlake, and released his first book, Contend , on October 13, 2026.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: The ACCESS Gatherings ACCESS is billed as “That Powerful Hour of Prayer.” Mitchell says it began more than twelve years ago as a family prayer hour in his parents’ home in Rex, Georgia, while his father was dying of cancer. After his father’s death the family kept the hour going, and it grew into church gatherings. In October 2025 it filled State Farm Arena in Atlanta and an overflow hall, with about 40,000 people reported. On October 10, 2026, ACCESS came to AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. The church said all 80,000 free tickets were claimed within eight hours. The evening moved through three parts called The Cross, The Warning, and The Cry, and it closed with the prayer “Maranatha! Come, Lord Jesus!” Mitchell says the event cost about three million dollars and that no admission or offering was taken. Two days later he posted on Facebook, “Just learned that a teenage girl was HEALED of deafness and removed her hearing aids last night at ACCESS in TX,” and added, “This to the glory of Christ.” No name, no family statement, and no medical record has been offered, and no independent report confirms it. A great crowd gathered to pray and to hear of the cross and the coming of Christ is no small thing, and no Christian should sneer at it. But the way Mitchell taught his church to understand ACCESS raises real problems, which the part on prayer below takes up.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: What He Gets Right Fairness comes first. A man should be judged by the whole of what he teaches, and Mitchell teaches a good deal that is true. Salvation by grace He denies salvation by works in plain words. His church’s statement says salvation is a gift of grace and is not earned by works. On The Breakfast Club he said, “You can never be enough to be accepted by God.” In a sermon on Matthew 15, about thirty-eight minutes in, he said of Christ, “He never broke the law,” spoke of him “exchanging his righteousness for your unrighteousness,” and told his people, “you’re not righteous because you have good behavior.” He went on, “we are only righteous if we stand in Christ.” That’s the heart of imputed righteousness, and he preaches it with conviction. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. Ephesians 2:8-9 (KJV) Sin, election, and judgment He affirms election. In October 2026 he told his church, “God in eternity past chose you saved you before the foundation of the world.” He preaches hell as real. He calls sin by its name, and his sermon on Matthew 18 that passed two million views told hearers, “Stop treating sin like a pet. Kill it before it kills you.” Readers of John Owen will hear the echo. In his sermon on the ten virgins he taught that the foolish virgins “represent every man and woman who thinks they are Christians, but they are really not.” That’s a needed word in a land full of false assurance. Money He rejects the prosperity gospel by name. Preaching on mountain-moving faith from Matthew 21 he said, “this ain’t prosperity gospel” and “this ain’t name it or claim it,” and he added, “we have no guarantees, yours is to just pray with faith.” He has taught that tithing “is not structured to be bound in the New Testament” and that “we give out of the generosity of our heart.” Preaching on Acts 2 he warned that the early church’s generosity “is not permission for gospel grifting.” The Holy Spirit On the Spirit he is more careful than many charismatics. He teaches that Spirit baptism is “that salvific moment when the Holy Spirit unites a person with the Lord Jesus Christ,” which ties it to conversion. He noted that some traditions place it later, but he did not press that view. He also teaches that the tongues of Pentecost were real human languages. Humility and counsel He tells his people, “He’s just a man.
